1	# UMH-Anchored Sparkplug B UNS Notes
2	
3	These notes describe a realistic home-lab architecture anchored on United Manufacturing Hub (UMH) Community, using Sparkplug B as the core industrial messaging and harmonization pattern, and floci as the local AWS-style IT/cloud emulation layer.[cite:80][cite:106][cite:112][cite:185] The goal is to build an end-to-end environment that feels production-like from Levels 1 through 4 while remaining based on open-source or free/community tools.[cite:3][cite:6][cite:68][cite:80][cite:185]
4	
5	## Purpose
6	
7	This architecture is meant to demonstrate how plant data can move from PLC-oriented OT systems into a Unified Namespace, then into historian, streaming, analytics, ML, and cloud-style IT services without requiring a real cloud account or paid software for the lab.[cite:80][cite:89][cite:182][cite:185] It is especially useful when the objective is to learn and prove the full data journey rather than just build a historian or dashboard.[cite:80][cite:83][cite:89]
8	
9	UMH is the anchor because it provides an integrated open-source data infrastructure with MQTT, Kafka, historian/storage, visualization, and a management/data-model layer.[cite:80][cite:106][cite:112] floci extends that design by acting as a local AWS emulator for S3, Lambda, Kinesis, MSK, Athena, Glue, Step Functions, EventBridge, RDS, and other cloud-shaped services that many enterprise architectures expect downstream of the UNS.[cite:182][cite:184][cite:185]
10	
11	## Why anchor on UMH
12	
13	UMH Community is useful when the lab should move quickly toward a complete end-to-end story while still staying aligned with realistic industrial architecture.[cite:80][cite:106][cite:112] Instead of wiring every data-infrastructure component by hand, UMH gives a coherent stack with the kinds of interfaces and patterns commonly used in industrial IoT and UNS deployments.[cite:80][cite:112]
14	
15	According to UMH’s architecture and product materials, UMH provides a data infrastructure centered around MQTT, Kafka, storage/historian, and modeling/visualization concepts suitable for industrial use.[cite:80][cite:106][cite:112] The Community License is free forever and can later be complemented with paid support or enterprise services without discarding the architecture developed in the lab.[cite:80]
16	
17	## Architecture summary
18	
19	A concise view of the architecture is:
20	
21	1. **Level 0**: synthetic plus benchmark data representing sensors and actuators.[cite:145][cite:150]
22	2. **Level 1/2**: PLC-world representation through OpenPLC or PLC-style tags and addresses.[cite:21][cite:33][cite:167]
23	3. **Level 3 OT/UNS backbone**: UMH Community running MQTT, Kafka, historian/storage, dashboards, and plant data modeling.[cite:80][cite:106][cite:112]
24	4. **Level 3/4 SCADA and OT consumers**: Ignition Maker Edition or trial consuming Sparkplug B data and operating as an OT application on top of the UNS.[cite:3][cite:6][cite:81][cite:84]
25	5. **Level 4 IT/cloud emulation**: floci acting as local AWS for lake, eventing, orchestration, and analytics-style services.[cite:182][cite:184][cite:185]
26	6. **Cross-cutting**: Python services for data replay, synthetic generation, enrichment, ML training, and edge inference publishing via MQTT/Sparkplug.[cite:90][cite:92][cite:100][cite:104]
27	
28	This creates a layered story that looks close to a production setup: OT systems and UNS on one side, IT/cloud consumers and pipelines on the other, with clear interfaces between them.[cite:80][cite:89][cite:185]
29	
30	## Core OT and UNS roles
31	
32	### Level 0: Synthetic and benchmark process reality
33	
34	The intended design keeps only Level 0 synthetic.[cite:145][cite:150] Industrial benchmark datasets and Python-generated signals represent sensors, actuators, equipment states, and operational context.[cite:145][cite:150][cite:151] Those signals are then shaped to look like PLC memory or cryptic controller tags before being published upward.[cite:163][cite:167]
35	
36	This matters because the project is not trying to show “clean analytics input.”[cite:150][cite:155] It is trying to show how messy controller-facing data becomes semantically harmonized through Sparkplug B and a Unified Namespace.[cite:162][cite:166][cite:168]
37	
38	### Level 1/2: PLC-world representation
39	
40	OpenPLC is a strong fit as a free/open-source controller stand-in because it behaves like a PLC runtime and can expose variables via industrial protocols such as Modbus TCP.[cite:21][cite:33] Even if some signals are produced directly by Python services, they should still be structured to resemble controller memory or cryptic tag names so the rest of the lab reflects real plant integration patterns.[cite:163][cite:167][cite:169]
41	
42	This level exists to answer the real industrial problem: source systems often do not present clean semantic models.[cite:163][cite:167] Instead, they present address-based or cryptic names that later need to be mapped to enterprise-facing meanings.[cite:162][cite:168]
43	
44	### Sparkplug B as the harmonization layer
45	
46	Sparkplug B is the semantic and transport pattern that turns PLC-world structures into stable industrial MQTT messages.[cite:78][cite:166] Its node/device birth messages, metric definitions, aliases, and datatypes give a consistent model that downstream consumers can rely on.[cite:78][cite:110][cite:166]
47	
48	In this UMH-anchored design, Sparkplug is the recommended way to move structured plant data into the UNS because it makes the relationship between source tags, asset identities, and semantic metrics explicit.[cite:162][cite:168][cite:89]
49	
50	### UMH as the Level 3 UNS backbone
51	
52	UMH acts as the core Level 3 data infrastructure.[cite:80][cite:106][cite:112] Based on its architecture and product pages, it provides a combination of MQTT, Kafka, historian/storage, visualization, and connector/data-model capabilities suitable for industrial data collection and harmonization.[cite:80][cite:106][cite:112]
53	
54	The practical roles UMH can play in the lab are:
55	
56	- **UNS event backbone** through MQTT and Kafka.[cite:80][cite:106]
57	- **Historian/time-series platform** through its bundled storage stack and integrated dashboards.[cite:80][cite:112]
58	- **Plant data modeling layer** for machine, line, and site structures that can align with Sparkplug identity choices.[cite:86][cite:106]
59	- **Operational management layer** for managing and observing the data infrastructure.[cite:80]
60	
61	The advantage of anchoring on UMH is that many data-infrastructure concerns are already assembled, which lets more effort go into plant modeling, harmonization, and downstream analytics rather than infrastructure plumbing.[cite:80][cite:112]
62	
63	## Ignition’s role in the UMH-anchored design
64	
65	Ignition Maker Edition or trial is still valuable in a UMH-centered architecture because it acts as a realistic OT consumer of the UNS rather than as the owner of the data backbone.[cite:3][cite:6][cite:81][cite:84] This separation is useful because it mirrors how many real organizations operate: a common industrial data platform feeds multiple OT and IT applications.[cite:80][cite:89]
66	
67	Ignition can be used for:
68	
69	- HMI and dashboard views for operators or engineers.[cite:3][cite:6]
70	- Alarm visualization or basic control-room style views.
71	- Validation that Sparkplug-modeled assets can be consumed by SCADA tools in a way that is still practical for operations.[cite:81][cite:84]
72	- Demonstrating how an OT application subscribes to and consumes the same harmonized data that IT and ML tools use.[cite:84][cite:89]
73	
74	Because Maker and trial are the same platform as licensed Ignition, the lab configuration is a realistic stepping stone to a future paid deployment.[cite:3][cite:6]
75	
76	## Neo4j knowledge graph integration
77	
78	### Why add Neo4j to the UMH-anchored architecture
79	
80	Neo4j is a strong addition when the lab should include a **knowledge graph** that connects assets, tags, events, maintenance history, work orders, material flow, and enterprise context in a relationship-oriented model rather than relying only on time-series and relational stores.[cite:238][cite:242] Knowledge-graph approaches are increasingly used for digital-twin-style integration because they are well suited to connected industrial context spanning multiple systems.[cite:234]
81	
82	In the UMH-anchored design, Neo4j should not replace UMH, the historian, or ERPNext.[cite:80][cite:89] Instead, it should sit beside them as a connected-context layer that preserves how physical assets, harmonized metrics, anomalies, maintenance actions, and enterprise objects relate to one another.[cite:234][cite:239]
83	
84	### What Neo4j should model
85	
86	A practical Neo4j model for this architecture should include nodes such as:
87	
88	- **Site, area, line, cell, and asset** for physical hierarchy.
89	- **PLC or source tag** for brownfield identifiers.[cite:163][cite:167]
90	- **Sparkplug metric / semantic signal** for harmonized OT variables.[cite:166][cite:168]
91	- **Event** for faults, alarms, downtime, changeovers, and batches.
92	- **ERPNext business nodes** such as work orders, materials, assets, inventory movements, and maintenance actions.[cite:227][cite:233]
93	
94	Important relationships include `PART_OF`, `HAS_METRIC`, `GENERATED_EVENT`, `RELATED_TO_WORK_ORDER`, `TRIGGERED_MAINTENANCE`, and `CONSUMED_MATERIAL`.[cite:234][cite:239] This structure makes cross-domain reasoning easier than relying on a historian alone.
95	
96	### Where Neo4j sits in the UMH stack
97	
98	Neo4j should sit on the **IT / knowledge / reasoning side** of the architecture, downstream of the harmonized UMH backbone and adjacent to ERP and analytical services.[cite:234][cite:239] A practical view is:
99	
100	1. Level 0 replay and synthetic generation create plant behavior.[cite:145][cite:150][cite:151]
101	2. PLC-world structures or OpenPLC preserve source realism.[cite:21][cite:33][cite:163][cite:167]
102	3. Sparkplug B and UMH provide the harmonized OT/UNS backbone.[cite:78][cite:80][cite:106][cite:112]
103	4. OT applications such as Ignition and historian/dashboard services consume operational data.[cite:3][cite:6][cite:80][cite:112]
104	5. Integration services derive enterprise events and contextual relationships for ERPNext and Neo4j.[cite:227][cite:233][cite:238]
105	6. Neo4j becomes the graph layer connecting operational, semantic, and enterprise context.[cite:234][cite:239]
106	
107	This means UMH remains the data backbone, while Neo4j adds relationship-rich context and advanced graph querying on top of that backbone.[cite:80][cite:234]
108	
109	### How Neo4j integrates with UMH, Sparkplug, and ERPNext
110	
111	Neo4j should consume from the **harmonized** side of the stack, using Sparkplug-structured data and UMH-managed downstream flows rather than raw disorganized source streams.[cite:78][cite:80][cite:89][cite:166] In practical terms, Python services or other integration processes can subscribe to UMH/Kafka or Sparkplug-derived streams and create graph nodes and relationships from them.[cite:80][cite:90][cite:238]
112	
113	This can support patterns such as:
114	
115	- Linking PLC/source tags to Sparkplug metric definitions and semantic asset nodes.[cite:163][cite:167][cite:168]
116	- Connecting events and anomalies to the assets and lines they affect.[cite:234]
117	- Linking ERPNext work orders and maintenance records to the equipment, batches, and events that produced them.[cite:227][cite:233]
118	- Building graph context for lineage, impact analysis, root-cause investigation, or future assistant workflows.[cite:239][cite:245]
119	
120	This makes Neo4j a semantic extension of the UMH-anchored UNS rather than a competing backbone.[cite:80][cite:234]
121	
122	### Python and Neo4j in the UMH-anchored design
123	
124	Even though UMH provides the plant-side platform, Python remains the most practical implementation language for Neo4j integration because Neo4j provides an official Python driver and Python is already central to replay, enrichment, ML, and ERP integration across the architecture.[cite:90][cite:92][cite:238][cite:242] Python services can therefore create and update graph structures as a normal part of the overall data flow rather than as a disconnected side project.[cite:90][cite:97][cite:238]
125	
126	### GraphRAG and future use cases
127	
128	Neo4j also creates a path to GraphRAG and graph-assisted industrial copilots.[cite:239][cite:245] Neo4j’s GraphRAG Python tooling is intended for combining graph relationships with retrieval workflows, which could later support maintenance reasoning, fault-chain analysis, genealogy, and context-aware assistance in the lab.[cite:245]
129	
130	### Neo4j resource links
131	
132	- Neo4j Python driver GitHub: <https://github.com/neo4j/neo4j-python-driver> [cite:238]
133	- Neo4j Python driver on PyPI: <https://pypi.org/project/neo4j-driver/> [cite:242]
134	- Neo4j GraphRAG Python package: <https://github.com/neo4j/neo4j-graphrag-python> [cite:245]
135	
136	## ERP / SAP-like integration with ERPNext
137	
138	### Why ERPNext fits the UMH-anchored architecture
139	
140	ERPNext is a strong open-source stand-in for SAP-like enterprise integration because it is positioned as open-source ERP software for manufacturing and can represent production, maintenance, logistics, and manufacturing-oriented business processes in one platform.[cite:227][cite:233] In the UMH-anchored design, that makes ERPNext a practical enterprise-side consumer of harmonized OT data.[cite:80][cite:227]
141	
142	ERPNext should sit on the **enterprise / business application side** of the architecture, downstream of UMH and the Sparkplug-harmonized UNS.[cite:80][cite:89][cite:227] It should receive curated operational events and business-relevant state changes rather than every raw telemetry update.[cite:89][cite:227]
143	
144	### What OT data should flow into ERPNext
145	
146	Good ERPNext integration targets in the lab include:
147	
148	- **Production / manufacturing**: work-order confirmations, completed counts, scrap counts, runtime/downtime summaries, batch completion, and machine or line state milestones.[cite:227]
149	- **Maintenance**: anomaly summaries, maintenance-triggering events, runtime thresholds, failure categories, and equipment condition indicators.[cite:233]
150	- **Logistics / inventory**: material consumption, inventory adjustments, finished-goods completion, WIP movement, and transfer-style business events inferred from harmonized line behavior.[cite:227][cite:233]
151	
152	This reflects a realistic enterprise integration pattern because ERP systems generally consume aggregated events and transactions rather than high-frequency raw tags.[cite:89][cite:227]
153	
154	### How ERPNext integrates into the UMH stack
155	
156	A practical UMH-anchored ERPNext flow is:
157	
158	1. Replay and synthetic services generate plant behavior.[cite:145][cite:150][cite:151]
159	2. PLC-world structures and Sparkplug publishers create harmonized OT data.[cite:21][cite:33][cite:78][cite:100]
160	3. UMH operates as the plant-side data backbone through MQTT, Kafka, storage, and dashboards.[cite:80][cite:106][cite:112]
161	4. Python or other integration services consume selected UMH/Kafka or Sparkplug-derived events and write curated business updates into ERPNext.[cite:80][cite:90][cite:227][cite:233]
162	
163	In this role, ERPNext becomes the SAP-like system for work execution feedback, maintenance and asset actions, logistics/inventory context, and manufacturing business records beyond the OT layer.[cite:227][cite:233]
164	
165	### Why ERPNext is useful here
166	
167	Adding ERPNext strengthens the UMH-anchored architecture because it shows how a plant-side data platform feeds enterprise systems instead of ending at dashboards, historians, and cloud emulation alone.[cite:80][cite:89][cite:227] It gives the lab a realistic enterprise application destination for production, maintenance, and logistics signals that have already been harmonized in the UNS.[cite:227][cite:233]
168	
169	### ERPNext resource links
170	
171	- ERPNext manufacturing overview: <https://frappe.io/erpnext/open-source-manufacturing-erp-software> [cite:227]
172	- ERPNext GitHub repository: <https://github.com/frappe/erpnext> [cite:233]
173	
174	## floci as the IT/cloud emulation layer
175	
176	### What floci is
177	
178	floci is a free, open-source local AWS emulator designed to expose AWS-shaped APIs for local development and testing.[cite:182][cite:184][cite:185] Its site and related materials describe support for a large set of AWS-like services through a local endpoint, including S3, DynamoDB, Kinesis, MSK, Lambda, Step Functions, EventBridge, RDS, Glue, Athena, OpenSearch, CloudWatch, and others.[cite:182][cite:184][cite:185]
179	
180	That makes floci a strong fit for this lab because it lets the environment simulate an AWS-style enterprise landing zone without needing an actual AWS account.[cite:182][cite:185] In effect, UMH can represent the on-prem or plant-side data platform while floci represents the enterprise cloud platform that consumes and extends that data.[cite:80][cite:182][cite:185]
181	
182	### Why floci fits this architecture
183	
184	Many modern industrial architectures move data from OT and UNS systems into cloud-native services for lake storage, serverless processing, orchestration, analytics, and ML.[cite:73][cite:89] floci lets the lab imitate those target patterns locally, so the architecture can be designed in a cloud-compatible way from the beginning.[cite:182][cite:184][cite:185]
185	
186	This is especially useful for learning and portability. Services developed against floci’s local AWS-like endpoints can later be pointed at actual AWS with much smaller changes than a full redesign would require.[cite:182][cite:184][cite:185]
187	
188	### Specific roles floci can play
189	
190	#### 1) Data lake and archival target
191	
192	floci’s S3 emulation can act as the object-store landing zone for industrial data exported from UMH or Kafka pipelines.[cite:182][cite:185] This is useful for:
193	
194	- Storing Parquet or CSV snapshots of historian or Kafka data.[cite:182][cite:185]
195	- Maintaining long-term analytical history separate from the operational historian.
196	- Feeding local AWS-style lakehouse patterns such as Glue catalog plus Athena querying.[cite:185]
197	
198	This role matters because it separates operational storage from analytical storage in a way that resembles many real enterprise designs.[cite:80][cite:185]
199	
200	#### 2) Streaming and eventing destination
201	
202	floci supports AWS-shaped streaming and eventing services such as Kinesis, MSK, SQS, SNS, and EventBridge.[cite:185] Those can be used to emulate how industrial events leave the UMH backbone and enter broader enterprise integration patterns.
203	
204	Examples include:
205	
206	- UMH Kafka topics mirrored or transformed into floci MSK/Kinesis streams.[cite:80][cite:185]
207	- Operational alerts or state changes sent through EventBridge or SNS-style patterns.[cite:185]
208	- Queue-based decoupling for downstream batch or serverless jobs with SQS.[cite:185]
209	
210	This helps demonstrate that the UNS is not only an OT construct; it is also a clean upstream source for enterprise event-driven architecture.[cite:89][cite:185]
211	
212	#### 3) Serverless processing and orchestration
213	
214	floci supports Lambda and Step Functions, which lets the lab simulate cloud-style batch and event-driven processing locally.[cite:182][cite:185] That opens several useful patterns:
215	
216	- Trigger a Lambda-like function when a file lands in S3-floci.[cite:185]
217	- Use Step Functions to orchestrate replay backfills, feature computation, or model-scoring pipelines.[cite:185]
218	- Use EventBridge to schedule recurring analytics or data-quality checks.[cite:185]
219	
220	This is a very practical way to demonstrate how harmonized industrial data could feed automated business and analytics workflows in a cloud platform without leaving the local lab.[cite:182][cite:185]
221	
222	#### 4) Analytics catalog and query layer
223	
224	floci includes Glue and Athena emulation as part of its AWS-shaped offering.[cite:185] These can be used to:
225	
226	- Register datasets written to S3-floci into a catalog.
227	- Query historical Parquet data with Athena-like semantics.
228	- Demonstrate cloud-warehouse or lakehouse consumption of UNS-origin data in a way that is familiar to enterprise teams.[cite:185]
229	
230	This complements DuckDB well: DuckDB is ideal for local developer-first analytics, while floci emulates the AWS-facing interfaces and workflows an enterprise data team may later expect.[cite:67][cite:72][cite:185]
231	
232	#### 5) Relational and search endpoints
233	
234	floci’s RDS and OpenSearch emulation can stand in for downstream application storage and search systems.[cite:185] For example:
235	
236	- Store curated analytical outputs or asset metadata in RDS-like Postgres or MySQL.[cite:185]
237	- Index event logs or enriched equipment timelines into OpenSearch-like endpoints.[cite:185]
238	
239	These are optional, but they make the lab more complete when the goal is to show that a UNS can feed many enterprise data products, not only dashboards and ML notebooks.[cite:89][cite:185]
240	
241	#### 6) Cloud-style observability
242	
243	floci’s CloudWatch-style metrics and logging can help emulate how platform teams observe applications and pipelines on the IT side.[cite:185] Python services that consume from UMH or floci can emit logs and metrics into CloudWatch-like endpoints to show how operational and cloud observability might coexist.[cite:185]
244	
245	## Python services in the UMH-anchored design
246	
247	Even though UMH anchors the infrastructure, Python still plays a major role in this architecture.[cite:90][cite:92][cite:100] Python is a natural fit for:
248	
249	- Replaying benchmark datasets as time-ordered plant signals.[cite:145][cite:150][cite:151]
250	- Generating additional analog and discrete synthetic signals.[cite:151][cite:156]
251	- Injecting realistic data messiness such as missing points or spikes.[cite:136][cite:141][cite:156]
252	- Mapping PLC-style variables into Sparkplug metrics.[cite:163][cite:167][cite:100]
253	- Consuming Kafka or S3-style data on the IT side and running ML or feature pipelines.[cite:67][cite:72][cite:185]
254	- Publishing edge inference results back into the UNS via MQTT/Sparkplug.[cite:97][cite:100][cite:104][cite:105]
255	
256	The key Python transport libraries remain Paho MQTT and PySparkplug.[cite:90][cite:99][cite:100][cite:104] This keeps the lab aligned with your preference for Python while still benefiting from UMH as a platform layer.[cite:90][cite:100]
257	
258	## Recommended end-to-end flow
259	
260	A practical end-to-end pattern for the UMH-anchored lab is:
261	
262	1. Load and augment benchmark datasets in Python.[cite:145][cite:150][cite:151]
263	2. Translate them into PLC-style tags or controller-facing structures.[cite:163][cite:167]
264	3. Publish harmonized Sparkplug B data into UMH’s MQTT backbone.[cite:78][cite:80][cite:106]
265	4. Let UMH fan that data into historian, dashboards, and Kafka-based downstream paths.[cite:80][cite:112]
266	5. Use Ignition as an OT consumer of the harmonized Sparkplug/UNS data.[cite:81][cite:84]
267	6. Bridge or export selected data into floci services such as S3, Athena, Lambda, Kinesis, or EventBridge.[cite:182][cite:185]
268	7. Run analytics and ML processes on the floci side or in Python services using floci as the cloud-shaped API layer.[cite:182][cite:185]
269	8. Publish inference or enriched outputs back into the UNS through Sparkplug B, where they become visible to both OT and IT consumers.[cite:97][cite:100][cite:104]
270	
271	This round-trip is what makes the lab especially valuable: it shows not only OT-to-IT flow, but also IT-to-edge feedback, which is necessary for demonstrating ML deployment and operationalization.[cite:71][cite:73][cite:101]
272	
273	## Why this is a strong educational architecture
274	
275	This architecture is strong for education because it stays close to real-world industrial patterns while remaining accessible and reproducible.[cite:80][cite:89][cite:185] It teaches the distinction between source-system tags, semantic harmonization, operational storage, event streaming, and enterprise cloud consumption without requiring a large production environment.[cite:162][cite:168][cite:185]
276	
277	It is also upgrade-friendly. The same overall design can later move from:
278	
279	- Ignition Maker/trial to licensed Ignition.[cite:3][cite:6]
280	- UMH Community to UMH with support or enterprise deployment practices.[cite:80][cite:106]
281	- floci endpoints to actual AWS services.[cite:182][cite:184][cite:185]
282	- Python replay/generation code to real plant data sources or vendor gateways.[cite:90][cite:100][cite:167]
283	
284	That means the architecture is not a throwaway lab. It is a learning environment that can gradually evolve toward something operationally serious.[cite:80][cite:89][cite:185]
285	
286	## Practical links
287	
288	### UMH
289	
290	- UMH docs: <https://umh.docs.umh.app/docs/> [cite:112]
291	- UMH architecture: <https://umh.docs.umh.app/docs/architecture/> [cite:106]
292	- UMH data infrastructure: <https://umh.docs.umh.app/docs/architecture/data-infrastructure/> [cite:80]
293	
294	### floci
295	
296	- floci site: <https://floci.io/floci/> [cite:185]
297	- floci GitHub: <https://github.com/floci-io/floci> [cite:180]
298	
299	### Supporting components
300	
301	- Ignition Maker Edition docs: <https://www.docs.inductiveautomation.com/docs/8.1/other-editions/ignition-maker-edition> [cite:6]
302	- Paho MQTT: <https://pypi.org/project/paho-mqtt/> [cite:90]
303	- PySparkplug: <https://github.com/matteosox/pysparkplug> [cite:100]
304	- OpenPLC references: [cite:21][cite:33]
305	
306	## Working conclusion
307	
308	In a UMH-anchored Sparkplug B UNS architecture, UMH should be treated as the plant-side data backbone, Sparkplug B should be treated as the harmonization and messaging contract, Ignition should be treated as a realistic OT consumer, and floci should be treated as the local AWS-style enterprise platform that receives, stores, analyzes, and operationalizes industrial data.[cite:80][cite:84][cite:89][cite:182][cite:185]
309	
310	That combination gives a powerful lab setup: realistic OT and UNS behavior on one side, realistic cloud and enterprise patterns on the other, and a clear migration path to paid or production-grade systems later without invalidating the structure you build now.[cite:3][cite:6][cite:80][cite:106][cite:182][cite:185]

# UMH-Anchored Sparkplug B UNS Notes

These notes describe a realistic home-lab architecture anchored on United Manufacturing Hub (UMH) Community, using Sparkplug B as the core industrial messaging and harmonization pattern, and floci as the local AWS-style IT/cloud emulation layer.[cite:80][cite:106][cite:112][cite:185] The goal is to build an end-to-end environment that feels production-like from Levels 1 through 4 while remaining based on open-source or free/community tools.[cite:3][cite:6][cite:68][cite:80][cite:185]

## Purpose

This architecture is meant to demonstrate how plant data can move from PLC-oriented OT systems into a Unified Namespace, then into historian, streaming, analytics, ML, and cloud-style IT services without requiring a real cloud account or paid software for the lab.[cite:80][cite:89][cite:182][cite:185] It is especially useful when the objective is to learn and prove the full data journey rather than just build a historian or dashboard.[cite:80][cite:83][cite:89]

UMH is the anchor because it provides an integrated open-source data infrastructure with MQTT, Kafka, historian/storage, visualization, and a management/data-model layer.[cite:80][cite:106][cite:112] floci extends that design by acting as a local AWS emulator for S3, Lambda, Kinesis, MSK, Athena, Glue, Step Functions, EventBridge, RDS, and other cloud-shaped services that many enterprise architectures expect downstream of the UNS.[cite:182][cite:184][cite:185]

## Why anchor on UMH

UMH Community is useful when the lab should move quickly toward a complete end-to-end story while still staying aligned with realistic industrial architecture.[cite:80][cite:106][cite:112] Instead of wiring every data-infrastructure component by hand, UMH gives a coherent stack with the kinds of interfaces and patterns commonly used in industrial IoT and UNS deployments.[cite:80][cite:112]

According to UMH’s architecture and product materials, UMH provides a data infrastructure centered around MQTT, Kafka, storage/historian, and modeling/visualization concepts suitable for industrial use.[cite:80][cite:106][cite:112] The Community License is free forever and can later be complemented with paid support or enterprise services without discarding the architecture developed in the lab.[cite:80]

## Architecture summary

A concise view of the architecture is:

1. **Level 0**: synthetic plus benchmark data representing sensors and actuators.[cite:145][cite:150]
2. **Level 1/2**: PLC-world representation through OpenPLC or PLC-style tags and addresses.[cite:21][cite:33][cite:167]
3. **Level 3 OT/UNS backbone**: UMH Community running MQTT, Kafka, historian/storage, dashboards, and plant data modeling.[cite:80][cite:106][cite:112]
4. **Level 3/4 SCADA and OT consumers**: Ignition Maker Edition or trial consuming Sparkplug B data and operating as an OT application on top of the UNS.[cite:3][cite:6][cite:81][cite:84]
5. **Level 4 IT/cloud emulation**: floci acting as local AWS for lake, eventing, orchestration, and analytics-style services.[cite:182][cite:184][cite:185]
6. **Cross-cutting**: Python services for data replay, synthetic generation, enrichment, ML training, and edge inference publishing via MQTT/Sparkplug.[cite:90][cite:92][cite:100][cite:104]

This creates a layered story that looks close to a production setup: OT systems and UNS on one side, IT/cloud consumers and pipelines on the other, with clear interfaces between them.[cite:80][cite:89][cite:185]

## Core OT and UNS roles

### Level 0: Synthetic and benchmark process reality

The intended design keeps only Level 0 synthetic.[cite:145][cite:150] Industrial benchmark datasets and Python-generated signals represent sensors, actuators, equipment states, and operational context.[cite:145][cite:150][cite:151] Those signals are then shaped to look like PLC memory or cryptic controller tags before being published upward.[cite:163][cite:167]

This matters because the project is not trying to show “clean analytics input.”[cite:150][cite:155] It is trying to show how messy controller-facing data becomes semantically harmonized through Sparkplug B and a Unified Namespace.[cite:162][cite:166][cite:168]

### Level 1/2: PLC-world representation

OpenPLC is a strong fit as a free/open-source controller stand-in because it behaves like a PLC runtime and can expose variables via industrial protocols such as Modbus TCP.[cite:21][cite:33] Even if some signals are produced directly by Python services, they should still be structured to resemble controller memory or cryptic tag names so the rest of the lab reflects real plant integration patterns.[cite:163][cite:167][cite:169]

This level exists to answer the real industrial problem: source systems often do not present clean semantic models.[cite:163][cite:167] Instead, they present address-based or cryptic names that later need to be mapped to enterprise-facing meanings.[cite:162][cite:168]

### Sparkplug B as the harmonization layer

Sparkplug B is the semantic and transport pattern that turns PLC-world structures into stable industrial MQTT messages.[cite:78][cite:166] Its node/device birth messages, metric definitions, aliases, and datatypes give a consistent model that downstream consumers can rely on.[cite:78][cite:110][cite:166]

In this UMH-anchored design, Sparkplug is the recommended way to move structured plant data into the UNS because it makes the relationship between source tags, asset identities, and semantic metrics explicit.[cite:162][cite:168][cite:89]

### UMH as the Level 3 UNS backbone

UMH acts as the core Level 3 data infrastructure.[cite:80][cite:106][cite:112] Based on its architecture and product pages, it provides a combination of MQTT, Kafka, historian/storage, visualization, and connector/data-model capabilities suitable for industrial data collection and harmonization.[cite:80][cite:106][cite:112]

The practical roles UMH can play in the lab are:

- **UNS event backbone** through MQTT and Kafka.[cite:80][cite:106]
- **Historian/time-series platform** through its bundled storage stack and integrated dashboards.[cite:80][cite:112]
- **Plant data modeling layer** for machine, line, and site structures that can align with Sparkplug identity choices.[cite:86][cite:106]
- **Operational management layer** for managing and observing the data infrastructure.[cite:80]

The advantage of anchoring on UMH is that many data-infrastructure concerns are already assembled, which lets more effort go into plant modeling, harmonization, and downstream analytics rather than infrastructure plumbing.[cite:80][cite:112]

## Ignition’s role in the UMH-anchored design

Ignition Maker Edition or trial is still valuable in a UMH-centered architecture because it acts as a realistic OT consumer of the UNS rather than as the owner of the data backbone.[cite:3][cite:6][cite:81][cite:84] This separation is useful because it mirrors how many real organizations operate: a common industrial data platform feeds multiple OT and IT applications.[cite:80][cite:89]

Ignition can be used for:

- HMI and dashboard views for operators or engineers.[cite:3][cite:6]
- Alarm visualization or basic control-room style views.
- Validation that Sparkplug-modeled assets can be consumed by SCADA tools in a way that is still practical for operations.[cite:81][cite:84]
- Demonstrating how an OT application subscribes to and consumes the same harmonized data that IT and ML tools use.[cite:84][cite:89]

Because Maker and trial are the same platform as licensed Ignition, the lab configuration is a realistic stepping stone to a future paid deployment.[cite:3][cite:6]

## Neo4j knowledge graph integration

### Why add Neo4j to the UMH-anchored architecture

Neo4j is a strong addition when the lab should include a **knowledge graph** that connects assets, tags, events, maintenance history, work orders, material flow, and enterprise context in a relationship-oriented model rather than relying only on time-series and relational stores.[cite:238][cite:242] Knowledge-graph approaches are increasingly used for digital-twin-style integration because they are well suited to connected industrial context spanning multiple systems.[cite:234]

In the UMH-anchored design, Neo4j should not replace UMH, the historian, or ERPNext.[cite:80][cite:89] Instead, it should sit beside them as a connected-context layer that preserves how physical assets, harmonized metrics, anomalies, maintenance actions, and enterprise objects relate to one another.[cite:234][cite:239]

### What Neo4j should model

A practical Neo4j model for this architecture should include nodes such as:

- **Site, area, line, cell, and asset** for physical hierarchy.
- **PLC or source tag** for brownfield identifiers.[cite:163][cite:167]
- **Sparkplug metric / semantic signal** for harmonized OT variables.[cite:166][cite:168]
- **Event** for faults, alarms, downtime, changeovers, and batches.
- **ERPNext business nodes** such as work orders, materials, assets, inventory movements, and maintenance actions.[cite:227][cite:233]

Important relationships include `PART_OF`, `HAS_METRIC`, `GENERATED_EVENT`, `RELATED_TO_WORK_ORDER`, `TRIGGERED_MAINTENANCE`, and `CONSUMED_MATERIAL`.[cite:234][cite:239] This structure makes cross-domain reasoning easier than relying on a historian alone.

### Where Neo4j sits in the UMH stack

Neo4j should sit on the **IT / knowledge / reasoning side** of the architecture, downstream of the harmonized UMH backbone and adjacent to ERP and analytical services.[cite:234][cite:239] A practical view is:

1. Level 0 replay and synthetic generation create plant behavior.[cite:145][cite:150][cite:151]
2. PLC-world structures or OpenPLC preserve source realism.[cite:21][cite:33][cite:163][cite:167]
3. Sparkplug B and UMH provide the harmonized OT/UNS backbone.[cite:78][cite:80][cite:106][cite:112]
4. OT applications such as Ignition and historian/dashboard services consume operational data.[cite:3][cite:6][cite:80][cite:112]
5. Integration services derive enterprise events and contextual relationships for ERPNext and Neo4j.[cite:227][cite:233][cite:238]
6. Neo4j becomes the graph layer connecting operational, semantic, and enterprise context.[cite:234][cite:239]

This means UMH remains the data backbone, while Neo4j adds relationship-rich context and advanced graph querying on top of that backbone.[cite:80][cite:234]

### How Neo4j integrates with UMH, Sparkplug, and ERPNext

Neo4j should consume from the **harmonized** side of the stack, using Sparkplug-structured data and UMH-managed downstream flows rather than raw disorganized source streams.[cite:78][cite:80][cite:89][cite:166] In practical terms, Python services or other integration processes can subscribe to UMH/Kafka or Sparkplug-derived streams and create graph nodes and relationships from them.[cite:80][cite:90][cite:238]

This can support patterns such as:

- Linking PLC/source tags to Sparkplug metric definitions and semantic asset nodes.[cite:163][cite:167][cite:168]
- Connecting events and anomalies to the assets and lines they affect.[cite:234]
- Linking ERPNext work orders and maintenance records to the equipment, batches, and events that produced them.[cite:227][cite:233]
- Building graph context for lineage, impact analysis, root-cause investigation, or future assistant workflows.[cite:239][cite:245]

This makes Neo4j a semantic extension of the UMH-anchored UNS rather than a competing backbone.[cite:80][cite:234]

### Python and Neo4j in the UMH-anchored design

Even though UMH provides the plant-side platform, Python remains the most practical implementation language for Neo4j integration because Neo4j provides an official Python driver and Python is already central to replay, enrichment, ML, and ERP integration across the architecture.[cite:90][cite:92][cite:238][cite:242] Python services can therefore create and update graph structures as a normal part of the overall data flow rather than as a disconnected side project.[cite:90][cite:97][cite:238]

### GraphRAG and future use cases

Neo4j also creates a path to GraphRAG and graph-assisted industrial copilots.[cite:239][cite:245] Neo4j’s GraphRAG Python tooling is intended for combining graph relationships with retrieval workflows, which could later support maintenance reasoning, fault-chain analysis, genealogy, and context-aware assistance in the lab.[cite:245]

### Neo4j resource links

- Neo4j Python driver GitHub: <https://github.com/neo4j/neo4j-python-driver> [cite:238]
- Neo4j Python driver on PyPI: <https://pypi.org/project/neo4j-driver/> [cite:242]
- Neo4j GraphRAG Python package: <https://github.com/neo4j/neo4j-graphrag-python> [cite:245]

## ERP / SAP-like integration with ERPNext

### Why ERPNext fits the UMH-anchored architecture

ERPNext is a strong open-source stand-in for SAP-like enterprise integration because it is positioned as open-source ERP software for manufacturing and can represent production, maintenance, logistics, and manufacturing-oriented business processes in one platform.[cite:227][cite:233] In the UMH-anchored design, that makes ERPNext a practical enterprise-side consumer of harmonized OT data.[cite:80][cite:227]

ERPNext should sit on the **enterprise / business application side** of the architecture, downstream of UMH and the Sparkplug-harmonized UNS.[cite:80][cite:89][cite:227] It should receive curated operational events and business-relevant state changes rather than every raw telemetry update.[cite:89][cite:227]

### What OT data should flow into ERPNext

Good ERPNext integration targets in the lab include:

- **Production / manufacturing**: work-order confirmations, completed counts, scrap counts, runtime/downtime summaries, batch completion, and machine or line state milestones.[cite:227]
- **Maintenance**: anomaly summaries, maintenance-triggering events, runtime thresholds, failure categories, and equipment condition indicators.[cite:233]
- **Logistics / inventory**: material consumption, inventory adjustments, finished-goods completion, WIP movement, and transfer-style business events inferred from harmonized line behavior.[cite:227][cite:233]

This reflects a realistic enterprise integration pattern because ERP systems generally consume aggregated events and transactions rather than high-frequency raw tags.[cite:89][cite:227]

### How ERPNext integrates into the UMH stack

A practical UMH-anchored ERPNext flow is:

1. Replay and synthetic services generate plant behavior.[cite:145][cite:150][cite:151]
2. PLC-world structures and Sparkplug publishers create harmonized OT data.[cite:21][cite:33][cite:78][cite:100]
3. UMH operates as the plant-side data backbone through MQTT, Kafka, storage, and dashboards.[cite:80][cite:106][cite:112]
4. Python or other integration services consume selected UMH/Kafka or Sparkplug-derived events and write curated business updates into ERPNext.[cite:80][cite:90][cite:227][cite:233]

In this role, ERPNext becomes the SAP-like system for work execution feedback, maintenance and asset actions, logistics/inventory context, and manufacturing business records beyond the OT layer.[cite:227][cite:233]

### Why ERPNext is useful here

Adding ERPNext strengthens the UMH-anchored architecture because it shows how a plant-side data platform feeds enterprise systems instead of ending at dashboards, historians, and cloud emulation alone.[cite:80][cite:89][cite:227] It gives the lab a realistic enterprise application destination for production, maintenance, and logistics signals that have already been harmonized in the UNS.[cite:227][cite:233]

### ERPNext resource links

- ERPNext manufacturing overview: <https://frappe.io/erpnext/open-source-manufacturing-erp-software> [cite:227]
- ERPNext GitHub repository: <https://github.com/frappe/erpnext> [cite:233]

## floci as the IT/cloud emulation layer

### What floci is

floci is a free, open-source local AWS emulator designed to expose AWS-shaped APIs for local development and testing.[cite:182][cite:184][cite:185] Its site and related materials describe support for a large set of AWS-like services through a local endpoint, including S3, DynamoDB, Kinesis, MSK, Lambda, Step Functions, EventBridge, RDS, Glue, Athena, OpenSearch, CloudWatch, and others.[cite:182][cite:184][cite:185]

That makes floci a strong fit for this lab because it lets the environment simulate an AWS-style enterprise landing zone without needing an actual AWS account.[cite:182][cite:185] In effect, UMH can represent the on-prem or plant-side data platform while floci represents the enterprise cloud platform that consumes and extends that data.[cite:80][cite:182][cite:185]

### Why floci fits this architecture

Many modern industrial architectures move data from OT and UNS systems into cloud-native services for lake storage, serverless processing, orchestration, analytics, and ML.[cite:73][cite:89] floci lets the lab imitate those target patterns locally, so the architecture can be designed in a cloud-compatible way from the beginning.[cite:182][cite:184][cite:185]

This is especially useful for learning and portability. Services developed against floci’s local AWS-like endpoints can later be pointed at actual AWS with much smaller changes than a full redesign would require.[cite:182][cite:184][cite:185]

### Specific roles floci can play

#### 1) Data lake and archival target

floci’s S3 emulation can act as the object-store landing zone for industrial data exported from UMH or Kafka pipelines.[cite:182][cite:185] This is useful for:

- Storing Parquet or CSV snapshots of historian or Kafka data.[cite:182][cite:185]
- Maintaining long-term analytical history separate from the operational historian.
- Feeding local AWS-style lakehouse patterns such as Glue catalog plus Athena querying.[cite:185]

This role matters because it separates operational storage from analytical storage in a way that resembles many real enterprise designs.[cite:80][cite:185]

#### 2) Streaming and eventing destination

floci supports AWS-shaped streaming and eventing services such as Kinesis, MSK, SQS, SNS, and EventBridge.[cite:185] Those can be used to emulate how industrial events leave the UMH backbone and enter broader enterprise integration patterns.

Examples include:

- UMH Kafka topics mirrored or transformed into floci MSK/Kinesis streams.[cite:80][cite:185]
- Operational alerts or state changes sent through EventBridge or SNS-style patterns.[cite:185]
- Queue-based decoupling for downstream batch or serverless jobs with SQS.[cite:185]

This helps demonstrate that the UNS is not only an OT construct; it is also a clean upstream source for enterprise event-driven architecture.[cite:89][cite:185]

#### 3) Serverless processing and orchestration

floci supports Lambda and Step Functions, which lets the lab simulate cloud-style batch and event-driven processing locally.[cite:182][cite:185] That opens several useful patterns:

- Trigger a Lambda-like function when a file lands in S3-floci.[cite:185]
- Use Step Functions to orchestrate replay backfills, feature computation, or model-scoring pipelines.[cite:185]
- Use EventBridge to schedule recurring analytics or data-quality checks.[cite:185]

This is a very practical way to demonstrate how harmonized industrial data could feed automated business and analytics workflows in a cloud platform without leaving the local lab.[cite:182][cite:185]

#### 4) Analytics catalog and query layer

floci includes Glue and Athena emulation as part of its AWS-shaped offering.[cite:185] These can be used to:

- Register datasets written to S3-floci into a catalog.
- Query historical Parquet data with Athena-like semantics.
- Demonstrate cloud-warehouse or lakehouse consumption of UNS-origin data in a way that is familiar to enterprise teams.[cite:185]

This complements DuckDB well: DuckDB is ideal for local developer-first analytics, while floci emulates the AWS-facing interfaces and workflows an enterprise data team may later expect.[cite:67][cite:72][cite:185]

#### 5) Relational and search endpoints

floci’s RDS and OpenSearch emulation can stand in for downstream application storage and search systems.[cite:185] For example:

- Store curated analytical outputs or asset metadata in RDS-like Postgres or MySQL.[cite:185]
- Index event logs or enriched equipment timelines into OpenSearch-like endpoints.[cite:185]

These are optional, but they make the lab more complete when the goal is to show that a UNS can feed many enterprise data products, not only dashboards and ML notebooks.[cite:89][cite:185]

#### 6) Cloud-style observability

floci’s CloudWatch-style metrics and logging can help emulate how platform teams observe applications and pipelines on the IT side.[cite:185] Python services that consume from UMH or floci can emit logs and metrics into CloudWatch-like endpoints to show how operational and cloud observability might coexist.[cite:185]

## Python services in the UMH-anchored design

Even though UMH anchors the infrastructure, Python still plays a major role in this architecture.[cite:90][cite:92][cite:100] Python is a natural fit for:

- Replaying benchmark datasets as time-ordered plant signals.[cite:145][cite:150][cite:151]
- Generating additional analog and discrete synthetic signals.[cite:151][cite:156]
- Injecting realistic data messiness such as missing points or spikes.[cite:136][cite:141][cite:156]
- Mapping PLC-style variables into Sparkplug metrics.[cite:163][cite:167][cite:100]
- Consuming Kafka or S3-style data on the IT side and running ML or feature pipelines.[cite:67][cite:72][cite:185]
- Publishing edge inference results back into the UNS via MQTT/Sparkplug.[cite:97][cite:100][cite:104][cite:105]

The key Python transport libraries remain Paho MQTT and PySparkplug.[cite:90][cite:99][cite:100][cite:104] This keeps the lab aligned with your preference for Python while still benefiting from UMH as a platform layer.[cite:90][cite:100]

## Recommended end-to-end flow

A practical end-to-end pattern for the UMH-anchored lab is:

1. Load and augment benchmark datasets in Python.[cite:145][cite:150][cite:151]
2. Translate them into PLC-style tags or controller-facing structures.[cite:163][cite:167]
3. Publish harmonized Sparkplug B data into UMH’s MQTT backbone.[cite:78][cite:80][cite:106]
4. Let UMH fan that data into historian, dashboards, and Kafka-based downstream paths.[cite:80][cite:112]
5. Use Ignition as an OT consumer of the harmonized Sparkplug/UNS data.[cite:81][cite:84]
6. Bridge or export selected data into floci services such as S3, Athena, Lambda, Kinesis, or EventBridge.[cite:182][cite:185]
7. Run analytics and ML processes on the floci side or in Python services using floci as the cloud-shaped API layer.[cite:182][cite:185]
8. Publish inference or enriched outputs back into the UNS through Sparkplug B, where they become visible to both OT and IT consumers.[cite:97][cite:100][cite:104]

This round-trip is what makes the lab especially valuable: it shows not only OT-to-IT flow, but also IT-to-edge feedback, which is necessary for demonstrating ML deployment and operationalization.[cite:71][cite:73][cite:101]

## Why this is a strong educational architecture

This architecture is strong for education because it stays close to real-world industrial patterns while remaining accessible and reproducible.[cite:80][cite:89][cite:185] It teaches the distinction between source-system tags, semantic harmonization, operational storage, event streaming, and enterprise cloud consumption without requiring a large production environment.[cite:162][cite:168][cite:185]

It is also upgrade-friendly. The same overall design can later move from:

- Ignition Maker/trial to licensed Ignition.[cite:3][cite:6]
- UMH Community to UMH with support or enterprise deployment practices.[cite:80][cite:106]
- floci endpoints to actual AWS services.[cite:182][cite:184][cite:185]
- Python replay/generation code to real plant data sources or vendor gateways.[cite:90][cite:100][cite:167]

That means the architecture is not a throwaway lab. It is a learning environment that can gradually evolve toward something operationally serious.[cite:80][cite:89][cite:185]

## Working conclusion

In a UMH-anchored Sparkplug B UNS architecture, UMH should be treated as the plant-side data backbone, Sparkplug B should be treated as the harmonization and messaging contract, Ignition should be treated as a realistic OT consumer, and floci should be treated as the local AWS-style enterprise platform that receives, stores, analyzes, and operationalizes industrial data.[cite:80][cite:84][cite:89][cite:182][cite:185]

That combination gives a powerful lab setup: realistic OT and UNS behavior on one side, realistic cloud and enterprise patterns on the other, and a clear migration path to paid or production-grade systems later without invalidating the structure you build now.[cite:3][cite:6][cite:80][cite:106][cite:182][cite:185]

1	# uns-sparkplug
2	
3	## STRENGTHS
4	- Forwarder-not-bridge (charter §4 'Broker topology... DECIDED') is exactly right: the charter's rationale (LWT death certificates, primary-host STATE, no control over what forwards) matches documented field experience that naive spBv1.0/# broker bridges drop/strand NBIRTHs and break Sparkplug session coherence (e.g. EMQX-bridge NBIRTH failures documented at industrialmonitordirect.com; Ignition MQTT Engine forum reports). Most designs get this wrong; this one names the exact failure mode before writing code.
5	- 'Sparkplug B as the contract — births, aliases, datatypes, lifecycle; not plain JSON-over-MQTT' (charter §9, AGENTS.md constraints) matches the Eclipse Sparkplug 3.0 intent: interoperable state management rather than ad-hoc payloads. The synthetic-data mapping table (synthetic_data_generation_notes.md 'Sparkplug B mapping') already carries group ID, edge node ID, device ID, metric name, alias, and datatype — the right metadata to be Sparkplug-correct from day one.
6	- Edge store-and-forward for site autonomy (charter §13.1 L1.2) and per-site edge broker + central enterprise broker is the documented multi-site UNS pattern (HiveMQ Sparkplug architecture guidance: local brokers give store-and-forward, low-latency local subscribers, reduced WAN traffic).
7	- Placing the central EMQX enterprise broker in the iDMZ as the sole OT/IT conduit with exactly three crossings (charter §13.8 Z1–Z4) matches the HiveMQ/Siemens 'broker as DMZ gateway' best practice and IEC 62443 zone/conduit thinking — an unusually correct zoning for a home-lab design.
8	- Scan-rate tied to process physics + RBE deadband with the 'deadband too wide hides slow drift' cascade check (charter §13.7 P1) matches practitioner RBE/historian guidance (Canary Labs, Sparkplug RBE model) — the design already anticipates the classic RBE-vs-analytics failure.
9	- 'UNS/Sparkplug carries OT real-time only; business data joins downstream' (charter §13.7 P8) is stated as an explicit principle and matches published UNS data-modeling guidance (UMH, HiveMQ): the broker is not an ERP bus.
10	- Closed-loop governance — model never actuates, controller executes, graded HITL, defense-in-depth clamps independent of the model path (charter §13.5 L6.5 + §13.7 P2/P3) — matches industry closed-loop ML guidance and exceeds what most lab designs specify.
11	
12	## MAJOR FINDINGS
13	
14	### [critical] Sparkplug's fixed topic namespace vs the 'lagos-chem/beaumont/...' ISA-95 topic root is unresolved — the two claims are mutually incompatible as written
15	GAP: The charter declares the UNS/topic root as 'lagos-chem' with example topic 'lagos-chem/beaumont/...' AND declares 'Sparkplug B throughout'. Sparkplug B fixes the topic to spBv1.0/{group_id}/{message_type}/{edge_node_id}/[{device_id}] — a topic literally starting with 'lagos-chem/' cannot exist on the wire in a pure Sparkplug system. No doc decides how the ISA-95 hierarchy is actually encoded: in group_id with delimiters (the 'Parris method', e.g. group_id='lagos-chem:beaumont:areaX'), in metric names / Sparkplug device hierarchy, or by having the enterprise tier republish decoded Sparkplug data onto plain-MQTT ISA-95 semantic topics (the pattern UMH and many UNS practitioners use). This choice determines what the site-forwarder publishes, what every IT consumer subscribes to, and whether 'UNS retained state' (see the retained-flag finding) can exist at all — it is the shape of the very namespace the lab exists to prove.
16	EVIDENCE: design/PROJECT_CHARTER.md §6 'Sites & ISA-95 identity (DECIDED)' ('UNS/topic root: lagos-chem ... the root of every UNS topic, e.g. lagos-chem/beaumont/...'); §4 layered-architecture table L3 row ('Sparkplug B throughout'); §9 ('Sparkplug B as the contract'). design/synthetic_data_generation_notes.md 'Sparkplug B mapping' lists group/node/device fields but records no ISA-95-encoding decision. Not addressed in §12 open decisions or §13 ledgers.
17	BEST PRACTICE: Real UNS implementations resolve this explicitly: HiveMQ's 'Implementing UNS with MQTT Sparkplug' documents the Parris method (whole ISA-95 path in group_id with a delimiter, later 'broken apart and republished into flat MQTT topics') and the Schultz method (tiered brokers + republish); Corso Systems and others document combining ISA-95 with Sparkplug via group_id/node_id conventions; a widely used alternative is Sparkplug at the edge tier + plain-MQTT ISA-95 semantic topics at the enterprise tier.
18	SOURCES: https://www.hivemq.com/blog/implementing-unified-namespace-uns-mqtt-sparkplug/, https://corsosystems.com/posts/using-isa-95-and-sparkplug-b-together, https://www.hivemq.com/blog/understanding-mqtt-topic-namespace-iiot/, https://neomatrixinc.com/blog/sparkplug-b-or-not-to-b-unified-namespace-architecture-considerations/
19	RECOMMENDATION: Add a charter decision (a new §12 item) BEFORE Phase 2: pick the encoding. A clean two-tier fit for this lab: site tier = pure Sparkplug (group_id='lagos-chem:<site>', edge_node_id per line/PLC, device_id per equipment); enterprise tier = the forwarder (or an EMQX-side republisher) decodes Sparkplug and ALSO publishes JSON onto plain-MQTT retained ISA-95 topics 'lagos-chem/<site>/<area>/<line>/<equipment>/<metric>' on EMQX. That teaches both schools (Sparkplug state management at the edge, browsable retained ISA-95 UNS at the enterprise) and makes the 'lagos-chem/beaumont/...' root real instead of aspirational. Record the trade-off either way.
20	
21	### [important] The site-forwarder's upward republication has no Sparkplug session design — sequence numbers, bdSeq, aliases, rebirth handling, and historical replay must be specified or Phase 4 will hit rebirth loops
22	GAP: The charter decides the forwarder 'subscribes locally and re-publishes a curated stream upward — preserving per-tier Sparkplug state' but never says HOW. To be Sparkplug-correct on the central tier, the forwarder must itself be a compliant Edge Node on EMQX: its own MQTT session with an NDEATH Will (bdSeq), its own NBIRTH declaring every conformed metric, its own per-session seq numbering (0–255), and its own alias space — raw pass-through of local NDATA payload bytes is invalid because aliases and seq are session-scoped to the SITE broker session. It must also implement the one mandatory command, Node Control/Rebirth (NCMD), from central-side consumers, and translate central rebirth requests into local rebirths when its own state is stale. Likewise its store-and-forward buffer (L1.2) must, on reconnect, publish a fresh NBIRTH (incremented bdSeq) FIRST, then flush buffered values with metric.is_historical=true and original timestamps so central consumers don't treat replayed data as live. None of this appears in any design doc; a naive implementation will be discarded by any compliant consumer (e.g. Ignition MQTT Engine) with continuous rebirth requests.
23	EVIDENCE: design/PROJECT_CHARTER.md §4 'Connection = a Python site-forwarder, NOT a raw broker bridge' paragraph (states the goal, not the mechanism); §13.1 L1.2 (store-and-forward, no Sparkplug semantics); HANDOFF.md §3 blocks C/D (walkthrough covers births/RBE and store-and-forward but no session/seq/alias/rebirth design).
24	BEST PRACTICE: Sparkplug 3.0 spec (Eclipse, Operational Behavior chapter): every Edge Node session requires Will-based NDEATH with bdSeq, NBIRTH before data, seq incrementing per message within the session, aliases defined in BIRTH only; 'Node Control/Rebirth' NCMD is the one command all Edge Nodes MUST implement; buffered/replayed values are flagged is_historical so hosts don't update real-time state. Field reports (Ignition forums, EMQX bridge knowledge-base) show exactly these failures when Sparkplug is relayed without a proper session.
25	SOURCES: https://github.com/eclipse-sparkplug/sparkplug/blob/master/specification/src/main/asciidoc/chapters/Sparkplug_5_Operational_Behavior.adoc, https://sparkplug.eclipse.org/specification/version/3.0/documents/sparkplug-specification-3.0.0.pdf, https://industrialmonitordirect.com/blogs/knowledgebase/emqx-mqtt-bridge-spbv10-edge-node-birth-certificate-fix, https://flowfuse.com/blog/2024/08/using-mqtt-sparkplugb-with-node-red/
26	RECOMMENDATION: Add a half-page 'forwarder Sparkplug contract' to the charter (or a design note) before Phase 4: forwarder = one Sparkplug Edge Node per site on EMQX (node_id = site), fresh NBIRTH/bdSeq per session, remapped aliases from the metric_registry, seq managed per session, NCMD Rebirth handled by replaying its conformed birth, and S&F flush = NBIRTH first then is_historical data in timestamp order. Sized for a home lab this is ~1 day of design and directly becomes the Phase 4 test list (it is also the best Sparkplug lesson in the whole lab).
27	
28	### [important] No Primary Host Application is designated on either tier — STATE is mentioned once but never assigned, though it is the mechanism that triggers store-and-forward
29	GAP: Sparkplug's availability model hinges on the Primary Host Application publishing retained STATE (ONLINE/OFFLINE, QoS 1) on spBv1.0/STATE/{host_id}; Edge Nodes configured with a primary host defer publishing and flush their store-and-forward buffers when STATE flips ONLINE. The charter cites 'primary-host STATE' as a reason not to bridge brokers, but no doc decides WHO the primary host is per tier: on the site tier (the site-forwarder? the local historian collector?) or on the central tier (the historian-ingest/Kafka-bridge service? Ignition?). Without this, the decided store-and-forward feature (L1.2) has no standard trigger, and the 'historian-less site' (L1.4) has no defined authority for when data may flow.
30	EVIDENCE: design/PROJECT_CHARTER.md §4 broker-topology paragraph (only mention of 'primary-host STATE'); §13.1 L1.2 (store-and-forward) and L1.4 (historian-less site) — neither names a host; HANDOFF.md §3 walkthrough agenda omits STATE/primary host entirely.
31	BEST PRACTICE: Sparkplug 3.0 spec: STATE messages MUST be retained UTF-8 'ONLINE'/'OFFLINE' at QoS 1 with a registered Will, published after CONNACK; Edge Nodes use primary-host STATE to gate publishing and to flush historical data on host recovery (Cirrus Link Chariot docs on the v3.0.0 STATE changes; HiveMQ 'Decoding the Operational Behavior of MQTT Sparkplug').
32	SOURCES: https://docs.chariot.io/display/CLD80/Changes+to+the+STATE+message+in+the+Sparkplug+v3.0.0+Specification, https://sparkplug.eclipse.org/specification/version/3.0/documents/sparkplug-specification-3.0.0.pdf, https://www.hivemq.com/blog/decoding-operational-behavior-mqtt-sparkplug-iiot/
33	RECOMMENDATION: Decide and document one line per tier: site tier — the site-forwarder IS the site's Primary Host Application (publishes STATE on Mosquitto; local Sparkplug publishers buffer when it is OFFLINE); central tier — the historian/Kafka ingest service is the primary host on EMQX (the forwarder buffers and flushes on its STATE ONLINE, which is exactly the L1.2 behavior implemented the standard way instead of ad hoc). Cheap to implement, and it converts L1.2 from a custom buffer into the real Sparkplug lesson.
34	
35	### [important] 'MQTT-retained' is used as if Sparkplug had retained state — Sparkplug B forbids the retain flag on operational messages; state comes from BIRTH messages held by host applications
36	GAP: Charter §13.1 L2.2 justifies 'no separate hot store' with 'TimescaleDB + MQTT-retained covers near-real-time', §12 #12 forbids Redis duplicating 'MQTT-retained', and §4 role-B describes the ODS as 'a SQL-queryable mirror of UNS retained state'. But under 'Sparkplug B throughout', NBIRTH/DBIRTH/NDATA/DDATA MUST NOT be retained (and are QoS 0, clean-session true / session-expiry 0); last-known-value lives in each consuming Host Application's in-memory state seeded by BIRTH messages — or in a 'Sparkplug Aware' broker's $sparkplug/certificates/# retained system topics, which neither Mosquitto nor EMQX provides natively (it is a HiveMQ extension concept from the 3.0 spec). So as written there is no retained state anywhere for the ODS 'current_state' to mirror. The conflation is harmless prose today but it silently props up two DECIDED items (L2.2, Redis exclusion) with a mechanism that won't exist.
37	EVIDENCE: design/PROJECT_CHARTER.md §13.1 L2.2 ('TimescaleDB + MQTT-retained covers near-real-time'); §12 #12 ('must not duplicate MQTT-retained / Timescale current_state'); §4 Postgres role-B ('a SQL-queryable mirror of UNS retained state'). Charter §7 also imports ISHE 'retained state' UNS semantics without noting the Sparkplug difference.
38	BEST PRACTICE: Sparkplug 3.0 spec + vendor guidance (i-flow 'What is Sparkplug B', Cedalo Mosquitto+Sparkplug): operational Sparkplug messages are never retained; consumers rebuild state from BIRTHs (issuing a Rebirth NCMD if they missed one). Retained-topic 'browsable current state' is the plain-MQTT UNS pattern; the Sparkplug 3.0 'Sparkplug Aware broker' optional feature republishes births retained on $sparkplug/certificates/# to bridge the two.
39	SOURCES: https://i-flow.io/en/ressources/what-is-sparkplug-b-pros-and-cons-of-the-standard/, https://sparkplug.eclipse.org/specification/version/3.0/documents/sparkplug-specification-3.0.0.pdf, https://www.cedalo.com/blog/mqtt-sparkplug-mosquitto
40	RECOMMENDATION: Fix the language and tie it to the topic-namespace decision: if you adopt the recommended enterprise-tier plain-MQTT ISA-95 republish, retained flags on those topics genuinely ARE the UNS retained state and L2.2/§12#12/role-B become literally true — state it that way. If you stay pure Sparkplug, replace 'MQTT-retained' with 'BIRTH-seeded last-known-value maintained by consuming hosts and mirrored in ods_core.current_state', and have the walkthrough teach why (a mosquitto_sub joining late sees nothing until a rebirth — a great live demo).
41	
42	### [important] The closed-loop writeback is described as 'a Sparkplug setpoint/command topic' — Sparkplug has no free-form command topics; the correct model is a Host Application issuing NCMD/DCMD on the broker the target Edge Node is connected to
43	GAP: Charter §13.5 L6.5 (and AGENTS.md Plane-4 text: 'approved command via the UNS (Sparkplug setpoint topic)') models the command as a topic you publish a setpoint onto. In Sparkplug, commands are NCMD/DCMD messages (QoS 0, not retained) addressed to spBv1.0/{group}/NCMD|DCMD/{edge_node}/[{device}], written by a Host Application; the Edge Node executes the write and confirms by publishing the new value in NDATA/DDATA (the read-back is the acknowledgment). Two consequences the docs don't state: (1) the DCMD must be published on the SITE Mosquitto where the target Edge Node holds its session — a command published only on central EMQX never reaches Beaumont's Edge Node — so the site-forwarder must consume the approved recommendation from EMQX and issue the local DCMD as the site's host application (§13.8's 'broker → forwarder → PLC-clamp → controller' gestures at this but the 'setpoint topic' mental model contradicts it); (2) the HITL console's confirmation signal should be the DDATA read-back of the setpoint metric, which is also the natural audit record.
44	EVIDENCE: design/PROJECT_CHARTER.md §13.5 L6.5 ('published to the UNS as a Sparkplug setpoint/command topic'); §13.8 final paragraph (command path mediated by iDMZ broker); AGENTS.md 'The three planes' item 4 ('UNS Sparkplug setpoint topic').
45	BEST PRACTICE: Sparkplug 3.0 spec Operational Behavior: NCMD for node-directed commands, DCMD for device writes (metric name + new value in payload); Edge Node writes to the device and reports via DDATA (FlowFuse Sparkplug implementation guide; HiveMQ operational-behavior article; Cirrus Link client docs). Only host applications should originate commands; delivery requires the target's own broker session.
46	SOURCES: https://github.com/eclipse-sparkplug/sparkplug/blob/master/specification/src/main/asciidoc/chapters/Sparkplug_5_Operational_Behavior.adoc, https://flowfuse.com/blog/2024/08/using-mqtt-sparkplugb-with-node-red/, https://www.hivemq.com/blog/decoding-operational-behavior-mqtt-sparkplug-iiot/
47	RECOMMENDATION: Reword L6.5 to the message model: HITL console approval → recommendation event down through EMQX (iDMZ crossing #3) → site-forwarder (acting as site host application) issues DCMD to the target Edge Node on the site Mosquitto → Edge Node performs the clamped OpenPLC/OPC-UA write → DDATA read-back confirms; console displays confirmed-vs-commanded. Add 'DCMD + read-back' to the Phase 6 test list. No new components needed — it is the same path with correct Sparkplug verbs.
48	
49	### [important] No decision on WHERE Sparkplug protobuf gets decoded for IT consumers, and no gap-filling policy for RBE data reaching the historian/lakehouse/ML
50	GAP: Sparkplug payloads are protobuf with session-scoped aliases — bytes forwarded into Kafka are opaque and even undecodable without the corresponding BIRTH (alias→name map). The charter routes 'harmonized telemetry up (EMQX → Kafka)' and Bronze validates 'incoming data against metric_registry' (P7), but no doc says who decodes: EMQX rule-engine schema-registry (a licensed feature, and it can't resolve aliases statefully), a Python UNS→Kafka bridge service that holds BIRTH state, or Spark from_protobuf in Bronze. Similarly, RBE means the historian receives only changes; ML feature pipelines (Phase 6, SPC/EWMA on regular windows) need a stated resampling/LOCF (last-observation-carried-forward) policy plus staleness/quality handling, or window features silently mix 'no change' with 'no data'. P1 covers deadband width but not this consumption-side completeness question.
51	EVIDENCE: design/PROJECT_CHARTER.md §4 L3/4 analytics row and §13.8 ('harmonized telemetry up (EMQX → Kafka)') — no decode point; §13.7 P7 (Bronze validates metrics, presupposing decoded data); §13.7 P1 (deadband, publish side only). No doc mentions protobuf decoding or LOCF/resampling for the historian/gold features.
52	BEST PRACTICE: Sparkplug consumers must be stateful: hold BIRTH metadata to resolve aliases before payloads are meaningful (Eclipse spec; EMQX's own Sparkplug codec docs exist precisely because raw payloads are opaque; Spark supports from_protobuf but not alias state). Historian practice with RBE sources is to store on-change values with source timestamps and resample/LOCF at query/feature time, propagating quality (Canary Labs RBE guidance; UMH data-modeling lesson notes Kafka consumers want self-describing decoded payloads).
53	SOURCES: https://docs.emqx.com/en/emqx/latest/data-integration/sparkplug.html, https://spark.apache.org/docs/latest/sql-data-sources-protobuf.html, https://blog.canarylabs.com/get-started-with-mqtt-sparkplug, https://learn.umh.app/lesson/data-modeling-in-the-unified-namespace-mqtt-kafka/
54	RECOMMENDATION: Decide: a single Python 'UNS→Kafka bridge' service on the IT side of the iDMZ subscribes to EMQX, maintains BIRTH state, decodes protobuf, resolves aliases via metric_registry, and publishes canonical JSON (Pydantic CanonicalTelemetry) to Kafka — one place where Sparkplug ends and IT begins, which also matches the lab's Pydantic-first principle. And add one line to P1: 'historian stores on-change with source timestamps; feature/SPC queries resample with LOCF + max-staleness quality flag.'
