# uns-sparkplug

## STRENGTHS
- Forwarder-not-bridge (charter §4 'Broker topology... DECIDED') is exactly right: the charter's rationale (LWT death certificates, primary-host STATE, no control over what forwards) matches documented field experience that naive spBv1.0/# broker bridges drop/strand NBIRTHs and break Sparkplug session coherence (e.g. EMQX-bridge NBIRTH failures documented at industrialmonitordirect.com; Ignition MQTT Engine forum reports). Most designs get this wrong; this one names the exact failure mode before writing code.
- 'Sparkplug B as the contract — births, aliases, datatypes, lifecycle; not plain JSON-over-MQTT' (charter §9, AGENTS.md constraints) matches the Eclipse Sparkplug 3.0 intent: interoperable state management rather than ad-hoc payloads. The synthetic-data mapping table (synthetic_data_generation_notes.md 'Sparkplug B mapping') already carries group ID, edge node ID, device ID, metric name, alias, and datatype — the right metadata to be Sparkplug-correct from day one.
- Edge store-and-forward for site autonomy (charter §13.1 L1.2) and per-site edge broker + central enterprise broker is the documented multi-site UNS pattern (HiveMQ Sparkplug architecture guidance: local brokers give store-and-forward, low-latency local subscribers, reduced WAN traffic).
- Placing the central EMQX enterprise broker in the iDMZ as the sole OT/IT conduit with exactly three crossings (charter §13.8 Z1–Z4) matches the HiveMQ/Siemens 'broker as DMZ gateway' best practice and IEC 62443 zone/conduit thinking — an unusually correct zoning for a home-lab design.
- Scan-rate tied to process physics + RBE deadband with the 'deadband too wide hides slow drift' cascade check (charter §13.7 P1) matches practitioner RBE/historian guidance (Canary Labs, Sparkplug RBE model) — the design already anticipates the classic RBE-vs-analytics failure.
- 'UNS/Sparkplug carries OT real-time only; business data joins downstream' (charter §13.7 P8) is stated as an explicit principle and matches published UNS data-modeling guidance (UMH, HiveMQ): the broker is not an ERP bus.
- Closed-loop governance — model never actuates, controller executes, graded HITL, defense-in-depth clamps independent of the model path (charter §13.5 L6.5 + §13.7 P2/P3) — matches industry closed-loop ML guidance and exceeds what most lab designs specify.

## MAJOR FINDINGS

### [critical] Sparkplug's fixed topic namespace vs the 'lagos-chem/beaumont/...' ISA-95 topic root is unresolved — the two claims are mutually incompatible as written
GAP: The charter declares the UNS/topic root as 'lagos-chem' with example topic 'lagos-chem/beaumont/...' AND declares 'Sparkplug B throughout'. Sparkplug B fixes the topic to spBv1.0/{group_id}/{message_type}/{edge_node_id}/[{device_id}] — a topic literally starting with 'lagos-chem/' cannot exist on the wire in a pure Sparkplug system. No doc decides how the ISA-95 hierarchy is actually encoded: in group_id with delimiters (the 'Parris method', e.g. group_id='lagos-chem:beaumont:areaX'), in metric names / Sparkplug device hierarchy, or by having the enterprise tier republish decoded Sparkplug data onto plain-MQTT ISA-95 semantic topics (the pattern UMH and many UNS practitioners use). This choice determines what the site-forwarder publishes, what every IT consumer subscribes to, and whether 'UNS retained state' (see the retained-flag finding) can exist at all — it is the shape of the very namespace the lab exists to prove.
EVIDENCE: design/PROJECT_CHARTER.md §6 'Sites & ISA-95 identity (DECIDED)' ('UNS/topic root: lagos-chem ... the root of every UNS topic, e.g. lagos-chem/beaumont/...'); §4 layered-architecture table L3 row ('Sparkplug B throughout'); §9 ('Sparkplug B as the contract'). design/synthetic_data_generation_notes.md 'Sparkplug B mapping' lists group/node/device fields but records no ISA-95-encoding decision. Not addressed in §12 open decisions or §13 ledgers.
BEST PRACTICE: Real UNS implementations resolve this explicitly: HiveMQ's 'Implementing UNS with MQTT Sparkplug' documents the Parris method (whole ISA-95 path in group_id with a delimiter, later 'broken apart and republished into flat MQTT topics') and the Schultz method (tiered brokers + republish); Corso Systems and others document combining ISA-95 with Sparkplug via group_id/node_id conventions; a widely used alternative is Sparkplug at the edge tier + plain-MQTT ISA-95 semantic topics at the enterprise tier.
SOURCES: https://www.hivemq.com/blog/implementing-unified-namespace-uns-mqtt-sparkplug/, https://corsosystems.com/posts/using-isa-95-and-sparkplug-b-together, https://www.hivemq.com/blog/understanding-mqtt-topic-namespace-iiot/, https://neomatrixinc.com/blog/sparkplug-b-or-not-to-b-unified-namespace-architecture-considerations/
RECOMMENDATION: Add a charter decision (a new §12 item) BEFORE Phase 2: pick the encoding. A clean two-tier fit for this lab: site tier = pure Sparkplug (group_id='lagos-chem:<site>', edge_node_id per line/PLC, device_id per equipment); enterprise tier = the forwarder (or an EMQX-side republisher) decodes Sparkplug and ALSO publishes JSON onto plain-MQTT retained ISA-95 topics 'lagos-chem/<site>/<area>/<line>/<equipment>/<metric>' on EMQX. That teaches both schools (Sparkplug state management at the edge, browsable retained ISA-95 UNS at the enterprise) and makes the 'lagos-chem/beaumont/...' root real instead of aspirational. Record the trade-off either way.

### [important] The site-forwarder's upward republication has no Sparkplug session design — sequence numbers, bdSeq, aliases, rebirth handling, and historical replay must be specified or Phase 4 will hit rebirth loops
GAP: The charter decides the forwarder 'subscribes locally and re-publishes a curated stream upward — preserving per-tier Sparkplug state' but never says HOW. To be Sparkplug-correct on the central tier, the forwarder must itself be a compliant Edge Node on EMQX: its own MQTT session with an NDEATH Will (bdSeq), its own NBIRTH declaring every conformed metric, its own per-session seq numbering (0–255), and its own alias space — raw pass-through of local NDATA payload bytes is invalid because aliases and seq are session-scoped to the SITE broker session. It must also implement the one mandatory command, Node Control/Rebirth (NCMD), from central-side consumers, and translate central rebirth requests into local rebirths when its own state is stale. Likewise its store-and-forward buffer (L1.2) must, on reconnect, publish a fresh NBIRTH (incremented bdSeq) FIRST, then flush buffered values with metric.is_historical=true and original timestamps so central consumers don't treat replayed data as live. None of this appears in any design doc; a naive implementation will be discarded by any compliant consumer (e.g. Ignition MQTT Engine) with continuous rebirth requests.
EVIDENCE: design/PROJECT_CHARTER.md §4 'Connection = a Python site-forwarder, NOT a raw broker bridge' paragraph (states the goal, not the mechanism); §13.1 L1.2 (store-and-forward, no Sparkplug semantics); HANDOFF.md §3 blocks C/D (walkthrough covers births/RBE and store-and-forward but no session/seq/alias/rebirth design).
BEST PRACTICE: Sparkplug 3.0 spec (Eclipse, Operational Behavior chapter): every Edge Node session requires Will-based NDEATH with bdSeq, NBIRTH before data, seq incrementing per message within the session, aliases defined in BIRTH only; 'Node Control/Rebirth' NCMD is the one command all Edge Nodes MUST implement; buffered/replayed values are flagged is_historical so hosts don't update real-time state. Field reports (Ignition forums, EMQX bridge knowledge-base) show exactly these failures when Sparkplug is relayed without a proper session.
SOURCES: https://github.com/eclipse-sparkplug/sparkplug/blob/master/specification/src/main/asciidoc/chapters/Sparkplug_5_Operational_Behavior.adoc, https://sparkplug.eclipse.org/specification/version/3.0/documents/sparkplug-specification-3.0.0.pdf, https://industrialmonitordirect.com/blogs/knowledgebase/emqx-mqtt-bridge-spbv10-edge-node-birth-certificate-fix, https://flowfuse.com/blog/2024/08/using-mqtt-sparkplugb-with-node-red/
RECOMMENDATION: Add a half-page 'forwarder Sparkplug contract' to the charter (or a design note) before Phase 4: forwarder = one Sparkplug Edge Node per site on EMQX (node_id = site), fresh NBIRTH/bdSeq per session, remapped aliases from the metric_registry, seq managed per session, NCMD Rebirth handled by replaying its conformed birth, and S&F flush = NBIRTH first then is_historical data in timestamp order. Sized for a home lab this is ~1 day of design and directly becomes the Phase 4 test list (it is also the best Sparkplug lesson in the whole lab).

### [important] No Primary Host Application is designated on either tier — STATE is mentioned once but never assigned, though it is the mechanism that triggers store-and-forward
GAP: Sparkplug's availability model hinges on the Primary Host Application publishing retained STATE (ONLINE/OFFLINE, QoS 1) on spBv1.0/STATE/{host_id}; Edge Nodes configured with a primary host defer publishing and flush their store-and-forward buffers when STATE flips ONLINE. The charter cites 'primary-host STATE' as a reason not to bridge brokers, but no doc decides WHO the primary host is per tier: on the site tier (the site-forwarder? the local historian collector?) or on the central tier (the historian-ingest/Kafka-bridge service? Ignition?). Without this, the decided store-and-forward feature (L1.2) has no standard trigger, and the 'historian-less site' (L1.4) has no defined authority for when data may flow.
EVIDENCE: design/PROJECT_CHARTER.md §4 broker-topology paragraph (only mention of 'primary-host STATE'); §13.1 L1.2 (store-and-forward) and L1.4 (historian-less site) — neither names a host; HANDOFF.md §3 walkthrough agenda omits STATE/primary host entirely.
BEST PRACTICE: Sparkplug 3.0 spec: STATE messages MUST be retained UTF-8 'ONLINE'/'OFFLINE' at QoS 1 with a registered Will, published after CONNACK; Edge Nodes use primary-host STATE to gate publishing and to flush historical data on host recovery (Cirrus Link Chariot docs on the v3.0.0 STATE changes; HiveMQ 'Decoding the Operational Behavior of MQTT Sparkplug').
SOURCES: https://docs.chariot.io/display/CLD80/Changes+to+the+STATE+message+in+the+Sparkplug+v3.0.0+Specification, https://sparkplug.eclipse.org/specification/version/3.0/documents/sparkplug-specification-3.0.0.pdf, https://www.hivemq.com/blog/decoding-operational-behavior-mqtt-sparkplug-iiot/
RECOMMENDATION: Decide and document one line per tier: site tier — the site-forwarder IS the site's Primary Host Application (publishes STATE on Mosquitto; local Sparkplug publishers buffer when it is OFFLINE); central tier — the historian/Kafka ingest service is the primary host on EMQX (the forwarder buffers and flushes on its STATE ONLINE, which is exactly the L1.2 behavior implemented the standard way instead of ad hoc). Cheap to implement, and it converts L1.2 from a custom buffer into the real Sparkplug lesson.

### [important] 'MQTT-retained' is used as if Sparkplug had retained state — Sparkplug B forbids the retain flag on operational messages; state comes from BIRTH messages held by host applications
GAP: Charter §13.1 L2.2 justifies 'no separate hot store' with 'TimescaleDB + MQTT-retained covers near-real-time', §12 #12 forbids Redis duplicating 'MQTT-retained', and §4 role-B describes the ODS as 'a SQL-queryable mirror of UNS retained state'. But under 'Sparkplug B throughout', NBIRTH/DBIRTH/NDATA/DDATA MUST NOT be retained (and are QoS 0, clean-session true / session-expiry 0); last-known-value lives in each consuming Host Application's in-memory state seeded by BIRTH messages — or in a 'Sparkplug Aware' broker's $sparkplug/certificates/# retained system topics, which neither Mosquitto nor EMQX provides natively (it is a HiveMQ extension concept from the 3.0 spec). So as written there is no retained state anywhere for the ODS 'current_state' to mirror. The conflation is harmless prose today but it silently props up two DECIDED items (L2.2, Redis exclusion) with a mechanism that won't exist.
EVIDENCE: design/PROJECT_CHARTER.md §13.1 L2.2 ('TimescaleDB + MQTT-retained covers near-real-time'); §12 #12 ('must not duplicate MQTT-retained / Timescale current_state'); §4 Postgres role-B ('a SQL-queryable mirror of UNS retained state'). Charter §7 also imports ISHE 'retained state' UNS semantics without noting the Sparkplug difference.
BEST PRACTICE: Sparkplug 3.0 spec + vendor guidance (i-flow 'What is Sparkplug B', Cedalo Mosquitto+Sparkplug): operational Sparkplug messages are never retained; consumers rebuild state from BIRTHs (issuing a Rebirth NCMD if they missed one). Retained-topic 'browsable current state' is the plain-MQTT UNS pattern; the Sparkplug 3.0 'Sparkplug Aware broker' optional feature republishes births retained on $sparkplug/certificates/# to bridge the two.
SOURCES: https://i-flow.io/en/ressources/what-is-sparkplug-b-pros-and-cons-of-the-standard/, https://sparkplug.eclipse.org/specification/version/3.0/documents/sparkplug-specification-3.0.0.pdf, https://www.cedalo.com/blog/mqtt-sparkplug-mosquitto
RECOMMENDATION: Fix the language and tie it to the topic-namespace decision: if you adopt the recommended enterprise-tier plain-MQTT ISA-95 republish, retained flags on those topics genuinely ARE the UNS retained state and L2.2/§12#12/role-B become literally true — state it that way. If you stay pure Sparkplug, replace 'MQTT-retained' with 'BIRTH-seeded last-known-value maintained by consuming hosts and mirrored in ods_core.current_state', and have the walkthrough teach why (a mosquitto_sub joining late sees nothing until a rebirth — a great live demo).

### [important] The closed-loop writeback is described as 'a Sparkplug setpoint/command topic' — Sparkplug has no free-form command topics; the correct model is a Host Application issuing NCMD/DCMD on the broker the target Edge Node is connected to
GAP: Charter §13.5 L6.5 (and AGENTS.md Plane-4 text: 'approved command via the UNS (Sparkplug setpoint topic)') models the command as a topic you publish a setpoint onto. In Sparkplug, commands are NCMD/DCMD messages (QoS 0, not retained) addressed to spBv1.0/{group}/NCMD|DCMD/{edge_node}/[{device}], written by a Host Application; the Edge Node executes the write and confirms by publishing the new value in NDATA/DDATA (the read-back is the acknowledgment). Two consequences the docs don't state: (1) the DCMD must be published on the SITE Mosquitto where the target Edge Node holds its session — a command published only on central EMQX never reaches Beaumont's Edge Node — so the site-forwarder must consume the approved recommendation from EMQX and issue the local DCMD as the site's host application (§13.8's 'broker → forwarder → PLC-clamp → controller' gestures at this but the 'setpoint topic' mental model contradicts it); (2) the HITL console's confirmation signal should be the DDATA read-back of the setpoint metric, which is also the natural audit record.
EVIDENCE: design/PROJECT_CHARTER.md §13.5 L6.5 ('published to the UNS as a Sparkplug setpoint/command topic'); §13.8 final paragraph (command path mediated by iDMZ broker); AGENTS.md 'The three planes' item 4 ('UNS Sparkplug setpoint topic').
BEST PRACTICE: Sparkplug 3.0 spec Operational Behavior: NCMD for node-directed commands, DCMD for device writes (metric name + new value in payload); Edge Node writes to the device and reports via DDATA (FlowFuse Sparkplug implementation guide; HiveMQ operational-behavior article; Cirrus Link client docs). Only host applications should originate commands; delivery requires the target's own broker session.
SOURCES: https://github.com/eclipse-sparkplug/sparkplug/blob/master/specification/src/main/asciidoc/chapters/Sparkplug_5_Operational_Behavior.adoc, https://flowfuse.com/blog/2024/08/using-mqtt-sparkplugb-with-node-red/, https://www.hivemq.com/blog/decoding-operational-behavior-mqtt-sparkplug-iiot/
RECOMMENDATION: Reword L6.5 to the message model: HITL console approval → recommendation event down through EMQX (iDMZ crossing #3) → site-forwarder (acting as site host application) issues DCMD to the target Edge Node on the site Mosquitto → Edge Node performs the clamped OpenPLC/OPC-UA write → DDATA read-back confirms; console displays confirmed-vs-commanded. Add 'DCMD + read-back' to the Phase 6 test list. No new components needed — it is the same path with correct Sparkplug verbs.

### [important] No decision on WHERE Sparkplug protobuf gets decoded for IT consumers, and no gap-filling policy for RBE data reaching the historian/lakehouse/ML
GAP: Sparkplug payloads are protobuf with session-scoped aliases — bytes forwarded into Kafka are opaque and even undecodable without the corresponding BIRTH (alias→name map). The charter routes 'harmonized telemetry up (EMQX → Kafka)' and Bronze validates 'incoming data against metric_registry' (P7), but no doc says who decodes: EMQX rule-engine schema-registry (a licensed feature, and it can't resolve aliases statefully), a Python UNS→Kafka bridge service that holds BIRTH state, or Spark from_protobuf in Bronze. Similarly, RBE means the historian receives only changes; ML feature pipelines (Phase 6, SPC/EWMA on regular windows) need a stated resampling/LOCF (last-observation-carried-forward) policy plus staleness/quality handling, or window features silently mix 'no change' with 'no data'. P1 covers deadband width but not this consumption-side completeness question.
EVIDENCE: design/PROJECT_CHARTER.md §4 L3/4 analytics row and §13.8 ('harmonized telemetry up (EMQX → Kafka)') — no decode point; §13.7 P7 (Bronze validates metrics, presupposing decoded data); §13.7 P1 (deadband, publish side only). No doc mentions protobuf decoding or LOCF/resampling for the historian/gold features.
BEST PRACTICE: Sparkplug consumers must be stateful: hold BIRTH metadata to resolve aliases before payloads are meaningful (Eclipse spec; EMQX's own Sparkplug codec docs exist precisely because raw payloads are opaque; Spark supports from_protobuf but not alias state). Historian practice with RBE sources is to store on-change values with source timestamps and resample/LOCF at query/feature time, propagating quality (Canary Labs RBE guidance; UMH data-modeling lesson notes Kafka consumers want self-describing decoded payloads).
SOURCES: https://docs.emqx.com/en/emqx/latest/data-integration/sparkplug.html, https://spark.apache.org/docs/latest/sql-data-sources-protobuf.html, https://blog.canarylabs.com/get-started-with-mqtt-sparkplug, https://learn.umh.app/lesson/data-modeling-in-the-unified-namespace-mqtt-kafka/
RECOMMENDATION: Decide: a single Python 'UNS→Kafka bridge' service on the IT side of the iDMZ subscribes to EMQX, maintains BIRTH state, decodes protobuf, resolves aliases via metric_registry, and publishes canonical JSON (Pydantic CanonicalTelemetry) to Kafka — one place where Sparkplug ends and IT begins, which also matches the lab's Pydantic-first principle. And add one line to P1: 'historian stores on-change with source timestamps; feature/SPC queries resample with LOCF + max-staleness quality flag.' Both fit the existing Phase 4/6 work; no new infrastructure.

## MINOR FINDINGS
- **The 'EMQX OSS' justification (rule engine, native data bridges, clustering) rests on features that were Enterprise-only before v5.9 and are license-gated for multi-node after it** — Charter §4 justifies central EMQX 'by its rule engine, native data bridges, and clustering.' In EMQX ≤5.8 open source, Kafka/Postgres data integrations and the Sparkplug/protobuf schema registry were Enterprise-only (OSS rule engine forwarded to webhooks/MQTT only). From v5.9, EMQX moved to BSL 1.1 with all features unified — free for single node, but clustering (>1 node) requires a license. None of the three cited justifications holds for a plain older 'OSS' deployment, and clustering is not free in any current version. → Pin the decision: 'EMQX ≥5.9, single node, BSL 1.1' in charter §4/§12 #2, and drop 'clustering' from the lab-phase justification (keep it as the enterprise upgrade path). If you adopt the Python UNS→Kafka bridge from the decode finding, the broker's native Kafka bridge becomes optional anyway — which is also better for the bare-metal learning goal.
- **Equipment-type templates (P6) are planned only as Pydantic types — Sparkplug B has native Templates (UDTs) that would put the same lesson on the wire** — Charter §13.7 P6 defines equipment classes as Pydantic types instantiated per asset — good, but it stops at the Python layer. Sparkplug B natively supports Templates: TemplateDefinitions published in NBIRTH and template instances per device, which is exactly the Ignition-UDT analog P6 names. Skipping the wire-level feature means the lab's Sparkplug contract never demonstrates the spec's own answer to type reuse, and Ignition (an OT consumer in the stack) would consume Sparkplug templates as UDTs automatically — a free, visible payoff. → When P6 is built (Phase 2/4), emit each Pydantic equipment class also as a Sparkplug TemplateDefinition in NBIRTH and publish instances per device for at least one equipment class (e.g. the pump class). 1	# tool-verification
2	
3	## STRENGTHS
4	- Two-tier broker with a Python site-forwarder instead of a raw spBv1.0/# bridge (charter section 4) matches vendor guidance that Sparkplug B state (LWT death certificates, seq numbers, primary-host STATE) does not survive naive broker bridging — the charter's reasoning is verified correct.
5	- Mosquitto as per-site edge broker is correctly scoped (charter section 4): Sparkplug B requires only MQTT 3.1.1 features (QoS 0/1, retained messages, Last Will) which Mosquitto fully provides; the optional Sparkplug 3.0 'Sparkplug Aware Broker' feature is not needed for the lab. CONFIRMED.
6	- 'floci' is real, not a typo for LocalStack (github.com/floci-io/floci, floci.io/aws): MIT-licensed local AWS emulator covering S3, Lambda, Kinesis Data Streams, Glue, Athena (via the DuckDB-powered floci-duck sidecar), RDS, MSK, Step Functions — all free with no paid tier. This choice actually dodges a trap: in LocalStack, Glue/Athena emulation is Pro/paid-tier, so the docs' L4 cloud-emulation plan (charter section 4 L4, section 13.4 Diagram 3) survives fact-checking intact.
7	- Keep-Kafka-over-Apache-Iggy reasoning (charter section 13.6) verified: Iggy is still in the Apache Incubator (entered Feb 2025, not yet a TLP as of mid-2026) and has no Kafka Connect/Debezium/Schema Registry ecosystem — replacing Kafka would indeed break the Phase 5a Debezium milestone. CONFIRMED sound.
8	- Databricks Free Edition (charter section 13.6) exists exactly as described: serverless-only, non-commercial, one workspace/one metastore, per-account quotas, with Unity Catalog and MLflow 3.x available — fit for the 'graduate-to managed lakehouse' milestone. CONFIRMED (docs.databricks.com/aws/en/getting-started/free-edition-limitations).
9	- Neo4j native vector index for GraphRAG with no separate vector DB (charter section 13 L5.2) verified: vector indexes shipped in Neo4j 5.11+ and are usable in Community Edition; neo4j-graphrag-python is Neo4j's current first-party GraphRAG package and manages those indexes programmatically. CONFIRMED.
10	- ERPNext on its own MariaDB (charter section 4) matches reality: Frappe/ERPNext officially requires MariaDB and PostgreSQL remains unsupported/not-production-ready for ERPNext, so isolating ERPNext's MariaDB from the Postgres estate is the correct call, and ERPNext's manufacturing module (BOM, work orders, production plans, job cards) covers the Plane 2 scope. CONFIRMED.
11	- OpenPLC for Beaumont (charter section 6, decision #4) verified: built-in Modbus TCP server (port 502, automatic IEC-address-to-register mapping) and all five IEC 61131-3 languages via OpenPLC Editor; its known limits (no certification, 10-50 ms scan times) are irrelevant at the lab's ~1 s cadence. CONFIRMED.
12	- asyncua for the Geismar OPC-UA server (charter section 13 L1.1) verified: FreeOpcUa/opcua-asyncio is the actively maintained Python OPC-UA library (releases through mid-2026) with a high-level Server API — a sound choice. CONFIRMED.
13	- Redis for the Phase-6 online feature store (charter section 12 #12) is license-safe: Redis 8 returned to genuine open source under AGPLv3 in May 2025, so calling it 'Redis (open source)' is now accurate; Valkey (BSD, CNCF-backed) exists as a drop-in fallback if AGPL ever matters. CONFIRMED with the Valkey note.
14	- TEP + Industrial IoT dataset anchoring (charter section 6) is real and well-chosen: the linked Harvard Dataverse TEP dataset (Rieth et al. 2017) is the standard fault-detection benchmark with 500 runs x 21 faults — statistically rich enough for the SPC/EWMA yield thesis (but see the cadence finding).
15	
16	## MAJOR FINDINGS
17	
18	### [important] EMQX justification is factually wrong: no 'EMQX OSS' with Kafka/Postgres bridges exists — Apache-2.0 versions never had them, and since v5.9 EMQX is BSL 1.1 with single-node production limit
19	GAP: The charter justifies the central broker as 'EMQX OSS ... rule engine, native data bridges, clustering.' Reality: in every Apache-2.0 open-source EMQX 5.x (through 5.8), data integrations were limited to MQTT and HTTP-webhook sinks — Kafka, Postgres, and all other native bridges were Enterprise-only. In May 2025 EMQX dropped the open-source edition entirely: from v5.9 there is one unified edition under Business Source License 1.1 (all Enterprise features included, converts to Apache-2.0 after 4 years), whose Additional Use Grant permits free production use of only a SINGLE node — clustering requires a paid license. So the three named justifications never coexisted in any free EMQX: the OSS editions had clustering but no bridges; the BSL edition has bridges but no free production cluster. HANDOFF.md Diagram 1 even depicts '1 EMQX cluster'.

- 'floci' is real, not a typo for LocalStack (github.com/floci-io/floci, floci.io/aws): MIT-licensed local AWS emulator covering S3, Lambda, Kinesis Data Streams, Glue, Athena (via the DuckDB-powered floci-duck sidecar), RDS, MSK, Step Functions — all free with no paid tier. CONFIRMED sound.

Grow it one row per service as phases land — it becomes the checklist that keeps Diagrams 2 and 3 honest.

Without a broker-side restriction on who may publish NCMD/DCMD/setpoint topics, 'no bypass' is unenforced (any broker client could command the PLC), and without a specified audit record the 'auditable' adjective is aspirational. For a simulated specialty-chemicals plant, the setpoint-change audit trail is the signature compliance artifact of the domain.
EVIDENCE: design/PROJECT_CHARTER.md §13.5 L6.5 ('single auditable UNS command path'), §13.7 P2/P3 (safety layers and graded HITL specified, audit not), §4 relational schema layout (no audit table); HANDOFF.md §3 block K (command path listed with no audit component).
BEST PRACTICE: Sparkplug operational-behavior guidance: use broker ACLs to allow only designated Host Applications to publish NCMD/DCMD to Edge Nodes. IEC 62443-3-3 FR2 'Use Control' incl. SR 2.8 auditable events (record of control actions with actor, timestamp, outcome). In chemicals/pharma, 21 CFR Part 11-style audit trails for operator-initiated setpoint changes (who, when, old/new value) are the reference pattern.
SOURCES: https://github.com/eclipse-sparkplug/sparkplug/blob/master/specification/src/main/asciidoc/chapters/Sparkplug_5_Operational_Behavior.adoc, https://simplerqms.com/21-cfr-part-11-audit-trail/, https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/products/collateral/security/isaiec-62443-3-3-wp.html
RECOMMENDATION: Decide and document now (it shapes the Phase 6 schema), build in Phase 6: (a) broker authz — only the HITL console identity may publish the Sparkplug command topic (pairs with the ACL finding); (b) one table, e.g. ods_core.command_audit: recommendation id, model + MLflow version, SHAP summary, proposed vs approved setpoint, approver, HITL level, safety-layer verdicts (envelope/PLC-clamp/independent-check), and timestamps at each hop (console publish → forwarder receipt → writeback result); (c) a small subscriber on the command topic that archives every message. This turns the lab's strongest claim into a queryable artifact.

### [important] Zone placement of ods_core contradicts itself: the consolidated TimescaleDB instance straddles the iDMZ
GAP: Charter §12 #7 / §4 co-locate ts_historian + ods_core + erp_shadow in ONE TimescaleDB instance, and §13.8 Z4 places the Timescale historian OT-side (Level 3). But HANDOFF §3 block I lists 'ods_core + identity_map (MDM analog)' under 'IT storage & analytics (L4–5)', and §4 boundary rule 4 has Neo4j (IT-side, Phase 5b) reading ods_core, with the lakehouse/erp_shadow joins also IT-side. One database instance cannot sit in two zones: as designed, IT-side systems (Neo4j, Spark, ERPNext shadow sync) must open direct DB connections into an OT-zone database — an undeclared iDMZ crossing that contradicts both Z4 and the three-flows claim, and it will surface as a wrong-looking arrow the moment Diagram 1 is walked end-to-end.
EVIDENCE: design/PROJECT_CHARTER.md §4 'Database topology (DECIDED)' + boundary rule 4 vs §13.8 Z4; HANDOFF.md §3 block I (ods_core under IT L4–5) vs block F (historian OT-side).
BEST PRACTICE: IEC 62443-3-2: an asset belongs to exactly one zone with one set of access requirements. NIST SP 800-82r3 / CPwE: data needed on both sides of the boundary is served by a DMZ-replicated store (historian mirror / staging DB in the iDMZ), never by cross-zone connections into an OT database.
SOURCES: https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/SpecialPublications/NIST.SP.800-82r3.pdf, https://www.dragos.com/blog/isa-iec-62443-concepts, https://softwaretoolbox.com/resources/what-is-industrial-dmz
RECOMMENDATION: Resolve explicitly in §13.8 (a Z5 row), before Diagram 1 locks. Cheapest consistent options: (a) split along the zone line — ts_historian stays OT-side, ods_core + erp_shadow move to an IT-side Postgres (the charter already calls splitting 'part of the upgrade-friendly story', so this only accelerates a planned seam); or (b) declare the consolidated instance an iDMZ-resident replicated store (the classic DMZ-historian pattern) and document the OT→iDMZ write and IT→iDMZ read conduits. Either is a Docker-network decision, not new software — but it must be one decision, not two contradictory ones.

### [important] No TLS on the one conduit that represents the untrusted WAN (site forwarders → iDMZ EMQX)
GAP: No design doc mentions transport security anywhere. In the lab's own narrative the forwarder→EMQX link is the inter-site WAN crossing — the exact link every reference pattern encrypts — and Sparkplug B itself defines no payload security; the spec defers entirely to MQTT/TLS, so a Sparkplug UNS without TLS on its exposed conduit has no confidentiality/integrity story at all. This is a concept gap, not skipped hardening: the standard iDMZ pattern is 'broker in the DMZ, firewall admits only 8883/443 inbound', and knowing why (and how certs are provisioned) is precisely the bare-metal lesson enterprise brokers later abstract away. Everything else (intra-site plaintext Mosquitto) is legitimately covered by the §10 hardening exclusion.
EVIDENCE: Absent from design/PROJECT_CHARTER.md §13.1 L1.3/L7.2 (boundary and secrets decided, transport never mentioned), §13.8, and all design/*_notes.md broker sections.
BEST PRACTICE: iDMZ broker guidance: MQTT servers in the DMZ behind a firewall admitting only ports 8883/443 (ManufacturingTomorrow 'MQTT and the Purdue Model'); EMQX production hardening: TLS 1.2/1.3 enforced on listeners, non-negotiable for boundary-crossing traffic; Cirrus Link/Sparkplug: TLS is the assumed transport security layer for Sparkplug infrastructures.
SOURCES: https://www.manufacturingtomorrow.com/article/2021/10/mqtt-and-the-purdue-model-work-together-for-iiot-security/17762, https://www.emqx.com/en/blog/security-hardening-emqx-iot-messaging-systems-part-3, https://cirrus-link.com/securing-mqtt-best-practices-for-a-robust-iot-ecosystem/
RECOMMENDATION: One evening in Phase 4: generate a lab CA (one openssl script), enable a TLS listener (8883) on EMQX only, have the four site-forwarders and the IT-side Kafka bridge connect over it (server-auth TLS is enough; mTLS is an optional stretch). Keep per-site Mosquitto plaintext and record that asymmetry in the ledger ('conduit encrypted, zone-internal traffic not — deliberate'). Add one line to L7.2.

## MINOR FINDINGS
- **No cyber-asset inventory per zone (the 62443 zone attribute the lab almost gets for free)** — ods_core.asset_master inventories PROCESS assets (ISA-95 hierarchy), but nothing inventories the lab's cyber assets — which services/containers exist, which zone and Docker network each belongs to, what it talks to. IEC 62443-3-2 lists asset inventory as a required attribute of every zone; it is also the input an asset owner needs to reason about a boundary at all. Since the whole plant is Docker Compose, this inventory is nearly free and would double as the ground truth for Diagrams 1–3 and the conduit table. → Add a zone/asset table to §13.8 (service → zone → Docker network → role → conduits used) and mirror it as labels on each docker-compose service (e.g. lab.zone: ot-beaumont / idmz / it). Grow it one row per service as phases land — it becomes the checklist that keeps Diagrams 2 and 3 honest.

3	## STRENGTHS
4	- ISA-95 network zoning is textbook-correct and explicitly reasoned: charter §13.8 Z3 places MES/LIMS/CMMS/quality + plant Postgres at ISA-95 Level 3 (below the iDMZ) and only ERP at Level 4, with the two-axis 'data domain vs network zone' distinction (§13.8 preamble) — a subtlety many real programs get wrong (ISA-95/IEC 62264, Purdue model).

9	- 'Business data joins downstream, not in the UNS' (charter §13.7 P8) matches established UNS/Sparkplug best practice: the broker carries OT real-time only, and transactional data on slower timescales joins in the ODS/lakehouse/graph.
10	- ERPNext consumes curated confirmations/events rather than raw telemetry (hand_built/python_centric notes ERP sections) — this mirrors the real ISA-95 L3↔L4 transaction pattern (schedule down, performance/confirmations up) that B2MML standardizes; the docs independently arrived at the industry norm.
11	- The tag-divergence roster is realistic per lineage: Allen-Bradley data-file addressing (N7:20) alongside ISA-5.1-style instrument tags (FIC101_PV), Siemens absolute addressing (DB10.DBD4, MW100), CygNet compound flat tags encoding hierarchy, imperial/metric/mixed units, and four status vocabularies (DOMAIN.md divergence table) — this spans the naming/addressing/unit/status dimensions real brownfield integrators actually face.
12	
13	## MAJOR FINDINGS
14	
15	### [critical] Continuous process (TEP) vs batch-oriented MES records — the ISA-88/ISA-106 tension is never acknowledged or decided
16	GAP: The simulated plant runs the Tennessee Eastman Process — a continuous CSTR reaction → separation → stripping process with no physical batches — yet the MES schema is batch-shaped (mes.production_order, mes.batch, mes.batch_step), the charter's Plane-3 flagship query is batch genealogy ('which batch ran on which reactor during which fault'), and §13.7 P9 adds a 'golden-batch' reference. ISA-88 (batch control: recipes, procedures, units, phases) is never mentioned in any design doc, nor is ISA-106 (its continuous-process counterpart), and no doc says what a 'batch' physically IS in a continuous plant. Without a decision, Phase 5a will seed batch tables whose rows have no defined mapping to the telemetry timeline, and the genealogy/identity-reconciliation lesson — the heart of Plane 3 — rests on an undefined join semantics.
17	EVIDENCE: PROJECT_CHARTER.md §4 'Relational schema layout' Home 2 (mes: production_order, batch, batch_step); §6 'Synthetic transactional data' ('batch genealogy', 'which batch ran on which reactor during which fault'); §13.7 P9 (golden-batch); DOMAIN.md 'The company' ('continuous reaction → separation → stripping process — the Tennessee Eastman process archetype'). ISA-88/ISA-106 absent from all files searched (charter, DOMAIN, all five design notes).
18	BEST PRACTICE: Industry distinguishes batch control (ANSI/ISA-88: recipes/procedures/units/phases, BatchML) from continuous operations (ISA-106 procedural automation, which explicitly adapted ISA-88 concepts to continuous processes). For continuous chemical production, traceability uses TIME-BASED lot definition: a 'lot' is a defined production time window (or grade campaign between transitions), and genealogy is computed by material-tracking models that integrate which raw-material lots were flowing into the unit during that window — not by discrete batch records. MES production accounting for continuous plants uses ISA-95 operations request/response (production runs), with material lot/sublot objects from ISA-95 Part 2.
19	SOURCES: https://www.isa.org/standards-and-publications/isa-standards/isa-88-standards, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ISA-88, https://www.yokogawa.com/us/library/resources/media-publications/isa-88-and-modular-automation/, https://investigationsquality.com/2025/10/24/material-tracking-models-in-continuous-manufacturing-development-validation-and-lifecycle-management/, https://www.datacor.com/resources/lot-tracking-traceability-guide
20	RECOMMENDATION: Add one charter decision (a §12 entry, ~half a page): 'LSC's process is continuous; production accounting is lot-based, not batch-based. mes.batch is reframed as mes.production_lot (or campaign/run) with explicit start_ts/end_ts and product grade; genealogy = time-window join of lot ↔ telemetry ↔ consumed material lots; the golden-batch pattern (P9) becomes golden-run per grade.' Note ISA-88 as consciously out (no batch units in scope) and ISA-106 as the applicable concept. This is a documentation + schema-naming decision now; it prevents a Phase 5a/5b schema and graph-model redesign and makes the genealogy demo conceptually correct.
21	
22	### [important] No ISA-18.2 alarm model behind the 'real-time alerting node' — alarms are modeled as bare threshold events
23	GAP: Charter L2.1 adds a real-time alerting node (UNS → rule thresholds → alert events) and ts_historian.events stores 'alarms/faults/downtime', but no doc references ISA-18.2/IEC 62682 alarm-management concepts: the alarm state machine (Normal → Unack-Alarm → Ack-Alarm → Return-to-Normal-Unack), priority assignment, acknowledgement, shelving/suppression, or flood/chattering handling. For a lab whose OT-consumer layer includes an operator console (HITL, P3) and whose TEP replay includes 21 fault scenarios that will naturally produce alarm floods, treating alarms as stateless threshold pings misses the single most standardized OT operational discipline above control itself.
24	EVIDENCE: PROJECT_CHARTER.md §13.1 L2.1 ('real-time alerting node (UNS → rule thresholds → alert events back to UNS/Kafka)'), §4 ts_historian schema ('events (alarms/faults/downtime)'), §8 Phase 3; hand_built_sparkplug_uns_notes.md Ignition section ('alarm visualization'). ISA-18.2 / IEC 62682 / EEMUA 191 appear nowhere.
25	BEST PRACTICE: ANSI/ISA-18.2 (and its international twin IEC 62682) define the alarm-management lifecycle: rationalization, priority, the alarm state model with acknowledgement, shelving, and flood/nuisance-alarm handling (chattering suppressed via deadband and on/off-delay). EEMUA 191 supplies the performance KPIs (alarms per operator per 10 minutes; flood = >10 alarms/10 min). Alarm objects in real SCADA/historians carry state + priority + ack, not just a threshold-crossing event.
26	SOURCES: https://www.exida.com/webinars/Recordings/understanding-the-alarm-management-lifecycle-of-isa-18.2-iec-62682, https://www.processvue.com/resources/alarm-management-guidelines/, https://www.isa.org/intech-home/2020/march-april/features/alarm-management-questions-that-everyone-asks, https://www.exida.com/Alarm-Management/Resources
27	RECOMMENDATION: Home-lab sized: define one Pydantic AlarmEvent model shaped by ISA-18.2 — fields for state (per the ISA-18.2 state machine), priority (3–4 levels), ack/shelve — and implement the state machine plus a simple chattering guard (deadband + on-delay) in the Phase 3 alerting node. Add ack/shelve buttons to the HITL operator console (it already exists in the design), and one Grafana panel of EEMUA-191-style alarm-rate KPIs. This is a few hundred lines and turns the alerting node into the bare-metal ISA-18.2 lesson; replaying a TEP fault then demonstrates a real alarm flood and why shelving/rationalization exist.
28	
29	### [important] Raw-counts → engineering-units scaling is missing from the divergence roster and the transform primitives
30	GAP: Every site in the divergence roster (DOMAIN.md) diverges on naming, unit system, and status vocabulary — but all apparently publish already-scaled engineering values. In a real brownfield Allen-Bradley SLC/PLC-5 plant, N7:20 is a 16-bit signed INTEGER data file: the value on the wire is raw ADC counts (e.g. 6208–31208 or 0–16383 for 4–20 mA) or integer-scaled values, requiring per-tag linear scaling (raw_min/raw_max → eu_min/eu_max) before it means anything. This 'one site sends raw counts, another sends scaled floats' problem is one of the classic harmonization messes, and the lab's three-stage mapping table (charter §6) carries unit/range/cadence but no scaling parameters; the §7 transform primitives cover unit conversion, status normalization, and timestamp coercion but not raw→EU scaling.
31	EVIDENCE: DOMAIN.md 'The cast of divergence' table (units row: imperial/metric/metric/mixed — no raw-vs-scaled dimension); PROJECT_CHARTER.md §6 mapping-table fields and §7 'Transform primitives — unit conversion, status normalization, timestamp coercion, cross-field data-quality flagging'; synthetic_data_generation_notes.md 'Step 2' mapping-table field list (unit of measure, expected range — no raw_min/raw_max/eu_min/eu_max).
32	BEST PRACTICE: PLC analog inputs deliver raw integer counts from the ADC, not engineering units; scaling (SCP/CPT in Allen-Bradley, NORM_X/SCALE_X in Siemens) with per-card raw ranges (AB 1769-IF4: 6208–31208; Siemens S7: 0/5530–27648) is a per-tag configuration that integrators routinely lose or mis-document — making raw-vs-scaled reconciliation a standard dimension of brownfield historian/UNS harmonization.
33	SOURCES: https://industrialmonitordirect.com/blogs/knowledgebase/scaling-4-20ma-analog-inputs-to-engineering-units-in-plcs, https://instrumentationtools.com/plc-analog-input-scaling/, https://industrialmonitordirect.com/blogs/knowledgebase/plc-analog-scaling-tutorial-engineering-units-vs-raw-values
34	RECOMMENDATION: Make Beaumont (the AB/N7 site — already the 'genuine memory-address lesson' site) publish RAW INTEGER COUNTS for its analog tags, and add four columns to the three-stage mapping table (raw_min, raw_max, eu_min, eu_max) plus one 'scale_linear' transform primitive. Zero new infrastructure; it deepens exactly the lesson Beaumont exists to teach and must be in the mapping-table schema (the spine) before Phase 0 freezes it.
35	
36	### [important] MES/LIMS schemas lack the ISA-95 Part 2 material model — genealogy has no material lots to trace
37	GAP: The role-A schemas (charter §4) define mes.production_order/batch/batch_step, lims.sample/lab_result/disposition, cmms.work_order, quality.nonconformance — but no material_definition or material_lot tables anywhere. Charter §6 promises 'material IDs' and 'CONSUMED_MATERIAL' graph edges, and the Plane-3 payoff is genealogy — yet genealogy is definitionally the consumed-lot → produced-lot linkage, which cannot be demonstrated without a material-lot object. As written, the graph can link batch↔reactor↔work-order↔lab-result but not raw-material-lot→product-lot, which is the query that makes genealogy commercially meaningful (recall scoping: 'which finished lots contain contaminated feedstock lot X?').
38	EVIDENCE: PROJECT_CHARTER.md §4 'Relational schema layout' Home 2 table (no material tables in mes/lims/cmms/quality); §6 'Synthetic transactional data' (mentions material IDs and 'CONSUMED_MATERIAL' only as context/edge names); §7 EngiGraph extracts (CONSUMED_MATERIAL edge). 
39	BEST PRACTICE: ISA-95 Part 2 defines the material model — material class, material definition, material lot, material sublot — as first-class objects, implemented in B2MML; MES lot-traceability practice records which material lots were consumed to produce which product lots (with processing conditions and quality data) as the genealogy backbone, with forward/backward trace as the standard query pair.
40	SOURCES: https://github.com/MESAInternational/B2MML-BatchML/releases, https://www.symestic.com/en-us/blog/mes/isa95, https://sgsystemsglobal.com/glossary/traceability-end-to-end-lot-genealogy/, https://www.siemens.com/en-us/technology/lot-traceability/
41	RECOMMENDATION: Add two tables to the mes schema in the charter's §4 layout: material_definition (product/feedstock catalog) and material_lot (lot_id, material_definition, quantity, produced_by/consumed_by production run, timestamps). The synthetic generator already plans material-consumption events (synthetic_data_generation_notes Step 3) — they just need a home table. This lands naturally with the finding-1 lot decision and costs one generator function; without it, Phase 5b's genealogy demo degrades to event correlation.
42	
43	### [important] P6 equipment-type templates stop at Pydantic — Sparkplug B's native Template (UDT) mechanism is never used
44	GAP: Charter §13.7 P6 defines equipment-type templates as Pydantic types instantiated per asset — the right pattern — but the design never mentions that Sparkplug B itself has a Template datatype: UDT-like type definitions published in the NBIRTH and referenced by template instances in DBIRTH, which Ignition's MQTT Engine materializes as UDT definitions/instances automatically. If templates live only in Python, the on-the-wire UNS carries flat metrics, Ignition (already in the stack as the SCADA consumer) sees no typed equipment, and the lab misses the real-world mechanism by which equipment classes propagate through a Sparkplug UNS — despite §9 declaring 'Sparkplug B as the contract — births, aliases, datatypes, lifecycle'.
45	EVIDENCE: PROJECT_CHARTER.md §13.7 P6 ('as a Pydantic type; instantiate per site/asset'); §9 'Sparkplug B as the contract' (lists births/aliases/datatypes/lifecycle — Templates absent); §7 ISHE extracts (Pydantic hierarchy). No design doc mentions Sparkplug Templates/UDT-over-Sparkplug.
46	BEST PRACTICE: The Sparkplug B specification includes Templates: reusable type definitions (metric sets with datatypes and parameters) published in birth certificates, the wire-level equivalent of Ignition UDTs; Ignition MQTT Engine converts received Sparkplug template definitions into Ignition UDT definitions and instances, which is the standard way equipment classes are shared across a Sparkplug UNS (Cirrus Link/Chariot docs, Opto22 Sparkplug guidance).
47	SOURCES: https://docs.chariot.io/display/CLD80/User+Defined+Types+(UDTs)+within+Transmission, https://documents.opto22.com/2357_Industrial_Strength_MQTT_Sparkplug_B.pdf, https://industrialmonitordirect.com/blogs/knowledgebase/configuring-udts-with-ignition-mqtt-engine-tags
48	RECOMMENDATION: When implementing P6 (Phase 2/4), emit each Pydantic equipment class as a Sparkplug Template definition in NBIRTH and each asset as a template instance in DBIRTH (verify PySparkplug supports Template metrics early — if not, this affects the library choice). Then observe Ignition auto-creating the UDT — that observation IS the lesson that P6 exists to teach, moved from Python-internal to the actual contract layer. Record it as a one-line refinement to P6 in the charter.
49	
50	### [important] identity_map is a bare crosswalk — the declared 'MDM analog' lacks match/survivorship/golden-record mechanics
51	GAP: Charter §13.1 L3.1 consciously rejects a separate MDM platform and names ods_core (asset_master + identity_map + metric_registry) 'the lab's MDM analog' — sound reasoning, not a gap. But the analog as specified is only a lookup: identity_map = (source_system, source_key) → canonical_identity (§4 boundary rule 2). What makes MDM a discipline — match rules (deterministic/probabilistic), survivorship policy (which source wins per attribute when CMMS and ERP disagree about the same pump), golden-record assembly, confidence and stewardship — is absent. Since the lab WILL have the same asset described by mes, cmms, ERPNext, and ET topology with conflicting attributes, the conflicts will occur; without survivorship the lesson silently degrades to 'maintain a mapping spreadsheet'.
52	EVIDENCE: PROJECT_CHARTER.md §4 boundary rule 2 ('Reconciliation lives in ods_core.identity_map — (source_system, source_key) → canonical_identity'); §13.1 L3.1 ('No CRM, no separate MDM — ods_core ... is the lab's MDM analog'). No doc mentions survivorship, match rules, or golden record.
53	BEST PRACTICE: Master-data practice builds the golden record via match (identify records referring to one real-world entity, deterministic + probabilistic) → merge → survivorship (rule-driven selection of the winning value per attribute, typically by source-priority and recency) → stewardship; survivorship rules per attribute are the core artifact distinguishing MDM from a static crosswalk (Profisee, Data Ladder, standard MDM literature).
54	SOURCES: https://dataladder.com/guide-to-data-survivorship-how-to-build-the-golden-record/, https://profisee.com/platform/golden-record-management/, https://justinlilly.com/master-data-management-golden-records-matching-and-survivorship
55	RECOMMENDATION: Keep the no-platform decision; upgrade the analog minimally: add match_rule, match_confidence, valid_from/valid_to, and steward columns to identity_map; write a one-page survivorship policy for asset_master (e.g. nameplate attributes: ET topology wins; maintenance status: CMMS wins; financial: ERP wins) and enforce it in the Python reconciliation service; include ONE deliberate fuzzy-match case in the synthetic data (e.g. 'P-101A' vs 'EQ-4471' vs 'Feed Pump A' with a typo) so probabilistic matching is exercised. A day of work in Phase 5a that makes the 'MDM analog' claim true.
56	
57	## MINOR FINDINGS
58	- **No standard unit-of-measure code list for the mapping table / metric_registry** — The three-stage mapping table and metric_registry carry 'unit' and unit-conversion factors (charter §6, §7, §9 'unit factors are data'), but no doc names a controlled unit vocabulary. With imperial/metric/mixed units across four sites plus LIMS results plus ERP quantities, free-text unit strings ('degF', '°F', 'DEG F') recreate inside the registry the exact divergence problem the registry exists to solve. → Adopt UNECE Rec 20 codes as the canonical 'unit' value in metric_registry, with a small units dimension table (code, display symbol, dimension, conversion-to-canonical factor). One YAML file in Phase 0; also gives Neo4j a clean hook to QUDT-style unit nodes later.
59	- **ISA-95 hierarchy vocabulary: 'line/cell' is the discrete-manufacturing level; a continuous chemical plant uses 'production unit', and 'equipment-class' is not a hierarchy level** — The charter's full path is 'enterprise → site → area → line/cell → equipment-class → equipment-id' (§6). Two vocabulary slips for a lab that teaches ISA-95: (1) at the work-center level, ISA-95 uses 'production unit' for continuous processes and 'process cell/unit' for batch — 'production line / work cell' is the discrete-manufacturing branch, the one branch LSC is NOT; (2) 'equipment class' in ISA-95 is a classification (type) orthogonal to the equipment hierarchy (instances) — embedding it as a topic level conflates type with instance (a known, defensible UNS-topic convention, but it should be a stated choice, not an unexamined one, in a teaching lab). → One-paragraph charter note: rename the level to 'production unit' (or state that 'line' is used loosely and why), and state explicitly that equipment-class appears in the UNS topic path as a deliberate navigability convention while asset_master keeps class as an attribute of the equipment instance per ISA-95. Do this before Phase 0 freezes the topic namespace — topic renames after historian data exists are painful.

- Deliberately misaligned business keys (batch 'B-2207', asset 'EQ-4471' vs OT 'site/line/reactor' identities), the no-cross-home-FK boundary rules, lane discipline, and system-of-record authority preservation (charter §4 boundary rules, §9) faithfully reproduce the real enterprise identity-reconciliation problem and correct system-of-record discipline — this is the pedagogically right design for the MDM lesson.
- 'Business data joins downstream, not in the UNS' (charter §13.7 P8) matches established UNS/Sparkplug best practice: the broker carries OT real-time only, and transactional data on slower timescales joins in the ODS/lakehouse/graph.
- ERPNext consumes curated confirmations/events rather than raw telemetry (hand_built/python_centric notes ERP sections) — this mirrors the real ISA-95 L3↔L4 transaction pattern (schedule down, performance/confirmations up) that B2MML standardizes; the docs independently arrived at the industry norm.
- The tag-divergence roster is realistic per lineage: Allen-Bradley data-file addressing (N7:20) alongside ISA-5.1-style instrument tags (FIC101_PV), Siemens absolute addressing (DB10.DBD4, MW100), CygNet compound flat tags encoding hierarchy, imperial/metric/mixed units, and four status vocabularies (DOMAIN.md divergence table) — this spans the naming/addressing/unit/status dimensions real brownfield integrators actually face.

## MAJOR FINDINGS

### [critical] Continuous process (TEP) vs batch-oriented MES records — the ISA-88/ISA-106 tension is never acknowledged or decided
GAP: The simulated plant runs the Tennessee Eastman Process — a continuous CSTR reaction → separation → stripping process with no physical batches — yet the MES schema is batch-shaped (mes.production_order, mes.batch, mes.batch_step), the charter's Plane-3 flagship query is batch genealogy ('which batch ran on which reactor during which fault'), and §13.7 P9 adds a 'golden-batch' reference. ISA-88 (batch control: recipes, procedures, units, phases) is never mentioned in any design doc, nor is ISA-106 (its continuous-process counterpart), and no doc says what a 'batch' physically IS in a continuous plant. Without a decision, Phase 5a will seed batch tables whose rows have no defined mapping to the telemetry timeline, and the genealogy/identity-reconciliation lesson — the heart of Plane 3 — rests on an undefined join semantics.
EVIDENCE: PROJECT_CHARTER.md §4 'Relational schema layout' Home 2 (mes: production_order, batch, batch_step); §6 'Synthetic transactional data' ('batch genealogy', 'which batch ran on which reactor during which fault'); §13.7 P9 (golden-batch); DOMAIN.md 'The company' ('continuous reaction → separation → stripping process — the Tennessee Eastman process archetype'). ISA-88/ISA-106 absent from all files searched (charter, DOMAIN, all five design notes).
BEST PRACTICE: Industry distinguishes batch control (ANSI/ISA-88: recipes/procedures/units/phases, BatchML) from continuous operations (ISA-106 procedural automation, which explicitly adapted ISA-88 concepts to continuous processes). For continuous chemical production, traceability uses TIME-BASED lot definition: a 'lot' is a defined production time window (or grade campaign between transitions), and genealogy is computed by material-tracking models that integrate which raw-material lots were flowing into the unit during that window — not by discrete batch records. MES production accounting for continuous plants uses ISA-95 operations request/response (production runs), with material lot/sublot objects from ISA-95 Part 2.
SOURCES: https://www.isa.org/standards-and-publications/isa-standards/isa-88-standards, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ISA-88, https://www.yokogawa.com/us/library/resources/media-publications/isa-88-and-modular-automation/, https://investigationsquality.com/2025/10/24/material-tracking-models-in-continuous-manufacturing-development-validation-and-lifecycle-management/, https://www.datacor.com/resources/lot-tracking-traceability-guide
RECOMMENDATION: Add one charter decision (a §12 entry, ~half a page): 'LSC's process is continuous; production accounting is lot-based, not batch-based. mes.batch is reframed as mes.production_lot (or campaign/run) with explicit start_ts/end_ts and product grade; genealogy = time-window join of lot ↔ telemetry ↔ consumed material lots; the golden-batch pattern (P9) becomes golden-run per grade.' Note ISA-88 as consciously out (no batch units in scope) and ISA-106 as the applicable concept. This is a documentation + schema-naming decision now; it prevents a Phase 5a/5b schema and graph-model redesign and makes the genealogy demo conceptually correct.

### [important] No ISA-18.2 alarm model behind the 'real-time alerting node' — alarms are modeled as bare threshold events
GAP: Charter L2.1 adds a real-time alerting node (UNS → rule thresholds → alert events) and ts_historian.events stores 'alarms/faults/downtime', but no doc references ISA-18.2/IEC 62682 alarm-management concepts: the alarm state machine (Normal → Unack-Alarm → Ack-Alarm → Return-to-Normal-Unack), priority assignment, acknowledgement, shelving/suppression, or flood/chattering handling. For a lab whose OT-consumer layer includes an operator console (HITL, P3) and whose TEP replay includes 21 fault scenarios that will naturally produce alarm floods, treating alarms as stateless threshold pings misses the single most standardized OT operational discipline above control itself.
EVIDENCE: PROJECT_CHARTER.md §13.1 L2.1 ('real-time alerting node (UNS → rule thresholds → alert events back to UNS/Kafka)'), §4 ts_historian schema ('events (alarms/faults/downtime)'), §8 Phase 3; hand_built_sparkplug_uns_notes.md Ignition section ('alarm visualization'). ISA-18.2 / IEC 62682 / EEMUA 191 appear nowhere.
BEST PRACTICE: ANSI/ISA-18.2 (and its international twin IEC 62682) define the alarm-management lifecycle: rationalization, priority, the alarm state model with acknowledgement, shelving, and flood/nuisance-alarm handling (chattering suppressed via deadband and on/off-delay). EEMUA 191 supplies the performance KPIs (alarms per operator per 10 minutes; flood = >10 alarms/10 min). Alarm objects in real SCADA/historians carry state + priority + ack, not just a threshold-crossing event.
SOURCES: https://www.exida.com/webinars/Recordings/understanding-the-alarm-management-lifecycle-of-isa-18.2-iec-62682, https://www.processvue.com/resources/alarm-management-guidelines/, https://www.isa.org/intech-home/2020/march-april/features/alarm-management-questions-that-everyone-asks, https://www.exida.com/Alarm-Management/Resources
RECOMMENDATION: Home-lab sized: define one Pydantic AlarmEvent model shaped by ISA-18.2 — fields for state (per the ISA-18.2 state machine), priority (3–4 levels), ack/shelve — and implement the state machine plus a simple chattering guard (deadband + on-delay) in the Phase 3 alerting node. Add ack/shelve buttons to the HITL operator console (it already exists in the design), and one Grafana panel of EEMUA-191-style alarm-rate KPIs. This is a few hundred lines and turns the alerting node into the bare-metal ISA-18.2 lesson; replaying a TEP fault then demonstrates a real alarm flood and why shelving/rationalization exist.

### [important] Raw-counts → engineering-units scaling is missing from the divergence roster and the transform primitives
GAP: Every site in the divergence roster (DOMAIN.md) diverges on naming, unit system, and status vocabulary — but all apparently publish already-scaled engineering values. In a real brownfield Allen-Bradley SLC/PLC-5 plant, N7:20 is a 16-bit signed INTEGER data file: the value on the wire is raw ADC counts (e.g. 6208–31208 or 0–16383 for 4–20 mA) or integer-scaled values, requiring per-tag linear scaling (raw_min/raw_max → eu_min/eu_max) before it means anything. This 'one site sends raw counts, another sends scaled floats' problem is one of the classic harmonization messes, and the lab's three-stage mapping table (charter §6) carries unit/range/cadence but no scaling parameters; the §7 transform primitives cover unit conversion, status normalization, and timestamp coercion but not raw→EU scaling.
EVIDENCE: DOMAIN.md 'The cast of divergence' table (units row: imperial/metric/metric/mixed — no raw-vs-scaled dimension); PROJECT_CHARTER.md §6 mapping-table fields and §7 'Transform primitives — unit conversion, status normalization, timestamp coercion, cross-field data-quality flagging'; synthetic_data_generation_notes.md 'Step 2' mapping-table field list (unit of measure, expected range — no raw_min/raw_max/eu_min/eu_max).
BEST PRACTICE: PLC analog inputs deliver raw integer counts from the ADC, not engineering units; scaling (SCP/CPT in Allen-Bradley, NORM_X/SCALE_X in Siemens) with per-card raw ranges (AB 1769-IF4: 6208–31208; Siemens S7: 0/5530–27648) is a per-tag configuration that integrators routinely lose or mis-document — making raw-vs-scaled reconciliation a standard dimension of brownfield historian/UNS harmonization.
SOURCES: https://industrialmonitordirect.com/blogs/knowledgebase/scaling-4-20ma-analog-inputs-to-engineering-units-in-plcs, https://instrumentationtools.com/plc-analog-input-scaling/, https://industrialmonitordirect.com/blogs/knowledgebase/plc-analog-scaling-tutorial-engineering-units-vs-raw-values
RECOMMENDATION: Make Beaumont (the AB/N7 site — already the 'genuine memory-address lesson' site) publish RAW INTEGER COUNTS for its analog tags, and add four columns to the three-stage mapping table (raw_min, raw_max, eu_min, eu_max) plus one 'scale_linear' transform primitive. Zero new infrastructure; it deepens exactly the lesson Beaumont exists to teach and must be in the mapping-table schema (the spine) before Phase 0 freezes it.

### [important] MES/LIMS schemas lack the ISA-95 Part 2 material model — genealogy has no material lots to trace
GAP: The role-A schemas (charter §4) define mes.production_order/batch/batch_step, lims.sample/lab_result/disposition, cmms.work_order, quality.nonconformance — but no material_definition or material_lot tables anywhere. Charter §6 promises 'material IDs' and 'CONSUMED_MATERIAL' graph edges, and the Plane-3 payoff is genealogy — yet genealogy is definitionally the consumed-lot → produced-lot linkage, which cannot be demonstrated without a material-lot object. As written, the graph can link batch↔reactor↔work-order↔lab-result but not raw-material-lot→product-lot, which is the query that makes genealogy commercially meaningful (recall scoping: 'which finished lots contain contaminated feedstock lot X?').
EVIDENCE: PROJECT_CHARTER.md §4 'Relational schema layout' Home 2 table (no material tables in mes/lims/cmms/quality); §6 'Synthetic transactional data' (mentions material IDs and 'CONSUMED_MATERIAL' only as context/edge names); §7 EngiGraph extracts (CONSUMED_MATERIAL edge). 
BEST PRACTICE: ISA-95 Part 2 defines the material model — material class, material definition, material lot, material sublot — as first-class objects, implemented in B2MML; MES lot-traceability practice records which material lots were consumed to produce which product lots (with processing conditions and quality data) as the genealogy backbone, with forward/backward trace as the standard query pair.
SOURCES: https://github.com/MESAInternational/B2MML-BatchML/releases, https://www.symestic.com/en-us/blog/mes/isa95, https://sgsystemsglobal.com/glossary/traceability-end-to-end-lot-genealogy/, https://www.siemens.com/en-us/technology/lot-traceability/
RECOMMENDATION: Add two tables to the mes schema in the charter's §4 layout: material_definition (product/feedstock catalog) and material_lot (lot_id, material_definition, quantity, produced_by/consumed_by production run, timestamps). The synthetic generator already plans material-consumption events (synthetic_data_generation_notes Step 3) — they just need a home table. This lands naturally with the finding-1 lot decision and costs one generator function; without it, Phase 5b's genealogy demo degrades to event correlation.

### [important] P6 equipment-type templates stop at Pydantic — Sparkplug B's native Template (UDT) mechanism is never used
GAP: Charter §13.7 P6 defines equipment-type templates as Pydantic types instantiated per asset — the right pattern — but the design never mentions that Sparkplug B itself has a Template datatype: UDT-like type definitions published in the NBIRTH and referenced by template instances in DBIRTH, which Ignition's MQTT Engine materializes as UDT definitions/instances automatically. If templates live only in Python, the on-the-wire UNS carries flat metrics, Ignition (already in the stack as the SCADA consumer) sees no typed equipment, and the lab misses the real-world mechanism by which equipment classes propagate through a Sparkplug UNS — despite §9 declaring 'Sparkplug B as the contract — births, aliases, datatypes, lifecycle'.
EVIDENCE: PROJECT_CHARTER.md §13.7 P6 ('as a Pydantic type; instantiate per site/asset'); §9 'Sparkplug B as the contract' (lists births/aliases/datatypes/lifecycle — Templates absent); §7 ISHE extracts (Pydantic hierarchy). No design doc mentions Sparkplug Templates/UDT-over-Sparkplug.
BEST PRACTICE: The Sparkplug B specification includes Templates: reusable type definitions (metric sets with datatypes and parameters) published in birth certificates, the wire-level equivalent of Ignition UDTs; Ignition MQTT Engine converts received Sparkplug template definitions into Ignition UDT definitions and instances, which is the standard way equipment classes are shared across a Sparkplug UNS (Cirrus Link/Chariot docs, Opto22 Sparkplug guidance).
SOURCES: https://docs.chariot.io/display/CLD80/User+Defined+Types+(UDTs)+within+Transmission, https://documents.opto22.com/2357_Industrial_Strength_MQTT_Sparkplug_B.pdf, https://industrialmonitordirect.com/blogs/knowledgebase/configuring-udts-with-ignition-mqtt-engine-tags
RECOMMENDATION: When implementing P6 (Phase 2/4), emit each Pydantic equipment class as a Sparkplug Template definition in NBIRTH and each asset as a template instance in DBIRTH (verify PySparkplug supports Template metrics early — if not, this affects the library choice). Then observe Ignition auto-creating the UDT — that observation IS the lesson that P6 exists to teach, moved from Python-internal to the actual contract layer. Record it as a one-line refinement to P6 in the charter.

### [important] identity_map is a bare crosswalk — the declared 'MDM analog' lacks match/survivorship/golden-record mechanics
GAP: Charter §13.1 L3.1 consciously rejects a separate MDM platform and names ods_core (asset_master + identity_map + metric_registry) 'the lab's MDM analog' — sound reasoning, not a gap. But the analog as specified is only a lookup: identity_map = (source_system, source_key) → canonical_identity (§4 boundary rule 2). What makes MDM a discipline — match rules (deterministic/probabilistic), survivorship policy (which source wins per attribute when CMMS and ERP disagree about the same pump), golden-record assembly, confidence and stewardship — is absent. Since the lab WILL have the same asset described by mes, cmms, ERPNext, and ET topology with conflicting attributes, the conflicts will occur; without survivorship the lesson silently degrades to 'maintain a mapping spreadsheet'.
EVIDENCE: PROJECT_CHARTER.md §4 boundary rule 2 ('Reconciliation lives in ods_core.identity_map — (source_system, source_key) → canonical_identity'); §13.1 L3.1 ('No CRM, no separate MDM — ods_core ... is the lab's MDM analog'). No doc mentions survivorship, match rules, or golden record.
BEST PRACTICE: Master-data practice builds the golden record via match (identify records referring to one real-world entity, deterministic + probabilistic) → merge → survivorship (rule-driven selection of the winning value per attribute, typically by source-priority and recency) → stewardship; survivorship rules per attribute are the core artifact distinguishing MDM from a static crosswalk (Profisee, Data Ladder, standard MDM literature).
SOURCES: https://dataladder.com/guide-to-data-survivorship-how-to-build-the-golden-record/, https://profisee.com/platform/golden-record-management/, https://justinlilly.com/master-data-management-golden-records-matching-and-survivorship
RECOMMENDATION: Keep the no-platform decision; upgrade the analog minimally: add match_rule, match_confidence, valid_from/valid_to, and steward columns to identity_map; write a one-page survivorship policy for asset_master (e.g. nameplate attributes: ET topology wins; maintenance status: CMMS wins; financial: ERP wins) and enforce it in the Python reconciliation service; include ONE deliberate fuzzy-match case in the synthetic data (e.g. 'P-101A' vs 'EQ-4471' vs 'Feed Pump A' with a typo) so probabilistic matching is exercised. A day of work in Phase 5a that makes the 'MDM analog' claim true.

## MINOR FINDINGS
- **No standard unit-of-measure code list for the mapping table / metric_registry** — The three-stage mapping table and metric_registry carry 'unit' and unit-conversion factors (charter §6, §7, §9 'unit factors are data'), but no doc names a controlled unit vocabulary. With imperial/metric/mixed units across four sites plus LIMS results plus ERP quantities, free-text unit strings ('degF', '°F', 'DEG F') recreate inside the registry the exact divergence problem the registry exists to solve. → Adopt UNECE Rec 20 codes as the canonical 'unit' value in metric_registry, with a small units dimension table (code, display symbol, dimension, conversion-to-canonical factor). One YAML file in Phase 0; also gives Neo4j a clean hook to QUDT-style unit nodes later.
- **ISA-95 hierarchy vocabulary: 'line/cell' is the discrete-manufacturing level; a continuous chemical plant uses 'production unit', and 'equipment-class' is not a hierarchy level** — The charter's full path is 'enterprise → site → area → line/cell → equipment-class → equipment-id' (§6). Two vocabulary slips for a lab that teaches ISA-95: (1) at the work-center level, ISA-95 uses 'production unit' for continuous processes and 'process cell/unit' for batch — 'production line / work cell' is the discrete-manufacturing branch, the one branch LSC is NOT; (2) 'equipment class' in ISA-95 is a classification (type) orthogonal to the equipment hierarchy (instances) — embedding it as a topic level conflates type with instance (a known, defensible UNS-topic convention, but it should be a stated choice, not an unexamined one, in a teaching lab). → One-paragraph charter note: rename the level to 'production unit' (or state that 'line' is used loosely and why), and state explicitly that equipment-class appears in the UNS topic path as a deliberate navigability convention while asset_master keeps class as an attribute of the equipment instance per ISA-95. Do this before Phase 0 freezes the topic namespace — topic renames after historian data exists are painful.

# streaming-data-eng

## STRENGTHS
- Two-tier broker joined by a Python site-forwarder instead of a raw spBv1.0/# broker bridge (charter §4) — correctly reasons from Sparkplug B's statefulness (LWT death certificates, primary-host STATE), matching HiveMQ's published guidance that naive bridging breaks Sparkplug session coherence. This is a subtle point many real deployments get wrong.
- The CDC crawl-walk-run plan (charter §8, 5a.1→5a.3) is textbook: Python poller emits Debezium-shaped envelopes ({before, after, op, ts_ms, source}) on Debezium's exact default topic naming {server}.{schema}.{table}, normalized through one ChangeEvent Pydantic model as a swap seam, with replication-slot/WAL-retention behavior named as an explicit learning goal — mirroring Debezium's own documented operational concerns (debezium.io PostgreSQL connector docs).
- 'Business data joins downstream, not in the UNS' (charter §13.7 P8) plus the storage-by-concern separation (§4) matches the industry consensus pattern (HiveMQ 'MQTT vs Kafka: friends not foes'; UMH data-modeling guidance): MQTT/Sparkplug carries OT real-time, Kafka carries the IT/analytics leg, business records join in the lakehouse/ODS — never through the broker.
- The governed metric_registry as an enforced contract (charter §13.7 P7 makes Bronze validate against it, drift → dead_letter) is a genuine data-contract practice, not just documentation — functionally what schema-registry compatibility enforcement does in enterprise Kafka stacks, expressed at the semantic-metric level. Per-field lineage + dead_letter table exceed typical home-lab designs.
- Edge store-and-forward (charter §13.1 L1.2) and the historian-less site (L1.4) are real edge-autonomy patterns adopted deliberately, and Kafka was consciously kept over Apache Iggy (§13.6) precisely because of the Connect/Debezium/Schema-Registry ecosystem — the reasoning explicitly names the registry ecosystem, showing awareness of the surrounding platform.
- Scan-rate/RBE-deadband policy classed by process physics (charter §13.7 P1: fast ~1s / supporting ~5s / environmental ~30s / state on-change, with the cascade check across every link) is a real industrial data-collection best practice rarely seen stated this explicitly in lab designs.
- The lake-catalog/governance gap is consciously acknowledged: charter §13.6 slots Databricks Free Edition (Delta Lake + Unity Catalog) as a graduate-to milestone explicitly to 'fill the lab's lake-catalog/governance gap' — a correct self-assessment rather than a blind spot.

## MAJOR FINDINGS

### [critical] No replay-clock design: TEP's 3-minute cadence vs the ~1s scan-rate policy, and wall-clock vs simulated-clock is undecided
GAP: The standard TEP benchmark datasets sample every 3 minutes (500 observations over 25h training / 48h test runs), yet charter §13.7 P1 mandates ~1s scan for fast process variables and requires that rate to 'hold across every link (replay → PLC/poll → Sparkplug RBE → historian)'. There is no upsampling/interpolation strategy anywhere — replaying 3-minute TEP data at a 1s scan produces 180 identical reads per sample (RBE then suppresses everything, so the fast-loop story collapses) unless values are interpolated or synthetic fast dynamics are layered on. Separately, the replay/orchestration layer mentions 'cadence, clock speed, pause/resume, backfill mode, live simulation mode' but never decides the clock model: are Sparkplug metric timestamps original-dataset time, rebased wall-clock time, or a simulated clock? Faster-than-real-time replay (explicitly planned for historian backfill) breaks SPC/EWMA windows, Grafana time ranges, Spark event-time watermarks, and TimescaleDB retention policies if timestamps aren't coherently rebased.
EVIDENCE: design/synthetic_data_generation_notes.md — '6) Replay/orchestration layer' and 'Recommended volume strategy' ('replay multiple runs at different speeds for backfill'); design/PROJECT_CHARTER.md §13.7 P1 (scan-rate policy) and §8 Phase 1 ('replay in time order'). Neither doc states TEP's native cadence or an interpolation/clock decision.
BEST PRACTICE: Replay/simulation systems (e.g. IBA IoT-data-simulator, DolphinDB replay, Deephaven simulated feeds) treat the replay clock as a first-class design: relative-timestamp rebasing to 'now', a single speed factor, and one clock master so every downstream event-time computation stays coherent. Standard TEP releases sample at 3-minute intervals (KeepFloyding TEP overview; BibMon TEP tutorial; Rieth et al. extended TEP dataset).

1	# ml-plane4

3	## STRENGTHS
4	- Graded HITL maturity ladder (charter §13.7 P3: L1 alert → L2 recommend → L3 closed-loop, with 'some metrics stay L1-only') matches how industrial closed-loop AI vendors (e.g. Imubit's advisory-then-closed-loop AIO progression) and the CPG reference actually stage autonomy — risk-based scoping of which loops ever go autonomous is genuine best practice.
5	- 'The model never actuates; the controller executes; the human gates' (§13.5 L6.5) with all writeback through a single auditable UNS command path and no edge→PLC bypass is exactly the APC/advisory-control command-mediation pattern — an auditable, revocable write path is what real advanced-control deployments require.
6	- Defense-in-depth writeback (§13.7 P2) with a PLC-side clamp that is hardcoded and independent of the model mirrors real APC clamping practice: the DCS/PLC enforces setpoint high/low limits regardless of what the optimizer requests. The layering instinct (model envelope ≠ controller clamp ≠ independent check) is correct.
7	- SPC-first detection (§13.7 P5: EWMA/CUSUM with ML tuning the chart, 'not generic anomaly detection') is the established, explainable yield/quality method — framing ML as adjusting chart parameters from covariates ('dynamic SPC') is a defensible, industry-grounded stance that most home labs get wrong by jumping straight to black-box anomaly detection.
8	- Explainability as a hard model-serving contract requirement (§13.7 P4 — every alert/recommendation carries feature attribution, rendered in the HITL console) is ahead of much industry practice and directly implements the operator-trust prerequisite that Google's own feature-attribution monitoring work and the model-cards literature emphasize.
9	- MLflow registry deploying the same model artifact to edge and cloud, plus the explicit online(Redis)/offline(gold) feature-store split (§13.1 L6.1/L6.2, §13.5 L6.4), is textbook MLOps reference architecture; per-site edge inference that survives WAN loss (L6.3) matches edge-ML best practice for OT.
10	- Scan-rate/deadband tied to process physics with the cascade check 'deadband too wide hides slow drift — scan rate decides whether the model can even see the problem' (§13.7 P1) is a subtle data-for-ML observability point that most enterprise programs miss.
11	- Business data joining downstream of the UNS (§13.7 P8) with LIMS results landing in gold means the structure needed for delayed-label model evaluation (predictions joined to later lab results) already exists — the lab is one decision away from teaching that correctly.
12	- Golden-reference concept (§13.7 P9) is a recognized high-value yield pattern (Rockwell/Kalypso golden-batch practice), and the doc already hedges 'golden-batch / golden-run', showing awareness of the batch-vs-continuous distinction.

16	### [critical] 'Independent safety-check service (GuardLogix analog)' conflates a BPCS-level software guard with a certified SIS layer
17	GAP: Charter §13.7 P2 layer 3 labels the independent safety-check service a 'GuardLogix analog'. GuardLogix is a SIL 3-certified safety controller — i.e., a Safety Instrumented System component under IEC 61511. 23	### [important] Graded HITL ladder is missing the shadow-mode rung and any promotion/demotion criteria
24	GAP: §13.7 P3 starts the ladder at L1 (alert). Industry norm — both generic MLOps and industrial closed-loop AI specifically — is to run every candidate model in SHADOW mode first: scoring live data, logging would-be alerts/recommendations, actuating and surfacing nothing, compared offline against outcomes.
