26	BEST PRACTICE: Shadow deployment before any user/process-facing stage is standard MLOps practice (SageMaker shadow variants; shadow-vs-canary literature), and closed-loop industrial AI vendors describe deploying the model 'in shadow mode alongside existing control systems' before advisory, then closed-loop, operation. Promotion gates are defined metrics over a defined shadow window (e.g., N days, precision/acceptance thresholds).
27	SOURCES: https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/machine-learning/deploy-shadow-ml-models-in-amazon-sagemaker/, https://www.qwak.com/post/shadow-deployment-vs-canary-release-of-machine-learning-models, https://imubit.com/articles/closed-loop-ai-in-manufacturing, https://christophergs.com/machine%20learning/2019/03/30/deploying-machine-learning-applications-in-shadow-mode/

This is a docs+one-topic change now; it also gives Phase 6 its natural first milestone (every model starts at L0).
29	
30	### [important] No model/data drift monitoring, no production model-performance monitoring, no retraining triggers — Prometheus is explicitly infra-only
31	GAP: §13.1 L7.1 scopes observability to 'container health, message rates, CDC lag, dead-letter counts, broker state'. Nothing anywhere monitors the MODELS in production: no feature/prediction drift detection, no performance tracking once deployed, no defined retraining trigger or cadence. This is doubly relevant because (a) the flagship use case's ground truth (yield/quality) arrives late via LIMS — the classic delayed-label problem requiring two monitoring loops (real-time proxy metrics: input/prediction drift; delayed loop: join predictions to lab results when they land in gold) — and (b) the P3 ladder's demotion and the P2 safety story both depend on knowing when a model has gone stale. The lab's structure (LIMS→CDC→gold, P8 downstream joins) already contains everything needed; the decision is simply absent. Charter §12 #10 defers ML *tooling*, but drift/performance monitoring is an architectural concern on par with the already-decided MLflow/feature-store items in §13.1.
32	EVIDENCE: design/PROJECT_CHARTER.md §13.1 L7.1 (observability scope), §13.2 (learning milestones list — no ML monitoring), §13.5, §13.7 P2–P5 (no monitoring/retraining mention); AGENTS.md build sequence Phase 6.
33	BEST PRACTICE: Production ML monitoring distinguishes data drift (input distribution shift) from concept drift (input→target relationship shift), uses proxy metrics (drift, prediction distribution) while labels are delayed and a second evaluation loop when ground truth arrives, and defines explicit retraining triggers (e.g., drift above threshold for N periods, or performance drop on label arrival). 34	SOURCES: https://www.evidentlyai.com/ml-in-production/model-monitoring, https://www.nannyml.com/blog/availability-of-ground-truth, https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/developers-practitioners/monitoring-feature-attributions-how-google-saved-one-largest-ml-services-trouble, https://www.evidentlyai.com/blog/ml-monitoring-metrics
35	RECOMMENDATION: Add one decision row (e.g., L6.6 'ML observability') to §13.1: per-model drift metrics (PSI/KS on inputs, prediction drift) computed by the serving layer and exported to the EXISTING Prometheus/Grafana; a scheduled 'label-join evaluation' job that scores past recommendations against LIMS results in gold (this is a beautiful lab lesson — it exercises Planes 1–3 to evaluate Plane 4); a stated retraining trigger policy (even 'manual retrain when drift alert fires' is fine for a lab, as long as the trigger is defined). 38	GAP: §13.5 L6.5's loop inserts a human approval step of unbounded latency between model output and controller writeback. 41	SOURCES: https://image-ppubs.uspto.gov/dirsearch-public/print/downloadPdf/11086310, https://imubit.com/articles/closed-loop-ai-in-manufacturing, https://www.evidentlyai.com/ml-in-production/model-monitoring

62	- **Models have no governance artifact — extend the metric_registry 'govern what you harmonize' pattern with model cards** — The lab governs harmonized METRICS exhaustively (owner/gatekeeper, definition, lineage — §4 metric_registry, §9 'govern what you harmonize') but the models that write setpoints back into the process have no equivalent: nothing records a model's intended use, authorized HITL level, training-data version, safety-envelope bounds, evaluation results, or known limitations. For an asset that can (at L3) drive the process, this is a bigger governance omission than an undocumented metric — and it's the natural home for several decisions other findings require recording (SHAP perturbation mode, promotion history, TTL class). → One markdown model card per registered model (template ~15 fields), stored with the model in MLflow and owned by a named gatekeeper — deliberately mirroring the metric_registry schema so Plane 4 governance is visibly the same pattern as Plane 1 governance. Required fields: intended use, max authorized HITL level, training dataset version (from the data-versioning finding), safety envelope, eval metrics, SHAP mode, known failure modes.
63	- **Training/serving skew guard beyond the store split is unstated: single feature-definition source for offline gold and online Redis** — §13.1 L6.2 / §13.5 L6.4 decide the online(Redis)/offline(gold) split, but the split alone does not prevent training/serving skew — it CREATES the opportunity for it if the Spark ETL that computes gold features and the edge Python that computes/serves online features implement the same feature (e.g., 'rolling 1-h mean reactor feed flow') twice, divergently. Nothing states that feature definitions are single-sourced, and the lab's config-over-code principle (§9) isn't extended to feature definitions. → One sentence in the charter (fits P6's template philosophy): feature definitions live once — as declarative entries (name, source metrics, window, aggregation) in the same config family as the mapping table — and both the Spark gold job and the edge/online computation are generated from or validated against them; additionally have the edge inference service log its input feature vector with each prediction (which the drift-monitoring and TTL findings need anyway).

GAP: §13.1 L7.1 scopes observability to 'container health, message rates, CDC lag, dead-letter counts, broker state'. Nothing anywhere monitors the MODELS in production: no feature/prediction drift detection, no performance tracking once deployed, no defined retraining trigger or cadence. This is doubly relevant because (a) the flagship use case's ground truth (yield/quality) arrives late via LIMS — the classic delayed-label problem requiring two monitoring loops (real-time proxy metrics: input/prediction drift; delayed loop: join predictions to lab results when they land in gold) — and (b) the P3 ladder's demotion and the P2 safety story both depend on knowing when a model has gone stale. The lab's structure (LIMS→CDC→gold, P8 downstream joins) already contains everything needed; the decision is simply absent. Charter §12 #10 defers ML *tooling*, but drift/performance monitoring is an architectural concern on par with the already-decided MLflow/feature-store items in §13.1.
EVIDENCE: design/PROJECT_CHARTER.md §13.1 L7.1 (observability scope), §13.2 (learning milestones list — no ML monitoring), §13.5, §13.7 P2–P5 (no monitoring/retraining mention); AGENTS.md build sequence Phase 6.
BEST PRACTICE: Production ML monitoring distinguishes data drift (input distribution shift) from concept drift (input→target relationship shift), uses proxy metrics (drift, prediction distribution) while labels are delayed and a second evaluation loop when ground truth arrives, and defines explicit retraining triggers (e.g., drift above threshold for N periods, or performance drop on label arrival). Evidently (OSS, exports to Prometheus/Grafana) and NannyML (delayed-ground-truth estimation) are the reference open-source implementations.
SOURCES: https://www.evidentlyai.com/ml-in-production/model-monitoring, https://www.nannyml.com/blog/availability-of-ground-truth, https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/developers-practitioners/monitoring-feature-attributions-how-google-saved-one-largest-ml-services-trouble, https://www.evidentlyai.com/blog/ml-monitoring-metrics
RECOMMENDATION: Add one decision row (e.g., L6.6 'ML observability') to §13.1: per-model drift metrics (PSI/KS on inputs, prediction drift) computed by the serving layer and exported to the EXISTING Prometheus/Grafana; a scheduled 'label-join evaluation' job that scores past recommendations against LIMS results in gold (this is a beautiful lab lesson — it exercises Planes 1–3 to evaluate Plane 4); a stated retraining trigger policy (even 'manual retrain when drift alert fires' is fine for a lab, as long as the trigger is defined). Evidently is a home-lab-sized library choice to note for Phase 6.

### [important] Recommendation staleness: no TTL/expiry or pre-write revalidation on the human-gated command path
GAP: §13.5 L6.5's loop inserts a human approval step of unbounded latency between model output and controller writeback. A setpoint recommendation computed against process state at time t can be invalid — or unsafe-adjacent — when approved 20 minutes later (process moved, mode changed, feed switched). The design has no concept of recommendation validity: no TTL, no input-state snapshot, and the P2 layers validate the VALUE (clamps/envelope), not whether the recommendation still applies to the CURRENT process state. P2's PLC-side clamp would pass a stale-but-in-bounds setpoint.
EVIDENCE: design/PROJECT_CHARTER.md §13.5 L6.5 (model → HITL console → approved command → UNS → writeback) and §13.7 P2 (all three layers are value-range checks); HANDOFF.md §3 block K.
BEST PRACTICE: Open-loop advisory / RTO / MPC-operator-support practice revalidates before implementation: steady-state detection and measurement-validity tests gate whether an optimized setpoint may be written, and advisory outputs are recomputed from current state rather than replayed. In MLOps terms, predictions carry freshness metadata and consumers reject expired ones.
SOURCES: https://image-ppubs.uspto.gov/dirsearch-public/print/downloadPdf/11086310, https://imubit.com/articles/closed-loop-ai-in-manufacturing, https://www.evidentlyai.com/ml-in-production/model-monitoring
RECOMMENDATION: Add to the recommendation Pydantic model (the serving contract that P4 already constrains): issued_at, valid_until (TTL per metric class — fast process vars get short TTLs, consistent with P1's physics classing), and a snapshot/hash of the input state it was computed from. HITL console greys out expired recommendations; the edge writeback service (P2 layer 2's natural home) re-checks live values against the snapshot bounds before writing and rejects with a 'stale — regenerate' event back into the UNS. Also note that approved commands should use Sparkplug NCMD/DCMD message types, keeping the command path spec-conformant.

### [important] SPC framing is univariate-only; TEP is the canonical MULTIVARIATE SPC benchmark and many of its faults are invisible to EWMA/CUSUM
GAP: §13.7 P5 frames detection as EWMA/CUSUM/adaptive-limit charts with ML tuning the parameters. EWMA and CUSUM are per-variable charts. TEP has 52 strongly cross-correlated variables, and it is THE literature benchmark for multivariate SPC precisely because several of its 21 faults shift the correlation structure without moving any single variable's mean far enough for a univariate chart to fire. A yield/production-leakage lesson taught only with univariate charts on this dataset will systematically miss the fault classes the dataset was designed to exercise — and will miss the industry-standard mechanic (PCA-based T²/SPE monitoring with contribution plots) that is the actual 'bare-metal SPC' for continuous chemical processes.
EVIDENCE: design/PROJECT_CHARTER.md §13.7 P5 ('EWMA / CUSUM / adaptive limits… not generic anomaly detection'); §6 (TEP: '52 variables — correlated, multivariate, 21 fault scenarios'); AGENTS.md 'SPC-first yield/quality detection' constraint.
BEST PRACTICE: Multivariate SPC on latent-variable models — Hotelling T² plus SPE/Q charts over PCA (or DPCA for autocorrelation), with contribution plots for fault diagnosis — is the established monitoring method for correlated continuous processes, validated on TEP across decades of process-monitoring literature (Bakdi & Kouadri 2018 adaptive-threshold PCA on TEP; DPCA-DR on TEP; JMP multivariate-control-chart TEP studies). Univariate EWMA/CUSUM complements, not replaces, it.
SOURCES: https://analyticalsciencejournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/cem.2978, https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0169743913000592, https://community.jmp.com/t5/Abstracts/Fault-Detection-and-Diagnosis-of-the-Tennessee-Eastman-Process/ev-p/756631
RECOMMENDATION: Extend P5 to a two-level SPC story, still fully 'SPC-first': (1) univariate EWMA/CUSUM on the handful of named yield-relevant metrics (unchanged), plus (2) PCA-based T²/SPE across the TEP unit's harmonized metric set, with contribution plots as the classical pre-SHAP diagnosis method — which pairs directly with P4 (contribution plot = the SPC-native feature attribution). scikit-learn PCA + ~50 lines of Python; no new infrastructure. This is arguably the single highest-leverage Phase 6 teaching upgrade available.

### [important] No dataset versioning: MLflow tracks models, nothing versions the training data behind them
GAP: §13.1 L6.1 decides MLflow for tracking/registry and L6.2 the feature-store split, but nothing versions the training datasets: gold Parquet is rewritten in place by Spark ETL, so a registered model cannot be traced to the exact data it was trained on, and retraining (finding above) is unreproducible. This contradicts the lab's own 'deterministic, reproducible transforms' principle (§9) at the ML layer. §13.6 acknowledges Unity Catalog later 'fills the lab's lake-catalog/governance gap', but that is the graduate-to phase — Phase 6's hand-built medallion trains models first, and the reproducibility concept is exactly what the hand-built phase exists to teach.
EVIDENCE: design/PROJECT_CHARTER.md §13.1 L6.1/L6.2 and §13.6 (Databricks/Delta deferred); §9 'Deterministic, reproducible transforms'; §12 #10. No DVC/lakeFS/snapshot convention anywhere.
BEST PRACTICE: Data versioning is a core MLOps reproducibility requirement: DVC (Git-anchored), lakeFS (object-store branching), or Delta time travel, with the dataset version logged as an MLflow run parameter so every registered model points at an immutable training snapshot.
SOURCES: https://lakefs.io/blog/scalable-ml-data-version-control-and-reproducibility/, https://www.databricks.com/blog/2019/02/04/introducing-delta-time-travel-for-large-scale-data-lakes.html, https://celso.ch/blog/data-science/how-we-implement-data-versioning-with-dvc-for-reproducibility/
RECOMMENDATION: Lab-sized, zero new services: adopt an immutable-snapshot convention — training extracts are written once to a versioned path (gold/training/{dataset}/{run_date_or_hash}/) and never overwritten; log path + content hash + row count as MLflow run params/tags. Note DVC as an optional learning milestone, and let Delta time travel be the §13.6 graduate-to version of the same concept (which makes the Databricks milestone teach MORE, since the hand-built pain will be fresh).

## MINOR FINDINGS
- **SHAP-on-every-recommendation needs cost/validity caveats: interventional-vs-conditional under correlated features, attribution ≠ causation, and non-tree models** — §13.7 P4 makes SHAP a hard requirement on every alert/recommendation, edge and cloud, and the console renders 'top factor: reactor feed-temp +4 °C (SHAP 0.47)' as the operator's WHY. Three unstated caveats: (1) TEP features are strongly correlated, and interventional TreeSHAP evaluates the model at out-of-distribution feature combinations under correlation, producing potentially misleading attributions; conditional/path-dependent SHAP instead spreads credit across correlated features — either choice changes the 'top factor' shown to the operator and must be a conscious, documented pick. (2) SHAP explains the MODEL, not the PROCESS: rendering an attribution as an actionable cause ('feed temp is why yield dropped') implies causality the method does not provide — a trust hazard when the operator acts on it. (3) The blanket requirement is only cheap for tree models (TreeSHAP is exact and millisecond-fast); if Phase 6 lands on EWMA-parameter models or NN forecasters, KernelSHAP is orders of magnitude slower and won't run per-message at the edge. → Keep P4 but add three sentences: (a) constrain L2/L3 recommendation models to classes with fast exact attribution (tree ensembles → TreeSHAP; linear/SPC-native → coefficients/contribution plots), with slower explainers allowed only in cloud/batch; (b) record the feature_perturbation choice (interventional vs tree_path_dependent) as a deliberate decision in the model card, noting the correlated-features effect; (c) phrase console text as model attribution, not cause ('model weighted feed-temp most'), and pair it with the SPC contribution plot from the multivariate-SPC finding for a process-side view.
- **Golden-batch reference needs restating for a continuous process: operating-envelope/golden-run per mode, not batch profile** — §13.7 P9 defines the reference as 'best-performing historical run per asset/SKU'. TEP is a CONTINUOUS process: there is no batch trajectory to align against (the golden-batch method's time-stamped phase profile is an ISA-88 batch concept). The correct continuous analog — which the doc gestures at with 'golden-run' but never defines — is a golden operating window: steady-state statistics (means/ranges/correlation structure) from the best-performing period, per operating MODE (TEP has multiple documented modes), against which live drift is measured. 'Per SKU' also doesn't map cleanly; 'per product grade/operating mode' does. Left as-is, Phase 6 could burn time trying to time-align a profile that doesn't exist. → One-paragraph edit to P9: define the reference as a 'golden operating window' per (asset, operating mode/product grade) — steady-state summary statistics + the PCA model fitted on the golden period (which then IS the T²/SPE baseline from the multivariate-SPC finding, unifying P5 and P9 into one artifact). Batch-style golden profiles can still be demonstrated on the IIoT machine dataset's run cycles if a batch flavor is wanted.
- **Alerting node + ML alerts + HITL console with no alarm-management concept (ISA-18.2): fatigue and trust-calibration unaddressed** — The lab builds a real-time alerting node (§13.1 L2.1), SPC alarms (P5), and L1/L2 ML notifications into one operator console — three independent alert producers — with no alarm-management layer: no prioritization/rationalization concept, no flood/suppression handling, no alarm-rate KPI, and no measure of operator trust (recommendation acceptance rate). In real deployments this is a primary failure mode: ML advisory systems die of recommendation fatigue and miscalibrated trust, and the CPG discovery pattern the charter adopted ('governance that preserves operator control') implicitly depends on it. §13.7 Tier-3 excludes connected-worker APPS, not alarm management on the alerting the lab does build. → Lab-sized: (1) add priority + suppression/deadband fields to the alert/recommendation Pydantic models and a one-page 'alarm philosophy' note (which alert classes exist, who they're for, what priority means) — this is metric_registry-style governance applied to alerts, extending the lab's own gatekeeper pattern; (2) two Grafana panels: alerts-per-hour by priority (the ISA-18.2 KPI) and recommendation acceptance rate (the trust metric — which also feeds the L2→L3 promotion gate from the shadow-stage finding).
- **Models have no governance artifact — extend the metric_registry 'govern what you harmonize' pattern with model cards** — The lab governs harmonized METRICS exhaustively (owner/gatekeeper, definition, lineage — §4 metric_registry, §9 'govern what you harmonize') but the models that write setpoints back into the process have no equivalent: nothing records a model's intended use, authorized HITL level, training-data version, safety-envelope bounds, evaluation results, or known limitations. For an asset that can (at L3) drive the process, this is a bigger governance omission than an undocumented metric — and it's the natural home for several decisions other findings require recording (SHAP perturbation mode, promotion history, TTL class). → One markdown model card per registered model (template ~15 fields), stored with the model in MLflow and owned by a named gatekeeper — deliberately mirroring the metric_registry schema so Plane 4 governance is visibly the same pattern as Plane 1 governance. Required fields: intended use, max authorized HITL level, training dataset version (from the data-versioning finding), safety envelope, eval metrics, SHAP mode, known failure modes.
- **Training/serving skew guard beyond the store split is unstated: single feature-definition source for offline gold and online Redis** — §13.1 L6.2 / §13.5 L6.4 decide the online(Redis)/offline(gold) split, but the split alone does not prevent training/serving skew — it CREATES the opportunity for it if the Spark ETL that computes gold features and the edge Python that computes/serves online features implement the same feature (e.g., 'rolling 1-h mean reactor feed flow') twice, divergently. Nothing states that feature definitions are single-sourced, and the lab's config-over-code principle (§9) isn't extended to feature definitions. → One sentence in the charter (fits P6's template philosophy): feature definitions live once — as declarative entries (name, source metrics, window, aggregation) in the same config family as the mapping table — and both the Spark gold job and the edge/online computation are generated from or validated against them; additionally have the edge inference service log its input feature vector with each prediction (which the drift-monitoring and TTL findings need anyway).

# plan-docs-quality

## STRENGTHS
- Decision-ledger discipline matches Architecture Decision Record (ADR) best practice (Nygard/adr.github.io): charter sections 12-13 record every decision with a date, rationale, alternatives, and strike-through supersession (e.g. #2 broker, #3 historian, 13.6 Iggy kept out with reasons). Most home labs have nothing like this; it is the single strongest documentation asset in the repo.
- OT/IT zoning (charter 13.8 Z1-Z4) is genuinely standards-grounded: Purdue/ISA-95 levels, IEC 62443 zone-and-conduit thinking, iDMZ at Level 3.5 with exactly three enumerated crossings, MES/LIMS/CMMS correctly placed at Level 3 (a mistake most references make), and the explicit data-domain vs network-zone axis separation. This matches ISA/IEC-62443-3-3 and Cisco CPwE iDMZ guidance (https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/products/collateral/security/isaiec-62443-3-3-wp.html).
- Sparkplug B is treated as a real contract, not JSON-over-MQTT — births, aliases, RBE, lifecycle — and the design correctly avoids the naive spBv1.0/# broker-bridge pitfall (stateful LWT/STATE breaks across tiers) via the Python site-forwarder. Sparkplug 3.0 is now an international standard, ISO/IEC 20237:2023 (https://www.iso.org/standard/86204.html), so anchoring the lab on it is validated industry practice.
- A testability thesis already exists in principle: 'cross-source equivalence' (charter section 9) as the proof of harmonization, ISHE behavior as a test oracle (section 7), and 'tests as executable understanding' (AGENTS.md). The raw material for phase acceptance criteria is all there — it just is not yet bound to phases (see finding).
- Closed-loop safety design (13.5/13.7 P2-P4) follows the independent-protection-layers concept: model never actuates, PLC-side clamps independent of the model, a safety check off the model write path, graded HITL, mandatory explainability. This is conceptually aligned with IEC 61511/ISA-84 layer-of-protection thinking, scaled correctly for a lab.
- Session/program hygiene exceeds typical solo-project practice: mandatory HANDOFF.md updates per session, branch-per-change PR discipline with documented failure post-mortems (the PR #7 dropped-commits lesson), and 'charter governs' precedence rules.
- Anonymization discipline holds under verification: the client-named reference file (design/SAMPLE_*.html) is correctly gitignored (gitignore line 175) and untracked; no client names appear in any tracked doc.
- The CDC plan (5a.1 Python poll emitting Debezium-shaped events -> 5a.2 one-table Debezium sandbox -> 5a.3 swap one source, all normalized through a canonical ChangeEvent adapter seam) is a textbook incremental swap-seam/strangler migration — a model for how the other learning milestones should be phased.

## MAJOR FINDINGS

### [important] Authoritative charter contradicts itself on Geismar's PLC realism (decision L1.1 not propagated)
GAP: Charter section 13.1 L1.1 (and section 4 L1/2 row, section 8 Phase 4) decides Geismar runs a REAL OPC-UA server (asyncua). But the charter's own section 6 site table still says Geismar 'Python-modeled', section 12 decision #4 still says 'ONE site runs a real OpenPLC' and #6 lists only 'Beaumont (AB, real OpenPLC)'. The same stale one-real-site framing survives in AGENTS.md's 'Architecture: data flow' ASCII block ('ONE site (Beaumont) real OpenPLC'), DOMAIN.md's era table ('the one real OpenPLC site') and cast-of-divergence table (Geismar 'Python-modeled'), README.md's data-strategy paragraph, and HANDOFF.md's closing build-sequence recap ('4 multi-site + central EMQX + OpenPLC site'). A new agent reading the charter's site table — the natural lookup point — would build Geismar Python-modeled and skip the OPC-UA learning milestone.
EVIDENCE: design/PROJECT_CHARTER.md section 6 site table (Geismar row), section 12 items #4 and #6 — vs sections 4, 8, 13.1 L1.1; AGENTS.md 'Architecture: data flow' block; design/DOMAIN.md 'How it grew' table (Beaumont row) and 'Cast of divergence' table (PLC-in-lab row); README.md 'Data strategy'; HANDOFF.md section 3 final build-sequence paragraph.
BEST PRACTICE: ADR/decision-record practice: when a decision is superseded or amended, every place that states the old decision is updated or marked superseded, so the record has one truth (Nygard ADR status discipline; 'charter governs' is the project's own stated rule in AGENTS.md 'Charter governs... mirror changes into README/AGENTS so they don't drift').

aiTitle: Review IT/OT integration best practices and documentation

content.text:
The review is done. I read every project document end-to-end, then ran an 8-lens multi-agent review (UNS/Sparkplug specialist, IEC 62443/Purdue security, ISA-95/ISA-88 modeling, streaming/data engineering, historian/OT operations, tool-by-tool fact-checking, industrial ML/closed-loop safety, and plan/documentation integrity), each grounded in current web research with cited standards and vendor sources. A verification pass adversarially checked the biggest findings (a rate-limit blip killed some verifier agents mid-run; I re-checked those claims against my own knowledge of the specs — the load-bearing ones below all hold).

**TLDR: The architecture-level design is genuinely strong — several decisions match or exceed documented industry best practice. But there are real gaps, and they cluster in an uncomfortable place: the Sparkplug B contract itself, the exact layer the lab exists to teach. There's also one conceptually *wrong* safety claim, a stale-decision drift problem inside the charter, and a set of "decide before the affected phase" items that aren't in any decision ledger.**

---

## What already matches or exceeds best practice (confirmed against industry sources)

- **Forwarder-not-bridge** (charter §4): rejecting a raw `spBv1.0/#` broker bridge because Sparkplug state (LWT death certificates, STATE) breaks across tiers is exactly right, and matches documented field failures. Most real deployments get this wrong.
- **EMQX-in-the-iDMZ zoning** (§13.8): broker-as-DMZ-conduit is a documented HiveMQ/Siemens pattern; MES/LIMS/CMMS at ISA-95 Level 3 (not IT) and the data-domain-vs-network-zone axis separation are both things real programs routinely get wrong.
- **"UNS carries OT real-time only; business joins downstream"** (P8), scan-rate-by-physics + deadband cascade check (P1), SPC-first detection (P5), graded HITL with model-never-actuates (P2/P3, L6.5) — all align with published guidance.
- **The decision-ledger discipline itself** (§12/§13) is ADR best practice most home labs never have, and the CDC crawl-walk-run plan (5a.1→5a.3) is a textbook swap-seam migration.

---

## Critical gaps — resolve before Diagram 1 locks / before Phase 0–2

**1. The Sparkplug topic namespace contradicts your ISA-95 UNS root — unresolved.** The charter declares topic root `lagos-chem/beaumont/...` *and* "Sparkplug B throughout." These are mutually incompatible as written: Sparkplug **fixes** topics to `spBv1.0/{group_id}/{msg_type}/{edge_node_id}/[{device_id}]` — a topic starting `lagos-chem/` cannot exist on the wire in a pure Sparkplug system. Real UNS practitioners resolve this explicitly (HiveMQ documents the "Parris method" — encode the ISA-95 path in `group_id` with delimiters — vs. republishing decoded Sparkplug onto plain-MQTT ISA-95 semantic topics at the enterprise tier). Recommended for this lab: pure Sparkplug at the site tier; the forwarder/central tier *also* republishes decoded values onto retained plain-MQTT ISA-95 topics on EMQX. That teaches both schools and makes `lagos-chem/beaumont/...` real instead of aspirational. Related: the charter's "MQTT-retained / UNS retained state" language (L2.2, §12 #12, role-B ODS) assumes retained state that pure Sparkplug **forbids** (operational messages are never retained; state comes from BIRTHs) — the republish decision is also what makes that language true.

**2. Continuous process vs. batch-shaped MES — the ISA-88/ISA-106 tension is never acknowledged.** TEP is a *continuous* process, yet the MES schema is `batch`/`batch_step`, the flagship Plane-3 query is batch genealogy, and P9 is "golden-batch." No doc defines what a "batch" physically is in a continuous plant. Industry answer: continuous plants use **time-based lot/campaign definitions** (ISA-106 territory), genealogy is a time-window join of lot ↔ telemetry ↔ consumed material lots, and the golden reference becomes a **golden operating window per mode/grade**, not a batch profile. Rename `mes.batch` → `mes.production_lot` with explicit start/end timestamps, and note ISA-88 as consciously out. Decide now — it's a schema-naming decision today and a Phase 5a/5b redesign later. Related gap: there are **no `material_definition`/`material_lot` tables** anywhere, yet genealogy is definitionally consumed-lot→produced-lot; without them the Plane 3 demo degrades to event correlation.

**3. The "GuardLogix analog" safety claim is conceptually wrong.** P2's "independent safety-check service (GuardLogix analog)" conflates a BPCS-level software guard with a **SIL-3 certified Safety Instrumented System**. Under IEC 61511, an SIS is a separate certified layer, functionally independent of the BPCS — a Python service on shared broker fabric is not an analog of it in any sense. All three of your layers are BPCS-level guards (which is fine!). Since you explicitly want the *concepts* right: reword layer 3, add a half-page LOPA/protection-layer note stating a real plant would have a certified SIS below all of this and the lab deliberately doesn't model one. Optional great teaching artifact: a hard-trip in Beaumont's OpenPLC ladder logic, labeled "uncertified SIS stand-in."

**4. No replay-clock design, and TEP's cadence breaks your own scan-rate policy.** The Rieth TEP datasets sample every **3 minutes**; P1 mandates ~1 s for fast process vars and requires the rate to "hold across every link." Replaying 3-minute data at 1 s gives 180 identical reads (RBE suppresses everything — the P1 lesson goes vacuous) or interpolated fake dynamics (which SPC then "detects"). Also undecided: wall-clock vs. simulated clock, timestamp rebasing, accelerated backfill vs. live mode. This is the Phase 1 foundation. Decide: one orchestrator-owned simulated clock with rebasing + speed factor; either re-class TEP variables into slower scan classes (honest, cheapest) and let the IIoT dataset carry the 1 s class, or run an open TEP simulator (tep2py etc.) at a finer step.

**5. The iDMZ conduit model doesn't survive your own Phase 5–6 components.** The load-bearing rule — *no IT-side system initiates connections into OT; all cross-boundary traffic terminates in the iDMZ* (NIST SP 800-82r3) — is never stated, and four already-decided components violate "exactly three crossings": Debezium must connect INTO OT-zone Postgres (run Kafka Connect as a dual-homed iDMZ container); MLflow model deployment to edge has no conduit (edge should poll outbound from an iDMZ staging point); the online Redis has no zone placement (put it per-site OT-side); Prometheus scrapes by *pulling* into OT (per-zone Prometheus federated, or an iDMZ pushgateway). Also: the consolidated TimescaleDB instance **straddles the zone boundary** — §13.8 Z4 puts the historian OT-side, but Neo4j/Spark/lakehouse (IT-side) read `ods_core` in the same instance. Split `ods_core`+`erp_shadow` to an IT-side Postgres (you already call the split "part of the upgrade-friendly story"), or declare the instance an iDMZ-resident replicated store. Add a conduit inventory table (source zone, dest zone, **initiator**, protocol, Docker network, phase) to §13.8 before Diagram 1 locks — these will otherwise propagate into Diagrams 2–3.

---

## Important gaps — decide/document before the affected phase

**Sparkplug mechanics (Phase 2–4)** — the deepest cluster, and also the best lessons in the lab:
- **Forwarder session design**: to be spec-correct on EMQX the forwarder must be a compliant Edge Node — own NBIRTH/NDEATH with bdSeq, own seq numbering (0–255), own alias space (aliases are session-scoped; raw pass-through of site NDATA is invalid), and must implement NCMD Rebirth. Naive relay ⇒ rebirth-request loops from any compliant consumer.
- **Primary Host designation**: STATE is cited but nobody is assigned as Primary Host per tier — yet it's the standard trigger for your decided store-and-forward. Suggestion: forwarder = site-tier primary host; historian/Kafka-ingest = central primary host.
- **Store-and-forward semantics**: buffer duration (= the historian-less site's max history-loss budget), oldest-first eviction, and replay flagged `is_historical` with original timestamps so alerting/`current_state` skip backfill. `is_historical` appears nowhere in the docs; it's the spec's mechanism for exactly this.
- **Commands are NCMD/DCMD, not a "setpoint topic"**: L6.5's mental model needs rewording — the DCMD must be issued on the *site* broker where the target Edge Node lives (console → EMQX → forwarder-as-site-host → DCMD → PLC write → DDATA read-back = the confirmation *and* the audit record).
- **Sparkplug Templates (UDTs)**: P6 stops at Pydantic; Sparkplug natively has Template definitions in NBIRTH which Ignition auto-materializes as UDTs — put the P6 lesson on the wire for at least one equipment class.

**Time & data integrity (Phases 1–6):**
- **No end-to-end time/delivery semantics**: `ts_historian.telemetry` needs `UNIQUE (ts, metric_id)` + `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` (hard to retrofit on a hypertable — decide before Phase 3); state the principle "at-least-once transport + idempotent sinks everywhere"; Spark milestone should explicitly include watermarks + dedup.
- **No quality-code model**: the `quality` column is undefined. Adopt OPC-style Good/Uncertain/Bad/Stale; map per source (OPC-UA StatusCodes at Geismar, Sparkplug quality property, Modbus = inferred-only at Beaumont — it's genuinely a **fifth divergence dimension** across your four sites); implement STALE-on-NDEATH; rule that SPC/ML consume only Good samples (a stale flatline fed to EWMA suppresses exactly the drift the flagship use case detects).
- **Time synchronization is never mentioned** — invisible on one Docker host, which is why it will go un-learned. Best teaching move: deliberately skew one site's replay clock and have the conforming step detect/correct it.
- **Raw-counts→EU scaling is missing from the divergence roster**: real AB `N7:20` holds raw integer counts (4–20 mA scaled), not engineering floats. Make Beaumont publish raw counts and add `raw_min/raw_max/eu_min/eu_max` columns — this must land **before Phase 0 freezes the mapping-table schema** (the spine).
- **Historian lifecycle unnamed**: compression policy (delay > longest outage drill), retention, continuous aggregates for dashboards, and a per-metric `interpolation_type` (step|linear) column for gap-filling RBE data.

**Contracts & governance (Phases 4–6):**
- **No Kafka wire-contract decision**: Pydantic protects Python↔Python only. Add Apicurio schema registry + Avro as part of the 5a.2 Debezium milestone (one container — same learn-by-building pattern as Redis/MLflow). Also undecided: UNS→Kafka topic/key design (few topics, asset-path as record key for per-asset ordering) and **where Sparkplug protobuf gets decoded** (recommend one Python UNS→Kafka bridge that holds BIRTH state — also fixes the EMQX licensing issue below).
- **Broker auth + per-client topic ACLs are absent** — your governance thesis ("forwarder controls what leaves the site") is currently enforced by nothing. Mosquitto `acl_file` + EMQX authz (Beaumont's credential may publish only its namespace) is pure config and *is itself the governance lesson*. Add TLS on the one WAN-representing conduit (forwarder→EMQX, port 8883); keep intra-site plaintext as a recorded conscious choice.
- **"Auditable command path" has no audit**: add `ods_core.command_audit` (recommendation, model version, SHAP summary, proposed vs. approved, approver, safety-layer verdicts, per-hop timestamps) and ACL-restrict command topics to the console identity. For a simulated chemicals plant this is the signature compliance artifact.
- **Bronze must stay immutable raw**: P7's wording lets validation divert records *before* Bronze; industry practice validates on Bronze→Silver promotion so rejects remain reprocessable. And **dead_letter has no redrive path** — specify the schema (full payload, error category, retry count, status) + a small redrive script; the unknown-tag → gatekeeper-fix → redrive loop is your best governance demo.
- **ISA-18.2 alarm model**: the alerting node is bare thresholds; add the alarm state machine (Normal→Unack→Ack→RTN), priority, shelving, chattering guard, and EEMUA-191 alarm-rate KPIs — TEP's 21 faults will produce genuine alarm floods, which is the lesson.

**Plane 4 (Phase 6):**
- **Add "L0 — Shadow" to the HITL ladder** with explicit promotion/demotion gates (industry norm before anything user-facing; the ladder currently starts at Alert).
- **No model/data drift monitoring or retraining triggers** — Prometheus is scoped infra-only. Your LIMS→CDC→gold path is the textbook *delayed-label* structure; a scheduled "join predictions to lab results" evaluation job exercises Planes 1–3 to evaluate Plane 4.
- **Recommendation staleness**: a setpoint approved 20 minutes later can be invalid — add `issued_at`/`valid_until`/input-state snapshot to the recommendation contract; edge writeback re-validates before writing.
- **SPC framing is univariate-only** — TEP is *the* multivariate-SPC benchmark; several of its 21 faults shift correlation structure without moving any single mean, invisible to EWMA/CUSUM. Add PCA-based T²/SPE with contribution plots (~50 lines of scikit-learn; contribution plots are the SPC-native cousin of P4's SHAP). Probably the single highest-leverage Phase 6 teaching upgrade.
- **Nothing versions training data** (contradicts your own §9 determinism principle at the ML layer): immutable snapshot paths + hash logged as MLflow params; Delta time travel becomes the §13.6 graduate-to version of the same concept. Also consider model cards mirroring the `metric_registry` gatekeeper pattern — Plane 4 governance as visibly the same pattern as Plane 1.

**Tool reality checks (all web-verified):**
- **EMQX**: the charter's justification ("EMQX OSS… rule engine, native data bridges, clustering") is factually wrong in every free version — Apache-2.0 5.x never had Kafka/Postgres bridges (Enterprise-only), and since May 2025 EMQX is **BSL 1.1, all features unified, free for a single node only** (clustering requires a license). Fix: pin "EMQX ≥5.9, single node, BSL," drop "clustering" from the lab justification, and the custom Python Kafka bridge (above) makes the native bridge optional anyway. HANDOFF's "1 EMQX cluster" label needs the same fix.
- **PySparkplug is self-declared Pre-Alpha** with undocumented Sparkplug 3.0 conformance — too load-bearing to treat as decided. Downgrade to "candidate, verify in Phase 2"; per your raw-mechanism principle, hand-roll the protobuf payload with paho-mqtt first anyway.
- **UMH pivoted**: your UMH notes describe UMH *Classic* (k8s bundle); the current product is **UMH Core** (single container, benthos-umh + embedded Redpanda — and no bundled Timescale/Grafana historian). Re-validate before drawing Diagram 2, or it depicts a legacy product. (Good news: benthos-umh has a stateful Sparkplug B input.)
- Confirmed fine: floci is real and covers your L4 services free (note a fallback: LocalStack Community gates Glue/Athena behind Pro — DuckDB covers that surface); TimescaleDB features you need (compression, continuous aggregates) are Community/TSL edition, vendor renamed TigerData 2025; Redis 8 is genuinely open source again (AGPLv3); Neo4j Community has the vector index; ERPNext-on-MariaDB is correct (Postgres unsupported); OpenPLC/asyncua/Databricks Free/keep-Kafka-over-Iggy all check out.

---

## Plan & documentation integrity

- **The charter contradicts itself on Geismar**: §13.1 L1.1 makes it a real OPC-UA site, but §6's site table, §12 #4/#6, AGENTS.md's ASCII flow, DOMAIN.md's tables, and README all still say "one real site / Geismar Python-modeled." A new agent reading the natural lookup point builds the wrong thing. One doc-sweep PR fixes all of it.
- **The four `*_notes.md` files present decided questions as open** (InfluxDB-vs-Timescale, "EMQX *or* Mosquitto") with no superseded banner, yet §11/README list them as current docs. Add 3-line "archived vision note — superseded by charter §4/§12/§13" banners. (Three of them also end with committed shell garbage: `DOCEOF && ls -l output/...`.)
- **Phase 4 is a big-bang of ~8 workstreams** while the thesis proof needs only three. Split 4a (2 Python-modeled sites → forwarders → EMQX → cross-source equivalence test green = the harmonization proof), 4b (swap in OpenPLC + OPC-UA sites), 4c (store-and-forward, Docker segmentation, historian-less site). You already did exactly this for Phase 5.
- **No per-phase exit criteria.** The raw material exists (§9 cross-source equivalence, ISHE test oracle) but is bound to no phase. Add an "Exit criteria" column — e.g., Phase 4a: "same physical event through all sites yields identical canonical output; pytest equivalence suite passes; unmapped tag → dead_letter, not silence."
- **No risk register, and the Phase-6 stack won't fit casually on one machine**: 4×Mosquitto + EMQX + Kafka + Debezium + Timescale + Postgres + Spark + Neo4j + ERPNext (4–8 GB alone) + Ignition + MLflow + Redis + floci + Prometheus ≈ 16–24 GB+ of containers. Mitigation is cheap: docker-compose profiles per phase so only the active slice runs, plus a documented host-RAM assumption.
- **Sequencing inversion**: Diagrams 2–3 gate Phase 0 but depict phases that are months-to-years away and inform nothing in Phase 0 (a pyproject skeleton + YAML mapping table). Meanwhile design has been complete since June 21 with zero code. Keep the Diagram 1 walkthrough (it's a legitimate learning artifact — and now has a substantial gap list to process), but timebox it, start Phase 0 right after Diagram 1 locks, and draw Diagrams 2–3 just-in-time (2 before the UMH re-platform, 3 before floci work).

---

**The pattern across everything:** your architecture decisions (what talks to what, which zone, which store) are consistently right; what's missing is the **protocol- and semantics-level contracts** one layer down — exactly the bare-metal layer you built this lab to learn, which makes almost every gap above a *lesson to schedule* rather than a flaw to patch. Nearly all of them are half-page charter decisions or single mapping-table columns if made now, and phase-blocking redesigns if discovered mid-build. The two hard "before Phase 0 freezes the spine" items are the Sparkplug/ISA-95 namespace encoding and the mapping-table schema additions (raw/EU scaling, quality mapping, interpolation type, source cadence).

The full findings (~40 majors + minors, each with doc citations, standard references, and source URLs) are parsed per-lens at `/private/tmp/claude-501/.../tasks/parsed/*.md`. If you'd like, next step I can: (a) fold this into the repo as a review doc + charter follow-up items on a branch/PR per your git convention, (b) do the quick doc-integrity sweep PR (Geismar drift, banners, DOCEOF lines), and/or (c) merge the gap list into the Diagram 1 walkthrough agenda in HANDOFF §3 so each block's "gap check" step already knows what to look for.

The latest version supports PostgreSQL 17 and 18. However, there are important version compatibility notes:

Based on the web search results, here's what I found regarding Neo4j's 2025 calendar versioning, community edition, and vector index features:

## Calendar Versioning

From January 2025 Neo4j Server adopted calendar versioning (CalVer). The Calendar versioning (CalVer) format, YYYY.MM.PATCH, is based on the year and month of the release, for example, 2025.01, 2025.02, and so on. The patch number is incremented for each release within the same month.

## Community Edition Support

Support or fixes are not guaranteed for the Community Edition. This contrasts with Enterprise Edition, which has dedicated support policies.

## Vector Index Support

Introduced VECTOR as a new type supported by Cypher, Block store format, and v6 drivers. Additionally, configuration settings specified in the OPTIONS map (which can, for example, be used when creating a vector index) are tied to a Neo4j version rather than a Cypher version, meaning updates to these settings will be supported in both Cypher 5 and Cypher 25.

## Latest Release Information

The search results reference various 2025 releases but don't specify a single "latest" release date. For the most current version information, you may want to check the official Neo4j downloads page or the Neo4j release notes archive directly.

# Domain Narrative — Lagos Specialty Chemicals

> A narrative backstory for the simulated enterprise. It exists to make the harmonization problem
> **concrete and memorable**: every technical quirk in the lab (why Beaumont speaks Allen-Bradley,
> why Geismar is metric, why Corpus Christi uses compound tags) traces to a business event here.
> This is fiction in service of learning — only **Level 0** is synthetic; see
> [`PROJECT_CHARTER.md`](PROJECT_CHARTER.md), which governs.

---

## The company

**Lagos Specialty Chemicals (LSC)** is a mid-cap specialty-chemicals manufacturer headquartered in
**Lagos, Nigeria**. It began in the 1990s blending industrial solvents and coatings additives for the
West African market, then grew — first organically, then aggressively **by acquisition** — into a
multinational producer of specialty intermediates and polymer additives.

Its plants run a continuous **reaction → separation → stripping** process (reactants in, two liquid
products + byproduct out — the Tennessee Eastman process archetype), supported by the usual rotating
equipment: feed pumps, recycle compressors, agitator motors, transfer pumps.

LSC's problem is the problem of every roll-up: **each plant was built or acquired at a different time,
by different engineers, on a different control platform, in a different unit system, with different tag
conventions.** Headquarters now wants enterprise-wide analytics, predictive maintenance, and an AI
copilot — but the operational data is fragmented across four incompatible dialects. That gap is the
entire reason this lab exists.

UNS root: **`lagos-chem`** · ISA-95 enterprise level: **Lagos Specialty Chemicals**.

---

## How it grew — and why the data is a mess

| Era | Event | Site | Control heritage | Why it looks the way it does |
|-----|-------|------|------------------|------------------------------|
| 1990s | Founding + first West African operations | *(HQ, not a lab site)* | — | Solvents/coatings origins; the corporate data culture |
| ~2005 | First US Gulf Coast plant (oldest asset) | **Beaumont, TX** | **Allen-Bradley** PLCs | Legacy **brownfield**; cryptic AB register tags (`N7:20`, `FIC101_PV`); imperial units; terse status codes. In the lab this is the **one real OpenPLC** site (Modbus TCP) — the genuine "memory address → meaning" lesson. |
| ~2012 | Acquired a competitor's plant, originally built by a European licensor/EPC | **Geismar, LA** | **Siemens** S7 | Despite being on the US coast, it was engineered to European standards: Siemens addressing (`DB10.DBD4`, `MW100`) and **metric** units (m³/h, kPa, °C). Verbose status strings. |
| ~2018 | Greenfield European expansion | **Rotterdam, NL** | Modern **Ignition / MQTT** stack | Newest, cleanest build: verbose semi-semantic nested names, metric units, its own status vocabulary. Looks "almost harmonized" already — but on its *own* terms. |
| ~2022 | Acquired a midstream/feedstock terminal to secure raw-material supply (backward integration) | **Corpus Christi, TX** | **CygNet** (oil-&-gas heritage) | Different industry entirely. Compound flat tags that **encode the hierarchy in the name** (`CC_NORTH_U12_FIC101`); mixed units. The "we bought an O&G asset and inherited its SCADA" story. |

The result: the **same physical reading** — say, a reactor feed-flow — exists under four unrelated
names, in two unit systems, with four status vocabularies, across four SCADA lineages. A human
engineer can squint and reconcile them; a machine cannot. Harmonization is the act of making the
machine able to.

The mess runs deeper than the four lineages. Within a single site, **tag modeling also varies by the
system integrator** LSC contracted for each project — so even one plant is internally inconsistent.
Today, getting analytics-ready data means engineers **pulling historian extracts by hand — sometimes
days of work** — and each site quietly treats its real-time data as **its own**, not an enterprise
asset. Meanwhile corporate IT is mid-flight on an **SAP ECC → S/4 migration**, so the business-record
layer is itself a moving target. HQ's response is not just "one namespace" but **one namespace that is
governed and reusable**: every harmonized metric gets an owner, a definition, and lineage — a data
product the whole enterprise can trust — while sites keep local autonomy (the *global-and-local* ask).

---

## The cast of divergence (what the lab must reconcile)

| Dimension | Beaumont | Geismar | Rotterdam | Corpus Christi |
|-----------|----------|---------|-----------|----------------|
| SCADA lineage | Allen-Bradley | Siemens | Ignition-style | CygNet |
| Tag style | AB register (`N7:20`) | Siemens address (`DB10.DBD4`) | verbose semantic | compound hierarchy-encoding |
| Units | imperial | metric | metric | mixed |
| Status codes | terse | verbose | own vocabulary | O&G-style |
| PLC in lab | **real OpenPLC** | Python-modeled | Python-modeled | Python-modeled |

This single roster deliberately spans **every harmonization dimension at once** — naming style, unit
system, status vocabulary, addressing scheme, and real-vs-modeled control — so the lab proves the
hard cases, not the easy one.

---

## The mission (what LSC is trying to achieve = the lab's four planes)

1. **Harmonize** the four dialects into **one Unified Namespace** (Sparkplug B / MQTT) — "same reality,
   one name" — and **govern** it as a reusable data product (owners, definitions, lineage).
2. **Record** curated operational events into enterprise systems (ERPNext) and reconcile them with the
   plant's transactional systems (MES/LIMS/CMMS/quality).
3. **Contextualize** everything into a **knowledge graph** (Neo4j) — assets, tags, events, batches,
   work orders, lab results, engineering topology — enabling cross-domain reasoning and a GraphRAG
   copilot.
4. **Apply** the foundation — traditional ML (flagship: **yield improvement / production-leakage**,
   delivered as human-in-the-loop, edge-executed recommendations) and a GenAI copilot.

Get there and LSC unlocks enterprise analytics, predictive maintenance, yield gains, and trustworthy
AI. That's the payoff the lab is built to demonstrate end to end.

West African market, then grew — first organically, then aggressively **by acquisition** — into a
multinational producer of specialty intermediates and polymer additives.

Its plants run a continuous **reaction → separation → stripping** process (reactants in, two liquid
products + byproduct out — the Tennessee Eastman process archetype), supported by the usual rotating
equipment: feed pumps, recycle compressors, agitator motors, transfer pumps.

LSC's problem is the problem of every roll-up: **each plant was built or acquired at a different time,
by different engineers, on a different control platform, in a different unit system, with different tag
conventions.** Headquarters now wants enterprise-wide analytics, predictive maintenance, and an AI
copilot — but the operational data is fragmented across four incompatible dialects. That gap is the
entire reason this lab exists.

UNS root: **`lagos-chem`** · ISA-95 enterprise level: **Lagos Specialty Chemicals**.

---

## How it grew — and why the data is a mess

| Era | Event | Site | Control heritage | Why it looks the way it does |
|-----|-------|------|------------------|------------------------------|
| 1990s | Founding + first West African operations | *(HQ, not a lab site)* | — | Solvents/coatings origins; the corporate data culture |
| ~2005 | First US Gulf Coast plant (oldest asset) | **Beaumont, TX** | **Allen-Bradley** PLCs | Legacy **brownfield**; cryptic AB register tags (`N7:20`, `FIC101_PV`); imperial units; terse status codes. In the lab this is one of **two real-protocol sites** — a real **OpenPLC** runtime (Modbus TCP) — the genuine "memory address → meaning" lesson. |
| ~2012 | Acquired a competitor's plant, originally built by a European licensor/EPC | **Geismar, LA** | **Siemens** S7 | Despite being on the US coast, it was engineered to European standards: Siemens addressing (`DB10.DBD4`, `MW100`) and **metric** units (m³/h, kPa, °C). Verbose status strings. In the lab: the **second real-protocol site** — a real **OPC-UA server** (`asyncua`), per charter §13 L1.1. |
| ~2018 | Greenfield European expansion | **Rotterdam, NL** | Modern **Ignition / MQTT** stack | Newest, cleanest build: verbose semi-semantic nested names, metric units, its own status vocabulary. Looks "almost harmonized" already — but on its *own* terms. |
| ~2022 | Acquired a midstream/feedstock terminal to secure raw-material supply (backward integration) | **Corpus Christi, TX** | **CygNet** (oil-&-gas heritage) | Different industry entirely. Compound flat tags that **encode the hierarchy in the name** (`CC_NORTH_U12_FIC101`); mixed units. The "we bought an O&G asset and inherited its SCADA" story. |

The result: the **same physical reading** — say, a reactor feed-flow — exists under four unrelated
names, in two unit systems, with four status vocabularies, across four SCADA lineages. A human
engineer can squint and reconcile them; a machine cannot. Harmonization is the act of making the
machine able to.

The mess runs deeper than the four lineages. Within a single site, **tag modeling also varies by the
system integrator** LSC contracted for each project — so even one plant is internally inconsistent.
Today, getting analytics-ready data means engineers **pulling historian extracts by hand — sometimes
days of work** — and each site quietly treats its real-time data as **its own**, not an enterprise
asset. Meanwhile corporate IT is mid-flight on an **SAP ECC → S/4 migration**, so the business-record
layer is itself a moving target. HQ's response is not just "one namespace" but **one namespace that is
governed and reusable**: every harmonized metric gets an owner, a definition, and lineage — a data
product the whole enterprise can trust — while sites keep local autonomy (the *global-and-local* ask).

---

## The cast of divergence (what the lab must reconcile)

| Dimension | Beaumont | Geismar | Rotterdam | Corpus Christi |
|-----------|----------|---------|-----------|----------------|
| SCADA lineage | Allen-Bradley | Siemens | Ignition-style | CygNet |
| Tag style | AB register (`N7:20`) | Siemens address (`DB10.DBD4`) | verbose semantic | compound hierarchy-encoding |
| Units | imperial | metric | metric | mixed |
| Status codes | terse | verbose | own vocabulary | O&G-style |
| PLC in lab | **real OpenPLC** | Python-modeled | Python-modeled | Python-modeled |

This single roster deliberately spans **every harmonization dimension at once** — naming style, unit
system, status vocabulary, addressing scheme, and real-vs-modeled control — so the lab proves the
hard cases, not the easy one.

---

## The mission (what LSC is trying to achieve = the lab's four planes)

1. **Harmonize** the four dialects into **one Unified Namespace** (Sparkplug B / MQTT) — "same reality,
   one name" — and **govern** it as a reusable data product (owners, definitions, lineage).
2. **Record** curated operational events into enterprise systems (ERPNext) and reconcile them with the
   plant's transactional systems (MES/LIMS/CMMS/quality).
3. **Contextualize** everything into a **knowledge graph** (Neo4j) — assets, tags, events, batches,
   work orders, lab results, engineering topology — enabling cross-domain reasoning and a GraphRAG
   copilot.
4. **Apply** the foundation — traditional ML (flagship: **yield improvement / production-leakage**,
   delivered as human-in-the-loop, edge-executed recommendations) and a GenAI copilot.

Get there and LSC unlocks enterprise analytics, predictive maintenance, yield gains, and trustworthy
AI. That's the payoff the lab is built to demonstrate end to end.

# Industrial Data Harmonization & Contextualization Home Lab

A home lab that **simulates a multi-site process / specialty-chemicals manufacturer** in which
similar operational realities are represented differently across sites — then **harmonizes** those
disparate OT representations into a common enterprise language through a Sparkplug B / MQTT
**Unified Namespace (UNS)**, and **contextualizes** the result into a knowledge graph meaningful to
OT, IT, analytics, ML, ERP, and graph-based reasoning systems.

This is a **learning environment and architecture prototype** — built to understand every layer of
a modern industrial data stack at the bare-metal level *before* adopting enterprise software that
abstracts those layers away.

> **Authoritative project definition:** [`design/PROJECT_CHARTER.md`](design/PROJECT_CHARTER.md).
> This README is a summary; the charter governs.
> **Continuing the work / new agent?** Start with [`HANDOFF.md`](HANDOFF.md) for current status and next steps.

## The problem being simulated

Different sites, lines, and machines represent the *same underlying reality* differently — local
PLC naming, controller memory structures, brownfield integrations, divergent tag taxonomies, and
even different integrators per project (so tags diverge *within* a site too). What should be
enterprise-comparable data arrives as site-specific, cryptic, inconsistent signals — and the cost is
operational: analytics data can take **days to assemble by hand**, real-time data stays **fragmented
and "owned" by sites**, and ML can't scale across the enterprise. The lab deliberately manufactures
this mess (same reality, different names per site), then proves it can be conformed to one namespace,
**governed as a reusable data product**, and enriched into connected context. The problem mirrors
real process/CPG transformation discovery (anonymized industry pains); see charter §2.

## The three planes

Sources span the classic **IT / OT / ET** divide: OT (SCADA/PLC tags), IT (on-prem
business-transactional data in PostgreSQL — MES/LIMS/CMMS/quality), and ET (engineering topology).

| Plane | What it does | Key tech |
|-------|--------------|----------|
| **1 — Harmonize** (OT) | synthetic Level 0 → PLC-world disguise → Sparkplug B → UNS; unit/status/timestamp normalization + per-field lineage | OpenPLC + **OPC-UA**, two-tier MQTT (**Mosquitto** edge + **EMQX** central, Python forwarder w/ store-and-forward), Sparkplug B, Ignition, **TimescaleDB**, Grafana |
| **2 — Record** (Enterprise) | curated operational events → SAP-like business records | ERPNext |
| **3 — Contextualize** (Knowledge) | UNS + IT transactional + ERP + asset topology → **identity reconciliation** → knowledge graph → reasoning | Neo4j (ISO 15926 / DEXPI-aligned ontology), GraphRAG |
| **4 — Apply** (Intelligence) | consumes Planes 1–3 — **Track A** traditional ML (predictive maintenance, anomaly, forecasting; **flagship: yield improvement / production-leakage, human-in-the-loop & edge-executed**; scored back to UNS) · **Track B** LLM/GenAI (retrieval, copilot via GraphRAG) | ML stack + LLM/GraphRAG *(tooling deferred to Phases 6–7)* |

relational/transactional (OLTP) → **PostgreSQL** (transactional source-of-record + derived ODS, the

> messaging, historian, analytics, ERP, knowledge graph, cloud — behaves like a real OT/IT stack
> assembled from open-source or free/community software.

- **Tennessee Eastman Process** — continuous chemical-process units (reactors, columns, loops)
- **Industrial IoT Dataset (Synthetic)** — rotating machines (pumps, compressors, motors)

The enterprise is **Lagos Specialty Chemicals** (UNS root `lagos-chem`), operating **4 sites** —
**Beaumont** (Allen-Bradley, real OpenPLC), **Geismar** (Siemens), **Rotterdam** (Ignition-style),
**Corpus Christi** (CygNet) — each running the same units/machines but on a different SCADA lineage
with deliberately divergent naming. Physical meaning is *assigned* at the mapping stage, anchored by

metric` — which is the spine of the lab. The table doubles as a **governed data-product catalog**
(each metric has an owner/"gatekeeper", definition, and lineage), so harmonized signals are reusable
without re-interpretation.

Postgres, with their own business keys deliberately *not* aligned to OT identities — extending the
"same reality, different representation" principle to transactional data and creating the
identity-reconciliation problem at the heart of Plane 3.

## Implementation approach

The three architecture notes are **phases of one architecture**, not competing projects:

- **Build & learn → hand-built + Python-centric.** Wire every component explicitly so each boundary
  is visible; Python is a first-class UNS participant, not just glue.
- **Abstraction (later) → UMH-anchored.** Replace the hand-wired backbone with United Manufacturing

# Industrial Data Harmonization & Contextualization Home Lab

A home lab that **simulates a multi-site process / specialty-chemicals manufacturer** in which
similar operational realities are represented differently across sites — then **harmonizes** those
disparate OT representations into a common enterprise language through a Sparkplug B / MQTT
**Unified Namespace (UNS)**, and **contextualizes** the result into a knowledge graph meaningful to
OT, IT, analytics, ML, ERP, and graph-based reasoning systems.

This is a **learning environment and architecture prototype** — built to understand every layer of
a modern industrial data stack at the bare-metal level *before* adopting enterprise software that
abstracts those layers away.

> **Authoritative project definition:** [`design/PROJECT_CHARTER.md`](design/PROJECT_CHARTER.md).
> This README is a summary; the charter governs.
> **Continuing the work / new agent?** Start with [`HANDOFF.md`](HANDOFF.md) for current status and next steps.

## The problem being simulated

Different sites, lines, and machines represent the *same underlying reality* differently — local
PLC naming, controller memory structures, brownfield integrations, divergent tag taxonomies, and
even different integrators per project (so tags diverge *within* a site too). What should be
enterprise-comparable data arrives as site-specific, cryptic, inconsistent signals — and the cost is
operational: analytics data can take **days to assemble by hand**, real-time data stays **fragmented
and "owned" by sites**, and ML can't scale across the enterprise. The lab deliberately manufactures
this mess (same reality, different names per site), then proves it can be conformed to one namespace,
**governed as a reusable data product**, and enriched into connected context. The problem mirrors
real process/CPG transformation discovery (anonymized industry pains); see charter §2.

## The three planes

Sources span the classic **IT / OT / ET** divide: OT (SCADA/PLC tags), IT (on-prem
business-transactional data in PostgreSQL — MES/LIMS/CMMS/quality), and ET (engineering topology).

| Plane | What it does | Key tech |
|-------|--------------|----------|
| **1 — Harmonize** (OT) | synthetic Level 0 → PLC-world disguise → Sparkplug B → UNS; unit/status/timestamp normalization + per-field lineage | OpenPLC + **OPC-UA**, two-tier MQTT (**Mosquitto** edge + **EMQX** central, Python forwarder w/ store-and-forward), Sparkplug B, Ignition, **TimescaleDB**, Grafana |
| **2 — Record** (Enterprise) | curated operational events → SAP-like business records | ERPNext |
| **3 — Contextualize** (Knowledge) | UNS + IT transactional + ERP + asset topology → **identity reconciliation** → knowledge graph → reasoning | Neo4j (ISO 15926 / DEXPI-aligned ontology), GraphRAG |
| **4 — Apply** (Intelligence) | consumes Planes 1–3 — **Track A** traditional ML (predictive maintenance, anomaly, forecasting; **flagship: yield improvement / production-leakage, human-in-the-loop & edge-executed**; scored back to UNS) · **Track B** LLM/GenAI (retrieval, copilot via GraphRAG) | ML stack + LLM/GraphRAG *(tooling deferred to Phases 6–7)* |

**Storage by concern (no overlap):** time-series → **TimescaleDB** historian;
relational/transactional (OLTP) → **PostgreSQL** (transactional source-of-record + derived ODS, the
ODS co-located in the Timescale instance); analytical (OLAP) → **medallion lakehouse** (Bronze/Silver/
Gold via **Spark ETL**) + **DuckDB** over Parquet; relationships → Neo4j; enterprise records → ERPNext.
Pipeline/infra observability via **Prometheus + Grafana**.

## Guiding principle

> Only **Level 0 (the physical world)** is synthetic. Everything above — PLC-facing structures,
> messaging, historian, analytics, ERP, knowledge graph, cloud — behaves like a real OT/IT stack
> assembled from open-source or free/community software.

## Data strategy

The domain is **data-driven, not dictated**, so realistic data is always available:

- **Tennessee Eastman Process** — continuous chemical-process units (reactors, columns, loops)
- **Industrial IoT Dataset (Synthetic)** — rotating machines (pumps, compressors, motors)

The enterprise is **Lagos Specialty Chemicals** (UNS root `lagos-chem`), operating **4 sites** —
**Beaumont** (Allen-Bradley, real OpenPLC/Modbus), **Geismar** (Siemens, real OPC-UA via `asyncua`),
**Rotterdam** (Ignition-style), **Corpus Christi** (CygNet) — each running the same units/machines but on a different SCADA lineage
with deliberately divergent naming. Physical meaning is *assigned* at the mapping stage, anchored by
the **three-stage name mapping table** — `friendly variable → site-specific PLC tag → Sparkplug
metric` — which is the spine of the lab. The table doubles as a **governed data-product catalog**
(each metric has an owner/"gatekeeper", definition, and lineage), so harmonized signals are reusable
without re-interpretation.

The generator also produces **synthetic relational tables** (MES/LIMS/CMMS/quality) seeded into
Postgres, with their own business keys deliberately *not* aligned to OT identities — extending the
"same reality, different representation" principle to transactional data and creating the
identity-reconciliation problem at the heart of Plane 3.

## Implementation approach

The three architecture notes are **phases of one architecture**, not competing projects:

- **Build & learn → hand-built + Python-centric.** Wire every component explicitly so each boundary
  is visible; Python is a first-class UNS participant, not just glue.
- **Abstraction (later) → UMH-anchored.** Replace the hand-wired backbone with United Manufacturing
  Hub Community once the internals are understood.

These styles are captured as **three full architecture diagrams** — hand-built/Python-centric ·
UMH-anchored · cloud-native (floci→AWS) — in the Eraser `scada_harmonization` workspace. The design
was benchmarked layer-by-layer against a real industrial-products target architecture (charter §13).

Every component is upgrade-friendly (OSS broker → enterprise; Ignition Maker → licensed; floci →
real AWS) without invalidating the design.

# Learning Log — Industrial Data Harmonization Home Lab

Durable concepts, gotchas, and glossary entries captured as the lab is designed and built.
Per the build cadence (AGENTS.md → "How we work"), when a component's teaching scaffolding is
pruned, the durable learning lands **here** so nothing is lost.

**How to use:** add entries as concepts appear (walkthroughs, build sessions, debugging).
One `##` section per component/theme; glossary at the bottom, alphabetized, plain-language.

---

## Concepts (per component)

*(seeded empty — filled during the Diagram 1 walkthrough and each build phase)*

## Gotchas

- **Eraser MCP:** the AI edit path (`update_diagram`) tends to reverse connection arrow
  directions — use `manually_update_diagram` (verbatim DSL) when direction matters.

---

## Glossary

- **CDC (change data capture)** — capturing inserts/updates/deletes from a database as an event
  stream; *log-based* CDC (Debezium reading the Postgres WAL) catches deletes and ordering that
  *poll-based* CDC misses.
- **Historian** — the OT time-series database of record for telemetry (here: TimescaleDB
  hypertables); stores value + timestamp + quality per sample.
- **Hypertable** — TimescaleDB's abstraction that auto-partitions a Postgres table by time into
  chunks, enabling compression, retention, and continuous aggregates.
- **iDMZ (industrial DMZ, "Level 3.5")** — the buffer zone between OT (Purdue Levels 0–3) and
  IT/enterprise (Levels 4–5); all cross-boundary traffic terminates there, and no IT-side system
  initiates connections into OT.
- **ISA-95** — the enterprise–control-system integration standard; source of the
  equipment hierarchy (enterprise → site → area → production unit → equipment) and the Level 0–4
  functional model.
- **NBIRTH / DBIRTH / NDATA / DDATA / NDEATH** — Sparkplug B message types: node/device birth
  certificates (declare all metrics + aliases), node/device data (changes only, by exception), and
  node death (via MQTT Last-Will). Consumers rebuild state from births — Sparkplug messages are
  *never* MQTT-retained.
- **OLTP / OLAP** — transactional workloads (many small concurrent writes; Postgres) vs analytical
  workloads (large read-heavy scans; DuckDB/lakehouse). One engine per concern.
- **Purdue model** — the classic OT network reference architecture (Levels 0–5) that the lab's
  OT / iDMZ / IT zoning follows (charter §13.8).
- **RBE (report by exception)** — publishing only when a value changes beyond a deadband, instead
  of on every scan; saves bandwidth but makes the historian store irregular, change-only samples
  (queries must gap-fill).
- **Sparkplug B** — an MQTT topic + protobuf payload specification (ISO/IEC 20237:2023) adding
  birth/death lifecycle, metric aliases, datatypes, and command semantics (NCMD/DCMD) on top of
  plain MQTT.
- **UNS (Unified Namespace)** — the single, hierarchically-organized, semantically-named event
  namespace through which all OT/IT systems publish and consume current plant state.
- **WAL (write-ahead log)** — Postgres's durability log; logical decoding of the WAL is what
  Debezium reads for CDC (a replication slot pins WAL until the connector consumes it).
